CoNKLIN, Past Grand Master, was ca1led to the chair and reed the
Annual Address of that officer to the Grand Lodge, as follows :..:..
BBBTHRRN 01' THK GRAND LoDGR 01' CALIFORNIA:-

Another year has rolled into eternity. The M. •. W. ·• Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of California has again assembled for its Forty.fourth Annual '
Communication, for the transaction of businesa, and especially for the consideration of the reports of its officers in respect to business transacted since the last
Annual Communication. As your Grand Master, I beg to submit my report.
During my incumbency it has been my misfortune to be out of health, and,
therefore, I have been unable to make the visits among the brethren that my in·
clination and duty dictated; however, when opportunity afforded, I have endeavored to give such counsel as would encourage iood work and promote harmony
and brotherly love. Further than this I have left the matter to the Grand
Lectnrer, feeling assured it was in excellent hands, as his report will verify.
It is now my pleaeant duty to report that the Craft is in a prosperous condition,
and that peace and harmony reign throughout the jurisdiction. There have been
five dispeusatiobs granted for the formation of _new Lodges in the jurisdiction
during the year, and about 200 brethren added to the membership,Jncreasing the
roll this year that number in comparison with last year.
On the twenty-seventh day of December, 1892, at the request of Ha1111Liian
Lodge, No. 21, at Honolulu, Hawaiian Islands, I deputed Bro. W. F. ALLEN, a
Past Master of eaid Lodge, to convene the Grand Lodge and proceed to lay the
corner-atone of the new Masonic Temple to be erected at that place, and in pur·

8

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 10,

suance of my direction Bro. ALLEN performed that duty in an imposing manner.
I am informed that everything passed off pleasantly, and that the ceremony was
witnessed by a vast concoursfl of people. The Hon. PAUL NEUMANN, the orator of
the day, was introduced by Bro. ALLEN, and delivered an eloquent oration.
On the sixteenth day of November, 1892, at the request of the Board of Trade at
San Jose, the Grand Lodge was convened for the purpose of laying the cornerstone of the new national Postoffice building about to be erected at that place. A
number of the Grand Officers were present. The duty was performed by the
Grand Lodge, assisted by the brethren of Santa Clara county. The Grand Orator
delivered the oration. San Jose Commandery of Knights Templar acted as escort.
On December 5th, 1892, and April 21st, 1893, I authorized the payment of assessments Nos. 2 and 3, of i1,000 each, to the "Masonic Temple ABBociation," as
per report and resolution of your Finance Committee at the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge in 1891, by which a subscription of $10,000 for the erec tion of a new Masonic Temple in this city was directed. I hesitated about authorizing these payments because much objection bad come to my knowledge as to
location, etc., the site selected being so far from the business center, and the
probability of a very long time elapsing before any revenue could be realized upon
the investment. I therefore met with the Board of Directors, and it was then
agreed there ~hould be no further aSBessments levied until the Communication of
the Grand Lodge this year, when a stockholdera' meeting should be called, a report submitted, and the Grand Lodge with themselves should decide whether they
should continue to levy and collect the assessments and proceed with the erection
of the new Masonic Temple, or the Association should go into liquidation, and
divide the proceeds among the stockholders. In pursuance of this agreement
they have called a stockholders' meeting, to be held Tuesday, October 10th, 1893,
at 8 o'clock P. M., in this building, and my desire is that the member3 may interest
themselves in this matter and as many as possible attend this meeting, (and
especially the officers and past officers of the Grand Lodge,) to give us the benefit
of their ad vice.
The Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home is progressing, and a suitable. and
very satisfactory site, comprising some 270 acres of land, of easy acceSB to San
.Francisco, the metropolis of the Pacific Coa11t, has been selected upon which to
erect the same. I refpr you to the report of the Trustees, which will be given
you at this Communication of the Grand Lodga, for details, and ha\'e nothing
but commenrlation for every act of the Board. The architect has furnished plans
in detail of a building to cost about $60,000, which has been adopted by the
Board. · Bro. WILLIAM F. PERRY, Secretary of the Board of Trustees, informed
me they had subscriptions amounting to about $60,000, and &88ured bequest.a
of R&Y about $2.'>,000, making in all thus far about '85,000. The institution
commends itself to the }'raternity, and is worthy the consideration of any brother
who is disposed to assist it by his influence or purse. On Wednesday, September
27th last, I authorized the Grand Secretary to draw a warrant in their favor upon
the Grand Treasurer for $10,000, the amount subscribed by this Grand Lodge,
as provided in report and resolution of your Finance Committee adopted a~ the
last Communication of the Grand Lodge.
Immediately after the close of the Communication of the Grand Lodge last
October, I reappointed Bros. ALBERT HANSON, NATHANIEL GREENE CURTIS and
GUSTAVUS LANGFORD SPEAR, as Trustees of the Masonic Widows' and Orphans'
Home, for three years, vice themselves-terms expired, and on the tenth day of

as I presume, been inclosed to the Grand Lecturer, as, with one or two exceptions'
they have not been sent to me. This seems to me correct, as the Grand Lectute;
is the custodian of the work which is given by him to the Inspectors, and through
them is, or should be, tr~nsmitted to the ~odges: . The Grand Lecturer Ahould go
at least once a year to mspect the work, impart mformation, and correct errors.
For this service the Grand Lodge should pay his actual expenses in addition to his
annnal salary. This 11ervice requires a good man, one accurate in the work . and
teapected by the Fraternity, and he should be a permanent officer. Thus, as sugj!88ted by Grand Master ESTEE in hie address in 1889, the work will be unifcrrm.
Such a man, I think, we possess in our pri;sent Grand Lecturer. The reports of
the Inspector3 to him enable him to make his report in detail.

I am indirectly informed that a circular letter, emanating from a Lodge, baa
been circulated throughout the jurisdlctioo, referring to a resolotioo to be otfered
at this Communication, advocatidk the setting apart of a small percentage of the
revenue of a Lodge for social purposes, feasts, etc., and evidently with the hope,
by this me11ns, to ioflaeoce legtslatioo in the Grand Lodge.
Now, io my opinion, the revenu~ of a Lodge is a sacred trust, for two purposesfirst, the actual expenses for running s11me; aod secondly, for charity among
the brethren and their families, to relieve distress, feed the huogry, clothe the
oaked, aod bury the dea.d. This we understood when we were received into the
iostitotlon, and it is virtually a ooutraot, aod we have no right, as a Lodge or as
lodividuals, to break this contract or pervert this trust into any other channel.
The Graod Lodge has decided this question absolutely several times, and why will
thA brethren still Insist?
Could not tbe members of the Lodg611, iu some way, form within themselves a
social club, ooosisteot with the Lodge teacbiogs, baviog their own fees and dues,
independent entirely from the Lodge, for these social purposes, making the fees aod
dues light, and bearing their own expenses. Yoo say, If we do this, all will not join,

By direction of Atlanta Lodge, No. 59, Atlanta, Ga., the body of Bro. A. 0.
LADD, a member of that Lodge, was, under the supervision of the Board, em·
balmed and shipped to his old home in Atlanta, Ga.
In regard to the matter of the charge of $73.50 against Mt. Olivet Lodge,
No. S, of Parkersburg, West Virginia, we would further report, that under cover
of May ~~th we received tbrongh the Grand Secretary or California a report from
Mt. Olivet Lodge, No. 3, in relation to the matter, from which it appears that tbe
Lodge wished this Board to wait until his estate was settled, when we might obtain
a reimbursement for the amount expended. We replied through our Grand Sec·
retary, under date of June 4th, sending them a copy of the original telegram under
which we acted, and also, after making dne inquiry, reporting that the amount of
the estate left was probably nothing. This report, under date of June 6th, 1893,
was forwarded to the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of West Virginia. No
further response has been had.

.At request of our Board, I wish to add to our annual report by calling special attention to the continued refusal of .Alcatraz Lodge, No. 244, to join our compact and
share with other Lodges in the many personal attentions uecessary for the r£:1ief of
the sick and needy and the burial of the dead. I am informed that that Lodge has
done a large amount of work during the past year and is prosperous, and we can
learn of no valid reason why they refuse. The matter has been under consideration
by them during this year, bot we learn of no action taken. In this connection we
call your attention to the comments of your committee on this matter as contained
in the proceedings, as follows: 1885, p. 218; 1886, p. 661; 1887, p. 187; 1888, p. 685;
and 1889, p. 215. Mere suggestions as to performance of duty seem, however, to
meet with but a deaf ear in this case.
Fraternally and respectfully,
FRBD L. BUTTON, Secretary.

The Boe.rd of Trustees of the Me.sonic Widows' and Orphans' Home herewith
submits the Beoood Annual Report of its transactions for the current year.
Regular meetings of the Board have been held throughout the year. A special
mee.tiog was held on the fourth day of May, for the purpose of a tteodiog the fooeral
services and burie.l of the lamented Brother Gsooos EDWIN WRITNBY, one of the
Truetees alld Vice-President of this Board.
The work of the preceding year, after our organization was completed, was
largely devoted to the viewing and loves.igatioo of sites, and to securing subscrip·
tloos to the funds of the Home. The result of these labors was a sobscriptioo list
amounting to 844, 759,50. Doring the present year we have added $12,883.00 to the
amount previoDBly subscribed.
The members of the Board have directed their attention me.ioly1to the investigation of the availability and desirability of the many sites olfered. A number of them
were olfered e.s donations, and were of sufficient acreage and value to merit serions
consideration; while, on the other hand, the sites oifered during the present year
were only to be obtained at their market value. Io our le.st Annual Report, in refer·
ring to the selection of a site, we ueed the following Iangoage, viz.:
" Wishing to ave.ii itself of the best advantages attainable, the Board still bolds
Its decision lo abeyance, with the assurance that in its floe.I action it will be ioflueooed solely by a desire to promote the best interests of the loatitution-eveo should
the resolt be a rejection of all proifered donations and the purchase of a site in the
best available locality."
.
With this purpose lo view, the Board convened at Masonic Temple, lo Bao Francisco, on the ninth day of February, 1893, to render its floe.I decision in the choice
of a site, which resulted in the selection of a tract of 268 acres of land, located at
Decoto, in Alameda Coooty. The distance pf the tract from the City of Bao Francisco Is twenty-seven miles. It is located one-half mile north of the track of the
broad gauge railway leading from Oakland to Bao Jose, and has a frontage. of 4000
feet on the couoty road leading from Haywards to Niles. The front portion of the
traot, comprising approximately sixty acres, is level. It is of rich alluvie.1 soil, and
well adapted to gardening, frnit raising and general farming. Beyond this Is a series
of low hills, well adapted to grain and the cultivation of early vegetables for the
markets of Bao Francisco. The rear portion of the tract extends well up towards
the summit of the ridge, and is mainly valuable for pasturage, fruit and forest
culture. There are several flowing springs on the premises, and we are now engaged
lo tunneling Into the hillside, for the purpose of developing a more bouotifol supply
of water for the domestic purposes of the home.

Among the important considerations that led to the choice of this site was Its
nearness to the center of population and its aooeaslbillty-lt being but thirty-6ve
minutes' ride from Oakland and Sao Jose, and one and ooe·quarter boors from San
Francisco. While there were diverse opinions among the members of the Board as
to the relative advantages.of the various sites, yet we have used opr best judgment
in an honest effort to select the best location, all things considered, and now that the
property is In onr posseBSioo we feel confident that this Gran'd Lodge and the frater•
nity at large will generally approve of the choice.
The cost of the tract will amount to $33,000, being about $125 per acre, of which
$17,500 has been paid in cash, and the balance iR due on an no matured mortgage
which was on the premises at the time of pnrchase, and which will not mature until
the 30th of November, 1894,
The title was Investigated and found perfect, and the deed was dnly executed to
this Board of Trustees, recorded in the Book of Deeds in the omce of the Oounty
Recorder of Alameda, and finally deposited with the Grand Secretary of this Grand
Lodge for safe keeping.
After the purchase of a site the Executive Committee was authorized to advertise for architectural designs for the proposed administration boildlng, which, when
ooDBtructed, should cost, say $66,000. 'fhiR resulted ID the presentation of some
beautifol designs by various architects, all of which were referred to the Executive
Committee for.inspection, with Instructions to report at the regolar meeting in September. Considering the great importance of this sobject, the Executive Committee
deemed it best to give all the time possible to a final submission of plans to the
Board; and while many admirable features were discovered lo most of the plans
submitted, the palm of honor was floe.Hy given to the designs of Brother W. H.
LILLIE, a member of (}olden (}ot,e Lodge, and the attention of the Grand Lodge is
oordially Invited to an inspection of the same.

We accord With the committee in the remarks relative to unifonnity of work.
We are fully of the opinion that, even were the ritual published in full and 11 copy
thereof placed in the hands of every officer, there would still be a. lack of uniformity. There might be approximate uniformity as regards the general execution
of the work; but not even this much is possible so far as phraaeology is concerned.

Past Grand Master PALMER J, PILLANS, as heretofore, presented the Report
on Correspondence. It is an excellent one. Several pages are appropriated to
California Proceedings for 1891, and liberal quotation is made therefrom. He
. fully endorses the sentiment expressed by Grand Master CONKLIN that " too much
law complicates affairs, and in time confuses by multiplicity." Bro. ELLIS receives much praise for his able report, frequent quotation from it being made.
We entirely agree with our brother that the Committee of Investigation in a
Lodge has nothing to do with the regularity of the petition of an applicant.
He considers the appointment of Representatives to other Grand Lodges as possessed of neither "present nor prospective usefulness," in which opinion, personally, we fully concur, because our observation and experience impel us to do so.
Bro. PILLANS, WI reporters should do, writes for the btanefit of the brethren of
his jurisdiction. He uses the scissors without stint, but very judiciously. We
quite agree with him as to the important influence of these reports in harmonizing
and molding opinions in Masonry, and in building up the Fraternity in the knowlc
edge of the Craft. And yet we sometimes think that this influence is far too much
circumscribed. If Grand Lodges could devise some means by which the proceedina-s could be made accessible to the brethren generally, much greater good would
be the result.
There are in Alabama two hundred and sixty-six Lodges, and a membership of
eleven thonsand one hundred and seventy-eight.

M>. W.·.

V.·.

Y our committee heartily concurs in the remarks of the Grand Master relative
to the burden thrown upon the Western Jurisdictions in relieving the necessities
of foreign brethren sojourning in our midst, and desire to express it as our judgment that, in view of the fact that such sojourners prefer continuing their affiliation with their parent Lodge, rather than transferring their support to us, it is be~ ·
coming and just that the Lodges to whom they owe allegiance and render support
should assume all such liability incurred, and in caee of their inability so to do,
the Grand Lodge having jurisdiction over such subordinate Lodge, should act in

1893.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

59

the premises. The sojourner's condition was forcibly and aptly illustrated by the
Grand Master'~ story of the "passage of the rapids," and the Justice of the foreign
brother transferring his membership, thereby sharing our burdens, wh.ile participating in our benefits, should be apparent to all. Nor should we lose sight of the
moral taught by the brothers who "bend the knee" in time of danger only. By
it we are admonished that the wise use of the ballot is indispensable to the purity
of our membership, and the applicant, whom it is deemed likely would find most
pleasure outside rather than within the Lodge-room, should be left to the full exercise of hiB preference.
This is one of the evils which afllict our western jurisdictions-an evil which it
seems very difficult to remedy, but one which should be in some equitable manner
disposed of. California can sympathize with Arizona in this matter, for we have
had an unusual call made upon our Lodges for aid to these sojourning brethren,
without any return. It is an easy matter for jurisdictions not thus afHicted, to
harp about Masonic charity, and all that; but if these jurisdictions had a little of
our experiences therewith, we opine that they would modify their opinions.

ARKANSAS.

The fifty-third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas was
held in the city of Little Rock, commencing on the fifteenth day of November,
1892,-the M.·. w.·. c. A. BRIDEWELL, Grand Master, presiding, and theR.·. W.·.
FAY Hll:Ml'BTEAD beiog Grand Secretary. Three hundred and sixty-six Lodges
were represented.
Opening this beautiful volume, the first thing to arrest our attention is a likeness of the new Masonic Temple. If we may form a conception of this building
from this representation we would say that it is a magnificent structure-one of
which our brethren of Arkansas may well be proud-of which the city of Little
R_ock can reasonably boast. The pinnacle of its great dome, ornamented with one

60

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 11,

of the principal emblems of the Fraternity, will constantly remind the brethren of
the Great Source from whom all their blessings flow. The building is a seven-story
structure, grand in its proportions, and beautiful in its style of architecture. Well
may our Arkansas brethren sing pieans of gladness that now the great undertaking
is completed. The Grand Master, in the opening of an admirable Address, thus
welcomes his brethren to this beautiful Temple:-

lt is with feelings of exquisite pleasure that I welcome you on this auspicious
occasion. For a half century past the Grand Lodge has been somewhat like the
A~a~ of the desert-a wanderer; but to-day we m~t in our home. Here i~ 01;1r
abid1Dg place, and during all the years to come will the Craft assemble "'ithlD
these walls. When Jolll'l HOWARD PAYNB wrote the immortal song, "Home,
Sweet Home." he builded far better than he knew, for he builded in the hearts of
his fellow-men, and erected therein a monument more enduring than brass or
marble. He struck a chord responsive in the heart of eve_ry human being, and expressed in words that feeling which is uppermost to-day ID every heart here; that
joy that sparkles in the eye; that peace that settles over us. as we cr!lss ~he threshold
of home. Y1!9, brethren, we are at home; and, I say again, that it gives me great
pleasure to bid you welcome to your home.
Eight decisions were reported.• We quote the fourth, considerable general
interest attaching at the present time to the question of visiting:No visitor has a right to demand to see the charter of a Lodge previous to his
examination. If he does ask for it he should be promptly refused. The privilege
of visiting is granted by the Lodge to a brother. The Lodge is not up for examination, but the visitor. The visitor must not ask a privilege <!f this sort of the
body, the legality of which he questi<J?lS. That WC?uld be an msult to the ,bojl.y
whose courtesy he solicits. The Worshipful Master IS solemnly charged at his ID·
stallation to carefully preserve the charter, "and in no case should it ever be out
of your imm&liate control." The ante-room is not the place for the charter, and
no one has a right to demand that the Worshipful Master surrender it in order
that some stranger may examine it. The visitor, before admission, is not upon an
equality with the Lodge. He asks it. He need not ask it if he is not satisfied.
The Lodge, on the other hand, asks no privilege, but examines the applicant to see
if he is worthy to ·enjoy the privilege sought. Let the visitor take his time to
examine the charter after he has been admitted into the Lodge-room, and even

Another matter we especially commend in the action of Grand Master MAXWELL, namely: bis refusal in a number of cases to grant dispensations to confer
the degrees in less than the regular time. He maintains, and rightly, that "Masonry is souie~hing more than a degree machine." He reasons that, " as the three
symbolic degrees are the foundation of the whole Masonic structure, too much
care can not be exercised in selecting the material out of which this foundation
shall be constructed, and ample time should be taken to see that the stones composing the foundation are properly and Maeonically laid." To all of which we say
"amen." It has become far too common in these latter days to railroad candidates through the three degrees, apparently with no higher object in view than to
qualify them for the Chapter, the Commandery, the Eastern Star, etc.; thus doing
violence to the Fraternity, and little if any good to the candidate. We visited a
Lodg:e not long ago, and heard a brother importuning the Master to hurry a brother
through the Master's degree because he wished to join the Eastern Star at the
sru:ne time that sister so and so did. This is not Masonry.

proceedings." If the Secretary's minutes are evidently incorrect in either of these
respects the Master undoubtedly has the power to refuse to put a motion to affirm
them before the needed correction is made. But it does not follow from this that
the Master has the prerogative or power to declare the minutes of the Lodge to he
confirmed; that power resides in the Lodge.
(3) '.l.'he Master of a Lodge has no power to suspend the Secretary, or any
elective officer, under any circumstances. He can be su•pended only by the Lodge
through charges re)Cularly preferred against him, a nd after due trial. The Grand
Master ca-n suspend him from the exercise of the duties of his office, pending the
examination of the charges.
(4) A verbal motion to amend an amendment to the by-laws that had been
offered in writing, would be in order.
•
(5) The Master has the right to make or second a motion; but, by general
usage, when the Master desires a certain motion to come before the Lodge, he requests some member to make it from the floor.

•

In connection with No. 3 above, we remark that it has been decided by the
Gr1md Lodge of California that when a Secretary neglects his duties and fails to
account for moneys collected by him, the Master may and should suspend him
from office, and cause charges to be preferred against him. Our Grand Lodge has
even gone farther than this and say that " the officers of a Lodge undertake when
they accept office, not only to qualify themselves to perform their official duties,
but to be _d iligent in performing them; and, if one neglects to perform such duties,
it is proper that the Master suspend him from .his office, and appoint in his place
another who is not only competent, but willing t o perform the duties. Your committee would not except even the Master from this role. The Master is not excepted, for he mmt qualify himself before be caii be installed; and if, after being
installed, be neglects to perform his duties, the Grand Master may, and upon well
verified complaint should, suspend him from his office." This is stringent; but it
is, neverthelet18, the decision of our Grand Lodge. In other respects the opinions
of the Committee of Jurispruclence in the District of Columbia are, we think, good
law; and in this also they are good law, but not to the extent recognized by our
Grand Lodge.

We do not agree with Bro. SINGLETON that a Mason has the right to any Masonic home which be may choose to select. He has the right w select any Masonic
home which be may think proper within the Grand Jurisdiction under whose laws
be lives. So says our sovereign Grand Lodge in its fundamental law.
Suppose, Bro. SINGLETON, that a member of a Lodge should come to a meeting
thereof in a drunken condition, as sometimes does happen, ought the Master to
admit him? We think there are times when protection to the inberests and the
peace and harmony of the Lodge would demand positive action on the part of the
Master. We grant that the cause for such action should be a strong one, and one
about which there can be no doubt. We think there is Masonic authority for such
action by the Master; certainly there is in our jurisdiction, if the decisions of our
Grand Lodge have any significancy.
Thie suite us:It has been our custom, in these reports, to notice such decisions of Grand Mas·
tare which were of a very decided l!hara.cter, differing from the general practice of
our own local laws, that our own brethren might he profited by the comparison.
We have never quoted any such for the mere purpoee of criticism. We believe
ea.ch Grand Lodge has the right, as well as power, to adopt its own rules for the
government of the Craft, and we have never desired to force any Grand Lodge to
measure their grain with 01.1r bushel. When we have entered at all into a contention it has been to defend ourselves against unjust criticisms of those who would
have all the world of Masonry adopt their peculiar ideas as practioed in their jurisdictions.
Bro. SINGLETON believes that a visiting brother has a right to demand to see
the charter of the Lodge which be asks to visit. If a charter is -prim.a facie evid ence of the regularity of a Lodge, why is not a dimit prim.a facie evidence of the
regularity of a Mason ? We think the charter is merely proximate evidence of
regularity. We think we know of clandestine Lodges that have ~arters; and we
think that it is the duty of a prother intending to visit to determine the character
of the Lodge by proper inquiry, outside of the charter.

71

But we are led to believe, from his review of Michigan, that our brother regards a diploma, or dimit, as prim.a facie evidence of the regularity and standing
of a Mason, and that such is the general usage. We have not so regarded it; nor
do we agree with him in his expressed OP.inion that very few Americans could pa'IS
examination in any country outside of the United States. We take it that exam.
inations are not conducted on the ritual in its phraseology. While we regard a
diploma or a dimit as good evidence, we do not regard it as sufficient evidence.
Our brother is not a believer in the "perfect man " doctrine. He seems to
think that moral qualification takes precedence over physical Individually we
think ho is right.
We have been much pleased with oiir brother's opinions and with bis manner
of expressing them. His report is instructive as well as pleasing; be writes for the
information of ·his brethren, and his brethren will d o well to read what be baa
written.

The one hundred and sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of

The portrait of the Grand Master appears as a frontispiece to the proceedings. ·
Thie representation indicates him to be a man of great intelligence and power, and
the indication is doubly confirmed by the character of his long and able address.
The.address is a masterpiece in Masonic literature; we have seldom read a more
beautiful specimen of word painting. The paper occupies some twenty-five pages
of closely printed matter. In his exordium he compares Masonry and its beneficent results to the Gulf Stream, "The Wandering Summer of the Sea," and to the
benign influences exerted thereby upon the earth and its inhabitants. The follow ing excerpts will give an idea of the 1lxcellence of sentiment and of the beauty of
diction characterizing this 11>ble paper:To me, this institution of Freemasonry, in its duty and its mission, has often
seemed like the great Gulf Stream. In the ages far agone it was divinely appointed to perform such trusts as would change the coldneBB of humanity into the
warmth of fraternal conduct-to carry its tender message of universal brotherhood into every clime, and bring the distant and frigid nature into close association with those near and warm. It wa8 intended to develop in soils apparently
so barren that naught eave the thistle could flourish there, a growth of sweetest
flowers to please the eye with their beauty and the senses with their perfume. It
was intended to create in man the knowledge that without assistance from other
hands and sympathy from other hearts he needs must suffer the very coldness of
death for want of warm and loving associations.
Again, like the same Gulf Stream, Masonry everywhere abides. When the
waters of life are cold, we find it warming them with its touch. Whep the air of
life is chill, we find its breath driving off the icy influence, and when the soil is
barren, we, discover its warmth giving vigor and vitality to the heavy clods. Like

Our plan of dealing with delinquents.}B p~nounce~ much simpler tha~ t~e
Idaho plan; but the question is asked, . Is it legal?
We answer that it is.
Every Grand Lodge is in itself supreme, and has perfect right to enact any pro·
vision in its Constitution that it may deem proper to enact, except such a pro·
vision as would contravene the recognized landmarks of the Fraternity. We
know of no fundamental or other principle of Masonry that is ignored or violated
by this plan. Its simplicity, its ju,tice, and its easiness of execution commend the
plan. We believe the time will come when it will be generally adopted.
We can assure our brother that he shall have a copy of Bro. ANDEBSON'B new
edition of Masonic Manual which contains the form for installation of Grand Offi·
cers. We will·be pleased to see the Grand Lodge of Idaho, under the guidance of
Bro. S'IEVENSON as Master of Ceremonies, give it a trial. •
Under Iowa, Bro. STEVENSON thus gives hie opinion of Masonry. We are not
ready to endorse it, and·yet we have a very exalted opi~ion of our Fraternity and
its teachings:W e care not for ourself whether Masonry originated yesterday or a million
years ago· it is g<>od enough for us. Its greatest glory lie11 in its n?ble deeds, not
in its history. It io for the present aud future, not the past. It is greater than
any church, sect, creed, or society of any description, and in our. op~nion stands ·
nearer to the throne of the Great .Jehovah than any other organization on earth.
This is our faith.

Under .A.rizo.n a we notice the following, which is well said, relative to the burdens Imposed upon Lodges in our weetem juriadictions by ~ojouming brethren,

No human tribunal has ever been clothed with such sovereignty in controlling
its affairs as is vested in the Grand Lodge of a Masonic jurisdiction-a tribunal
from whose decisions there is no appeal. How important it is then that such a
body should have a Constitution and laws-a code of government-representing
those underlying principles of oar ancient Fraternity which are now recognized in
the government of Masonic Lodges throughout the world. How important, too,
that this instrument should be clear and unmistakable in its language, free from
all obscurity, subject to but one interpretation, firm in its construction, yet of that
conservative character which balances all extremes and forms a bulwark against
ignorance and against oppression. We always find that the evils incident to government a.re least where the functions and powers of that government are limited
1>y certain well defined laws. Thus our Constitution and laws limit the powers of
the Grand Lodge itself and encompass the prerogatives of the Grand Master, who
is, of himself, but a creature of the Constitution.
The Grand Master reports fraternal relations with sister Grand Lodges as
being most pleasant and harmonious in every respect, with the single exception of
a difference of opinion between the Grand Master of New York and himself relative to the Representative of the Grand Lodge 9f lndian Territory near that of
New York. It appears that the Grand Master of New York, the M.'. W.". WILLIAM SHERER, had requested that the appointment of the Representative of the
Grand Lod11e of Indian Territory near the Grand Lodge of New York should be
recalled, without stating any reason for the request. Grand Master BENNETT decli~ed to recall the appointment, and his Grand Lodge endorsed his action. We
incline to t.he opinion that the same comity should exist among Grand Lodges as
among nations in reference to Ministers at their respective courts. We trust that
good counsels may prevail in this unfortunate diversity of opinion, and that fraternal relations may be continued between these Grand Lodges.
The views of the Grand Master on tbe temperance question have no uncertain
ring. We are in favor of temperance. Masonry is a moral institution, and cannot afford to give countenance to anything that Aavors of immorality.

oring and benefiting the Craft.

Whilst highly complimenting most of the Secretarie.s of the subordinate Lodges
for the promptness and care manifested in their reports, he is compelled to ani·
madvert in somewhat stringent terms to the lack of promptness, and ·the careleeeness of others. No position in a subordinate Lodg'l has more important work,

The R.-. W. '. RoREBT W. HILL, D. D., Grand Orator, presented for publication in the proceedings a very able exposition of his views of "The M&Ronic
Ideal of Manliness." This ideal, be maintains, embraces the physical standard of
the ancient Athenians, and the men~! standard of the sophists, with the super~
added excellencies of a pure morality. Masonry, he thinks, ia not exempt from
the operation of the law which controls every society, namely, that every Aociety,
whether social, political or ceremonial, exists for the perpetuation of ideals; that
modem societies are not exempt from the dominance of ideals.• He thinks that
Masonry exists because it is the embodjment of certain standards of thought and
character, and because there exists in it an ideal which ha• attractive powers that
gives vitality to the institution, and claim to the consideration of thoughtful men;
that it existR because it has ever approached and sought to reach forward to its
ideal of excellence. He thinks, rightly, that a Mason who would command the
respect of his brethren, and who would bring no discredit upon the Fraternity,
must have strongly developed characteristics of manliness; that he must be a well
balanced man, mentally endowed as well as physically able, and so morally developed as to understand hie relations with hie fellow-men; that he must be so
spiritually quickened as to exhibit in his life the influence of a religious spirit and •
a personal conception of his obligalions to the Supreme Architect of the Universe.
He considers the physically perfect ideal of the old masters a.n impoBBibilitv; that
it is no lonj!'er an unalterable rule and landmark that perfect development of the
physical ma.n is absolutely essential to membership in the Order; that mental deVtllopment and moral excellence are essential requirements for membership.
The whole oration is prolific of suggestive thought, and worthy of close study.
on the part of his brethren-creditable alike to the author and his Grand Lodge.

In compliance with instructions of the Grand Lodge at the Communication
held in August, 1892, the Grand Master ha.d called a meeting of the several Lodges
in the Okl..boma. District. The Convention as9embled at Oklahoma City, on the
tenth day of November, 1892. There were present the Masters. and Wardens of
all the Lodites in the District. The whole number of Lodges represented was ten.
A vote being had upon the proposition to form a separate Grand Lodge, it was
unanimously carried.
The Committee on Constitution reported, recommending the adoption of' the
constitution, by-laws, cOde of trials, uniform code of by-laws for constituent
Lodges, and the regulations of the Grand Lodge of Indian Territory, with changes
in name and boundary, and date of meeting, and a few others. The recommendation of the committee was adopted, Grand Officers were elected, and the
Convention adjourned .. In the afternoon the officers of the new Grand Lodge
were duly installed, the action of the Convention was duly ratified and confirmed,
and the Grand Lodge of Oklahoma was proclaimed legally organized, made independent, and declared entitled to all the prerogatives of a leitally constituted Grand
Lodge, and to the especial consideration of all Grand Lodges in communication
with the Grand Lodge of Indian Territory. We congratulate the new Grand
Lodge on its auspicious beginning. May prosperity attend it.
The reports of the Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer show a healthful condition of Grand Lodge finances.

·

From the num\>er of custodians and .assistant Grand Lecturer9 it might reasonably be expected that Kansas would soon be perfect in ritual; but, then, we pre.
some that Kansas, like all our western jurisdictions, is afflicted with the presence
of those wiseacres who always annoy and injure our Lodges by their caviling and
their disposition to obtrude upon us the work of the particular jurisdiction from
which they hail, or rather their ignorance of the work of their jurisdict ion. We
were Grand Lecturer at one time, and the greatest trial to which 01lr patience and
good nature was subjected was the attempt on the part of sojourners and others to
impress us with how this particular part of the ritual was in Maine or Georgia or
Texas or this jurisdiction or that. If visitors and sojourners would be governed
by the rule of silence in this regard they would confer a favor. We bad a stereotyped answer for all such parties to the effect that they were in California, and
common manners dictated that they should take the ritual as they found it. There
is no use to try t o have uniformity of phraseology or execution so long as unauthorized parties have liberty to obtrude their peculiar notions of how this thing or that
ought to be. The Grand Master of Kansas is about right. Let the Grand -Lodge
put its foot down in positiveneBB, and say this is the work, adopt, learn, and use it
or hand in. your charter.

People have their periods of adversity and prosperity. The people of Louisiana
have experienced their full share of the former, and barely their modicum of the
latter. ·rhe lE:ssons of adversity, however so valuable, affect budine8.'!.> society,
public and private life. In such times no one escapes. The Masonic .!fraternity
came under its all pervading influence. Up to 1873 the Lodges prospered,. and
numbered on their rolls 7780 members. Then gathered the clouds of adversity.
Misfortunes came, heads were bowed, many went to their long homes. For fourteen years there was an annual decrease in the number of members; and in 1888
we were reduced to 3601. Hut the deep of the valley was reached.
The poet tells us:...:.
" Sweet are the uses of adversity,
Which, like the toad, u1dy and venomous,
Wears yet a precious jewel in its head."
If the people during these fourtee~ years were apparently less devotional,
omitted to gather into the Lodges, it was from no failure or lack of inherent force
in the teachings of Masonry. Its teachinll's and usefulness were 11s grand during
that period as when they first came to light up the. heart of man.
The clouds that bun~ around and overshadowed the Lodges in this jurisdiction,
in 1888 began to break and scatter. The days brightened as the cloudq rolled
away. The Lodges again began to refill; the members of the Order awakened
from their lethargy; prayers were said, and songs of rejoicing were again heard
within the sacred walls of the Lodge-rooms. And as the Fraternity began to remount the hill of prosperity, the ne?lessity for a Temple took more earnest and
practical shape. TWo years ago it was resolved the house SHOULD BE BUILT.
The spirit that formed that resolve took shape
" .And gave to airy nothing
A local habitation and a name."

late, never doubting that success would crown their labors. To-day they hnve
their reward in beholding this princely house, beautiful in form, grand in proportions, Gothic in outline, with sufficient of graceful trncery and pointed arch to give
to the whole a most pleasmg and noble appearance.

We mingle our rejoicings and congratulations with those of the Louisiana

This Grand Lodge goes further in applying Its own law of jurisdiction without

The old law of perpetual jurisdiction in cases of rejection has been very generally
modified; Bot we know of no Grand Lodge, save the Grand Lodge of California,
that bolds that an accepted candidate does not remain the work of the accepting
Lodge, until released by it, or the law of its jurisdiction.
Formerly in most, if not all, jurisdictions, there was no definite time in which an
election lapsed; &nd the jurisdiction over an elected candidate was practically perpetual. But in most jurisdictions the law has been modified by prescribing a time
within which a candidate must present himself to receive the degrees, or lose the
benefit-of his election. In Maine and very many other jurisdictions that time is one
year· in California it iR three months. Now, it is generally held that Masonic comity

This matter brings out another feature in California practice that is not general,
Every affiliated Mason in California may object to the initiation of a candidate in any

rejection by ballot. · In Texas they allow every affiliated Mason in the State to bal·

We like the Texas law, and upon the same principle the lJallfornia law is wise. It

The first paragraph in the above Is a very sweeping assertion, and one not borne

California holds tbat, when a party has been elected to receive the degrees in a

exercise. Buch a thing as the lapsing of an election is not recognized. The failure
of a party to present himself for initiation simply forfeits his fee, bot does not annal
his election.
But even if the election lapsed at the expiration of three months, the by-law
would not infringe upon any principle of Masonic comity. No party coming into
tbe jurisdiction of California from another jurisdiction could apj>IY to a Lodge in
California until he had been In the State for the period of one year.

The eighteenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Manitoba was
held in the city of Winnil'68", commencing on the fourteenth day of June, 1893,the M.-. W.'. DAVID JAMES GooGIN, ,Grand MaBter, presiding, and the .R.·. W.·.
WILLIAM G. Soon being Grand Secretary. Thirty.five Lodges were repreeented.
Six Special Communications had been held for the laying of corner-stones and
other purposes. That of July 31st, 1892, was held for the purpose of performing
the sad and solemn duty of attending the funeral of the late Grand Master, the
Bro.
M.-. w.·. JOHN W. H. WILSON. The Deputy Grand Master, the .R.-.
GoooIN, paid a graceful tribute to the memory of ·the distinguished brother.
In the opening of a brief address the Grand Master feelingly, in view of the
}088 eustained by his own Grand Lodge in the death of Grand Master WILSON, expreeeed the sympathy of the Grand Lodge with sister jurisdictions that had suf.
fered from the heavy hand of death.
The Grand Master reports but two decisions-both eminently sensible. The
first was the refusal of a request for permiBBion to confer the degrees of Masonry
upon a former 'resident of Manitoba who bad been residing for the last two years
in Montana, and was now on a visit to Manitoba. The reason given for the request was that this party might save the pittance of difference between the Montana and Manitoba entrance fees.
The second · was a refusal of a request to heal a clandestinely made Mason.
We quote the reply of the Grand Master to this request as a matter of good information to our own brethren : -

w. ..

" It is very neceasary to distinguish between the irregukr.rly made Mason and
the clandeatinel11 made Mason. The former has been made in a legally constituted
Lodge, but not in strict conformity with some of its laws. The latter baa been
made or is said to have been made in an illegally constituted body. The former
may be healed; the latter, in my judgment, cannot. He is practically a profane,
and must apply as such if he desires to become a Mason.
The Grand Master reports a steady increase in membership in the Lodges. He
kindly reminds some of the Masters of Lodges that they had either forgotten or
ignored the section of the Constitution relative to dues, in permitting members to
become delinquent.
He represents that the ritual and ceremonial work, and the methode of busineBB
are, perhaps, more satisfactory than at any former period. In this connection he
very truthfully saye that "these are useful means to great ends, but perfection in
these may indicate a soulless Pbariseeism." He pleads "for the spirit rather than
the form, for the practice rather than the profession."
The Grand Master closes his very excellent ad~esa with some ver! pointed ·in·
terrogatoriea relative to how far the brethren are striving to comply with their
Masonic professions; and adds some well-timed suggestions as to bow Masone
should act towards themselves, toward one another, and toward the great Fraternity which they profeBB to love so earnestly.
'l'he reports of the several District Deputy Grand Masters show that the
Lodgea generally are in good oondition, and that good work is going bravely on.
From the report of Grand Secretary SooTT, we learn that two Lodges had been
constituted, and that two new Lodges had been formed, vie learn, also, that the
financial condition of the Grand Lodge continues good.
Resolutions recognizing the Grand Lodges of Victoria and Oklahoma, and wel·
"coming them with the great body of Grand LOdge Jurisdictions, weN ~opted.
There is no report on Correspondence.

The Report on Correspondence was presented by Bro. E. T. SoHULTZ. It is a

among which we find California for 1891 receiving a seven-page notice of a very
complime9tary character.
·
'
Bro. SoHULTZ believes that when an applicant is averse to a1011aring, he should
be permitted to affirm. So do we. Generally accefited law recognizes this as just
an.d right, and the one term is quite as comprehelll!ive as the other.
He considers the deprivation of all rights, privileges and charities of the Fraternity as quite a severe enough penalty for non.affiliation after the period of six
months. ThiB is the rule in California, and we think it quite severe enough. Still
California. like other jurisdictions, is compelled to complain of the evil of nonaffiliation. It seeme impossible to devise anv means by which the evil can be repressed. We are of opinion that n.o ~lan ever will be adopted until the causes
which lead to it are more fully investigated and understood. Grand Lodges may
"endeavor to fix the status of non-affiliateS within their borders;" but as in all the
past these endeavors will fail, unless the root of the evil is eradicated. We are of

1893.]

Grand Lod!Je of OaHifornia.

opinion that the primary cause of so much non-affiliation is al;tributa?le to the f~ct
that, in these latter days, we are too eager to make Masons~to mduct parties
· to the Order-and too indifferent about perfecting the ashlars after we have sethem. There is too much profeuion and not enough application and exercise of Masonic principles. We don't believe that punitory measures will cure the

Bro. SCHULTZ believes that acquittal on charges preferred against a brother is
bar to a second arraignment and trial for the same offense. Our own Grand
0
~ge bas on several occasions decided that an acquittal ie no bar to a second trial
for the same offense; but, subsequently, they so far modified prior decisions ae to
say that a judgment of acquittal by the subordinate Lodge should not be dis~urbed
or reversed by the Committee on Grievances or by the Grand Lodge, except ID ~e
of gross violation of Masonic law by the trial commi&11ioners, or by the Lodge acqoittinl{. Personally we think that in Mo.sonic, as in civil juriBpnidence, no one
should be placed twice in jeopardy for the same offense.
Our brother does not believe in cheap Masonry. Neither do we; but we do not
believe in a monetary standard of qualifica.tion. We do believe that it is desirable
in the interests of Masonry to admit all-" good men and true " who come knocking
at our doors. It is equally desirable, and imperatively necessary, to prevent the
admission of all unworthy per.mos. Perfection of manhood, as humanity.is, should
be the standard of qualification for the privileges and benefits of our Institution.
In ~heee latter days we seem inclined to make filthy lucre the standard by which
to me 118ure character; certainly, the observation of every one will confirm the fact
that there are many, alas I too many, in our Lodges mainly through the influence
of the almighty dollar, and not because of any personal merit. It is equally true
that many a one who would be a tower of strength for the good of the ]fraternity
is barred the privilege of entrance. Our brother seems not to understand the conditions of California as at present existing. Tbirtv dollars with the chanited conditions of to-day is a greater sum than three times thirty were thirty years ago.
It is just because that good men feel that they cannot afford to pay $50, and tie it
up from the use of their families, and supplement it by high monthly dues, that
they do not seek entrance to our Masonic Lodges. Tbe old regulations adopted
no such exorbitant entrance fees or dues as we find at present in California; nor
do any of our sister jurisdictions• .We have yet to learn that it ever.was the in·
tention of Masonry to convert our Lodges into banking institutions; grander sentiments characterized the fathers of our Fraternity. Now-a-days it is no uncommon
thing to bear Masons boasting of the plethoric condition of their Lodge treasuries
more than they do of the lofty character of the brethren. The taxes imposed upon
the Order are an injury to it, and are preventing our ;-oung men from seeking admission to our Lodges. Many who would be an honor to the Order are driven off
into other organizations because in a pecuniary sense they feel, just as our brother
does, that they have no business to seek entrance inte the Fraternity. 'l'he unwisdom of high entrance fees is showing itself visibly in many parts of our State,
and it will show itself clearly in its effects upon_the treasuries of our Lodges. 'l'he
revenues of a Lodge for clwri.ty and incidental expenses arise not from entrance
fees but from the monthly dues; and our Lodges, and' even our Grand Lodge, are
standing in opposition to their highest financial interests in thus barring out those
who would be in all respects, and who in other institutions are, moat excellent
members. The times have chanl{ed in California, and Masonry in regard to its
monetary matters must change. "Slugs" are no longer picked up in a day, and
Grand Master CONKLIN is right. Everything in Californi2' pas p~ed beyond the

After carefully examining the Standing Orders and Regulations of the Grand
Lodge of Maryland, we are not at all surprised to find Bro. SOHULTZ agreeing so
closely with Bro. ELLIS. These Orders and Regulations are very like.our own and
the principles embodied in our Constitution.
We desire to say to the brethren of Maryland that California is not a believer
in the · doctrine of "prerogatives." We believe that the Grand M11Ster is subject
to the restrictions of our Constitution, and can he held amenable for a violation of
its provisions. Our predecessors. must have overlooked a decision made by our
Grand "Lodge, away back in its early history, to the effect that it is the sense of
the Grand Lodge that the Grand Master is but a creature of the Grand Lodge,
with no implied powers inherent or divine.
Bro. SoHULTZ objects to the deprival of the rights of the Fraternity for nonpayment of dues by a statutory regulation, when for the most heinous offenees a
brother cannot be deprived of those rights without due and regular trial. It seems
to us that deprive.I by statutory regulation is a very just and a very convenient
mode of dealing with those who are derelict in the payment of dues. It seems,
too, that it is giving a great degree of ch~ritable consideration to the brother derelict, in that it does not deem him 1tUilty of a Masonic offense. Civil law abounds
in just such provisions. The payment of dues is a consideration for the privileges
and benefits arising from membership in the Lodge; failure of consideration brings
along with it failure or suspension of privilege, And from this suspension the
brother can at any moment relieve himself. Not so the brother who has been deprived of rights by due and regular trial. No partic~lar disgrace or ignominy of
punishment attaches to the former-much to the latter. California operate1 upon
this plan, and deems it a very expedient one.
We are in accord with Bro. SoHULTZ In holding that Lodges under dispensation
do not, and should not, have all the rights and powers that belong to regularly
constituted Lodges. In this jurisdiction such Lodges, in addition to the right to
make Masons, are, under our Constitution, ent.itled to send delegates to the Grand
Lodge. In the Grand Lodge such delegates may be permitted to speak, but ·shall
have no vote. We are not prepared to admit, however, that these Lodges are
creatures of the Grand Master. They are creatures of the Constitution by action
of the Grand Master under the provisions thereof.

In introducing the R.·. W.·. CHARLES C. DAMS, Grand Master BRIGGS alluded
so appropriately to the contemplated Home, that we must copy a part of what he
says; it is as applicable in California as in MaBSachusetts :-

1 am in favor of this proposed Masonic work, and our newly-elected Senior and
Junior Wardens both authorize me to say that it has their hearty co-o~tion.
Such a charity would not only help tho~e in need, but would directly benefit the
Lodges by placing before them a worthy cause, to which they could bend their energies. There are poor, aged and afflicted Masons, destitute and helpless orphans,
in this jurisdiction. As a Fraternity teaching charity, have we done our whole
duty towards them? I reci>gnize the temporary charita.ble work done, but are
there not more permanent demands? A reform school is not the place for our
brothers' children. Their care, welfare and education are our duty, and this duty
is one which we should hasten to discharge. Let us make a beginning. It may
require time to accomplish it; but let us press on wisely and perseveringly, and a
monument of Masonic charity will be erected which will honor the brotherhood.

The following excerpt from the eloquent remarks of Bro. SOLON W. STEVENS is
llllggestive:W e hear various societies discussing the great questions of the day, and every
man has to do what he considers to be right in regard to them; but whatever be
his political creed, his religious creed, I still firmly believe that the highest type of
good citizenship is a Master Mason. Oh, that men would "catch on," (as the boys
say), to the grand ideas of living to-day ! I am not talking politics, but I want to
say sdmething about citizenship. There are a number of questions of the day
which every ~ood Mason Rhould take to heart. Is the immigration question safely
settled ? Is your public school question safely settled? It is for you, Masons, to
take these things home, and remember that the duties of the coming day, even of
the present moment, rests upon you as citizens of America; and let it be so inspiring that as the years roll by, the fact, the idea, shall pervade the land that Freemasonry is synonymous with honest and just citizenship!

position of Grand Master in Michigan is far from being a sinecure. Several pages

Forty-six decisions are reported. No. 1 is to the effect that the Grand Lecturer is. authorized to furnish keys to the work to subordinate Lodges, they paying him for the same. This we regard as an exceedingly unwise provision, harmful not alone to the jurisdiction in which such action is permitted, but entailing
harm up0n other jurisdictions.
Some of our brother correspondents will attack No. 8, which is to the effect
that a Lodge may refuse to grant a dimit to a brother of Michigan who desires to
join a Lodge in Ohio. The dimit spould be granted, but the brother receiving it
should not be permitted to join a Lodge in a Grand Jurisdiction in which he does
not reside. It appears, however, that in Michigan a Lodge is not required to
grant dimits to brothers applying therefor; the Lodge is the judge of the sufficiency or insufficiency of the .,reasons for asking a dimit. In which we do not
concur. Freely come, freely go, is a principle that should ohtain in all jurisdictions.
No. 15 is eminently sound, and is in accord with the doctrine held in our own
jurisdiction. We give it in full, because we feel that too much care cannot be
manifested in scanning the character of those who seek such privileges, and be·
cause we are oognizant of the fact that Committees of Investigation seldom discharge their duties with that degree of care which should be exercised in all
cases:I believe it perfectly proper that an opportunity be given the brethren, before
ballot is taken for the degrees, to give the Lodge such information as they may be
in poesession of r1>lative to candidates. In a great many instances, part1cularl;r
in larger Lodges, this is the only means the brothers have of knowing the candidate or his qualifications.
Of the remaining decisions many are in full accord with what baa always been
held in California as good law ; some are such as we cannot endOYse ; others are
merely local in character.
Dispensatidhs for the formation of five new Lodges had been granted.
The Grand Master very strongly urges the consolidation of Lodges wherever
,uoh action will be beneficial to the Craft, remarking that one good, strong Lodge
. is of much more value to the Craft than two or more weak Lodges. In this we
heartily concur. We have entirely too many weak, sickly. Lodges that are not
only of no vaiue to the Order, but are a very decided detriment to it. California
is not an exception in this respect.
The Grand Master " speaks by the book" when he refers to the salary of the
Grand Secretary. He baa bad an experience of over seventeen years in the position of Grand Secretary, and hence knows that $800 is not a moiety of what
ought to be paid to an officer burdened as the Grand Secretary of Michigan is
with the labors incident to so many Lodges as are in his jurisdiction. Michigan
stands twelfth in number of Lodges, and fifth in membership, among the Grand
Lodges of the United States, and yet is forty-ninth in amount per Lodge, and
lowest in amount per capita paid for the services of Grand Secretary. It must be
taken into the account that.heretofore the Grand Secretary has been Chairman
of the Committee on Correspondence, for which he rooeives-nothing I The
Grand Lodge subsequently adopted an amendment to. the Grand Lodge By-Laws
raising the salary of the Grand Secretary to $1500. It shou\d have been $3000 if
we are to estimate it by the amount of work required.

The Committee on Appeala and Grievances reported that no appeals, grievances

The Report on Correspondence was prepared and presented by Bro. IRTING
ToDD. It is a brief but well written review of the proceedings of fifty-one Grand
Lodges, California for 1891 being among the number.
Our brother, in harmony with the custom prevailing in his Grand Lodge, disapproves of the practice of printing in the proceedings the names of the individual
members of the several subordinate Lodges. Hie remarks on this subject are pertinent and worthy of careful consideration. We have often asked the question,
"What benefit results from publishing the names?" It will be seen by reference
to the last proceedings of our Grand Lodge that two hundred and fifty-seven pages,
or almost one-half of the book, are appropriated to this purpose. It may be well
to enquire as to whether the labor and the expense incident to this publishing of
the names could not be devoted to something of more profit. Speaking for ourself, we fail to see a benefit resulting at all commensurate with the outlay incident;
indeed, we have very seldom, if ever, had occasion to advert to these lists, nor
have we at any time seen any use made of them in our Lodges; and we frankly
confeBB that the 111ere fact of a name being found in these lists would be of very
little weight with us in determining the statue of one claiming it. It has long
appeared to us that much that is printed in Grand Lodge proceedings in these
latter days might better be omitted.
Under Iowa, our brother expresses himself in unmistakable terms in reference
to Grand Lodge libraries. Again we are inclined to agree with him, and we are
led to do so by the fact that our own excellent library seems to have served the
purpose more of ornament than of utility. We are not opposed to these libraries,
but we are of the opinion that they should be confined to their legitimate place
and extent. In these days of extensive free libraries and of library associations
there seems to us no occasion for adding works of miscellaneous character. The
course pnreued by some of our Grand Secretaries is calculated to emburden Masonry
in their jurisdictions with an expense that has little of benefit resulting.
We cannot agree with :Sro. TODD that a Past Master has any right to open and
preside over a Lodge in the absence of the Master and Wardens.
In the main, we are in full accord with our brother in the opinions expniseed
by him. He writes as one who knows whereof he speaks; and what he says is
said in terms that admit of no doubtful meaning. Hie review, though brief, i1
very comprehensive, and thus rendered very interesting. Hie work indicates him
to be an experienced con~enser.

uniformity as ie contemplated ·in the adoption of a National Ritual is not possible;

The Address of the Grand Master is an able paper, a record of much work, and
full of excellent Masonic sentiment.
Peace and prosperity ltad attended the Craft, and foreign relations remain harmonlons. The growth of the Lodges is represented as greater than ever before.
'In taking a rettospect of the year, the Grand Master submits to bis brethren very
many pertinent inqniries, which, bad we the space, we wonld transfer in body to
these pages as a help to the brethren of our own jurisdiction for self-examination.
The Grand Master is a firm believer in practical Freemasonry-that practical
Freemasonry which makes a man a better citizen; which prefers the Craftsman to
the profane; which leads us to protect the weak, to defend the viriooris, and reverence the holy ties of home; which will go on foot and ont of the way to render service in time of need; which will extend the hand with hearty grip; which wlll rai~e
• a fallen brother; which will not be satisfied with merely admonishing and coon·
seling, bot is willing to aid and assist; which watches over the widow and the
orphan, defending them from oppreBSlon, and warming and feeding and clothing
them, without letting the left know. what the right band doeth.
Bro. SL!UGHTBR represents that, soon after entering upon his duties, he addreBSed
a circular letter to every Lodge, requesting that more attention be given to the so·
cial featore of Freemasonry, advising that at least four special meetings during the
year should be devoted to this purpose, aud that to these meetings the· wives, sisters and danghters of the members shoold be invite.d. The reqoest had been very
generally complied with, and the Fraternity had been streugtbened by the better
acquaintance and oloser onion that had resnlted. We are much inclined to favor

Oor brother seems to be a believer in the ancient character of Masonry. So are
we; bot we are not prepared to believe that in its present form it can be traced
back quite as far as some of our brethren attempt to trace it. Masonry, in oor
opinion, like every other human institot.ion, is an evolution. We do not doubt the
ancient .character of the teachings of Masonry; llke troth, they are from everlasting
to everlasting. Bnt, as to the manner of setting oot the teachings of Masonry, we
think that changes have freqnentiy occurred, and are still taking place. Masonry

we are in accord with Bro. WAIT in his opinion to the effect that a dlmit with
proof of identity is "lawful Information," and entitles the pOtll!essnr to the privilege
of visitation without any proof, except that which establishes the fact that he Is the
rightfal holder of such dimit. The dimit expressly recommends the possesaor as a

Bro. WAIT ably maintains the doctrine that a Grand Lodge does not lose its character as a sovereign power by submitting all propositions for change in its Constitu·
tion to the subordinate Lodges. lt seems to os, however, that the Lodges being
creatures cf the Grand Ledge, and deriving their powers from the Grand Lodge,
cannot control the U-rand Lodge. The legislative powers of the Grand Lodge ex·
tend to every case of legislation not expressly delegated .by itself to the subordinate
Lodges. It is subject to no control, except that of the Ancient Landmarks of the
Order, and of the Constitution and Regulations adopted by itself in aceord with the
Ancient Landmarks.
The decision of the Grand Lodge of California is "that, if, apon the state of the
vote being declared, a member shall annoaMe to the Lodge that he has voted contrary to his intention by accident, the ballot may be retaken for correction." It
seems to as that common sense, as well as common justice, demands that correction
of that which is wrong should be made.
·
Bro. WAIT thinks that the Ledge or the Master thereof has the right to admit a
visitor unless there are good Masonic reasons shown. for denying him the privilege.
So think we. This reminds os of a case that came under oor notice in one of cor
Lodges. A colored brother was visiting a Lodge; he was sitting in the Lodge-room
prior to the opening of the Lodge, when in walked a member cf the Lodge. Beholding the colored brother, the member, turning upon the heel, walked oot,remarking in the hearing of the Master, that he would not sit in a Lodge when such a visitor was admitted. The Master very promptly, and we think very rightly, replied to
him that he had the undoubted right to sit outside. Beason shoold always be given
for objection to a visitor. The reason can be given quietly to the Master, whose prerogative it Is to decide whether the reason is well-founded or not.

The question had been raised as to the right of Chapters of the Eastern Star to
occupy Masonic Lodge-rooms. Whilst we recognize the Eastern Star as a side issue,
we have never been able to see why the conferring of these '1egrees in a Masonic

opinion that, if Masons and Masonic Lodges wogld show a little more consideration

If we comprehend the force of oar brother's language under Maine, we infer that
he is a believer in perpetual jurisdiction. It is onr opinion that there is a marked
difference between reception of a degree and a rejection on application. In the
former case the party receiving the degree remains the material of the Lodge conferring the degree, and the remaining degrees can not be conferred by any other
Lodge without the permission of the Lodge that conferred the degree; in the latter
case, npon removal from the jurisdiction of the Lodge, the Lodge has no longer any
claim npon the party. Under our jurisdiction any party rejected may subsequently
apply to any Lodge within whose territory he resides, after the expiration of the
constitutional period; but an applicant who has received a degree In a Lodge anywhere can not receive the remaining degree or degrees in any other Lodge without
consent of the Lodge that conferred the degree. In this as in tbe case of members
of Lodges it may be said that there exist the two kinds of jnrisdictlon-the personal
and the geographical. Over the rejectod applicant the Lodge holds its jurisdiction,
or rather h,olds the right to exercise jurisdiction so long as the applicant resides
within its territory; iD: the other case, It retains jurisdiction wherever the party may
be.
·
We have been greatly pleased and benefited by a perusal of this able report.
We commend it to onr brethren for the Masonic Information which it contains.
Whilst on some points we dilfer, yet, in the main we are in accord, and we are compelled to admire the fraternal spirit which our brother manifests in combatting views
not in accord with his own. Masons and Masonry are benefited by such reviews.
We regret that we cannot dwell longer with Bro. WA..IT.

transferring it to these pages:·while assembled for labor In our Annual Oommunication, we experience hours of
pleasure in the renewal and cementing of fraternal friendships, and yet through these
times of labor and pleasure there r.ome thoughts of sadness.
Each year we miss the faces and the voices of some whose labors for the Craft,
and whose social disposition, won the love of their brethren.
Our own work to·day reminds ns of the labors of those who toiled before us, and
our new acqnaiutances recall old friendships.
The true Craftsman cannot be forgetful. The trne brother always remembers.
Hence we cannot forget them whose personal presence is gone from us, and
whose voice can no longer be heard to urge to action or inspire courage and hope in
our noble Institution.
While the Grand Lodge is for living men, it is for men who are governed by living
forces, foroes set in motion often and surviving men who have been called up hil(ber.
One of the most real of living things is the name or memory which is thrilling,
Inspiring, and fnll of power.
In justice to ourselves, we cannot leave unnoticed the names added year by year
to the number of the fraternal dead, or Ignore the memories of men whose presence
was our joy, whose labors were our confidence, and whose inftuence is our in·
·spiration.
·
If propriety did not prompt it, atfection would demand that we call the roll of
those departed since our last Communication.
Not only is this a sacred tribute paid to worth and goodness, and the expression
of the heart's feeling which no body of men can atford to repress, but it is an enoonragement to the living, that their services to the Grand Lodge and their atfection
for their brethren shall not be forgotten with the moment of their removal, but shall
live on perpetual record among Masons.
While urging men to fidelity to the trusts we have reposed in them, we may be
helped by considering those who have been faithful to the end, and whoAe mention
at such times as this may be the crown of loving remembrances brethren place upon
the record of their lives, while they resolve to imitate and emulate those so justly
honored.

The following will apply in the case of our California Home:There are few human institutions so enduring as a well-endowed charity. ID
every European country there are charitable foundations still doing their beneficent
work, though their origin is lost in the obscurity of centuries, and their founders'
names come down to us mingled with the legends of the remotest past. Long after
this building shall have riaen in its beauty, performed its work, and fallen to decay,
the charity established here will, through countless ages, educate the young and
smooth the pathway of declining years. Here will be the moet enduring monument,
not only to the work and teachings of Freemasonry at the close or the nineteenth
century, bnt also to the noble and generous men who are making this work poesible.
Here the prattle of children and the thanks of the aged will bless the names of those
who now are showing the teachings of Freemasonry in our fair State, in a way that
will compel the admiration and the emulation of our sister States.

Grand Orator O. H. TB.A.VBBB delivered an address whicldsa credit to himself and
an honor to the young Grand Lodge. If space permitted we woold transfer it
bodily to these pages. We cllll a few thoughts therefrom, because they snit us, and
onght to snit all:It has been said that we attach too much importance to the age of Masonry.
With me, age goes but for little. It neither adds to nor detracts from intrinsic merit.
'.rhe Son is no more essential to the preservation of animal and vegetable lire, and
has no greater power to-day than on the morning of its creation, nor have the thousand cycles of time already passed added one whit to its brilliancy or usefulness; but
I have a great deal more confidence in it than if I knew it was made but yesterday
or last year. I know it will rise again to-morrow. Time bas proved its worth and
stability; and whatever time approves may be aooep$ed as worthy of the highest

155

trnst Age, while It may not add to Intrinsic value, still inspires reverence and reect· and any organization which has survived the wreck and ruin of time; and
c~me~ to os gray-haired with longevity, commands our confidence and elicits our admiration. " To be hidden amougst crowds," says· D&Qu1NOY, "is •ublime; to come
down hidden amongst crowds from distant generations is doubly sublime."
All the years that sleep in the tomb of the past can add no sincerity to faith, the
aged locks of time can give no intensity to hope, the triumphant deeds of the ages
dead cau· impart no worth to charity-these are what they are find them when and
where yon may. Masonry inscribed these virtues oil her banner while yet the
onod Jloor of the Temple ·was incomplete; and we revere and honor Masoorv, not
::-erely because these virtues are old, but because Masonry has proven their efficacy
by a long continued practice of them.
·
Every principle that Mas 0 ory inculcates, every truth it teaches, is of scriptural
origin. But while this is true, M"sonry is not 11 religions lostltotloo. I use the word
religions as synonymous with Christian. The fact that all the doctrines and teachings of Masonry are drawn from the Bible has impressed many with the idea that
J(asoory is a religious institution; and, indeed, some Masons believe that it ia a religion-a good religion-so good they do not desire any other, and are willing to
chance lfeaveo on their fidelity to Masonry. Now, no man ever did or ever will get
to Beaven on Masonry. He will get there just as soon on a railroad. Masonry
never was dePigoed· as a vehicle to dead-beat milk and cider Ohristiaos Into
Beaven.
Bot, on the other hand, Masonry is neither delstical nor atheistical; it teaches the
existence of a Supreme Being-the existence of God; not any kind of a God-not
that nature is God-not that yon may have a vague. indistinct notion that somewhere
in the realms of space there is something, yon don't know what, that you recognize
as God; but it teaches the God of the Bible; and the Mason who has not pot his trust
in this God Is dishonest and untrue if he does not Immediately pay up his dues, take
a dimlt, and forever quit the Order.
Concerning how tliis Organization has prospered, the number of Its membership,
the amount of good it has done, I shall say nothing, It were Masonic immodesty to
go about. over the country parading in statistics, increase of membership, the amount
in dollars and cents of benevolence practiced, and the extent or volume of our
charity. Charity is not puffed op and does not vaont itself. The left hand should
have no knowledge of what the right hand does.
I will say this, however, that our people an!l onr. oonotry are better adapted to
the growth, development and prosperity of Masonry than any other/eopltt. Inconsistent with oppression aotl tyranny in goveromeut in every form an to any degree,
antagonistic to bigotry and intolerance in religion of any creed, at war with the
artificial distinction of caste and vect-repoblican, cosmopolitan in all its teachings,
It oao attqijn its highest aim, accomplish its exalted mission lo its fullest extent only
among a people free in government aoJ io religion-for tyranny dwarfs the growth
and bigotry blights tbe fruits of genuine fraternity.
. And of all the people on the face of the earth, ours are by education, instinct
and nature the most given to charity. Whenever want demands, Americans respond
with lavish hand. Yon will search history in vain for examples and parallels of soch
instances of benevolence and charity, as shown by our people when contributing to
the relief of the sufferers by the Obioago lire, and to the people of the south during
the yellow fever scourge. The afllictions of the people were almost forirotten in
their heartfelt gratitude for the· benevolence of their brethren. More even than
this: The generosity of our people is not circumscribed by any consideration of relationship or ties of consanguinity. When there came to oor ears across the Atlantic's waters the wail or Ireland's woe, we promptly gave of our substance to her
starvi\lg children, and brought again the sunshine of domestic happiness to many 11
sorrow-stricken home. Very naturally then we woold look for thrift in such 11
oonotry and among such people. And as freedom is congenial to the growth of
Masonry, so is Masonry conducive to the highest appreciation of freedom.
.To per.petnate our Order lo its simplicity and purity, it is only necessary that we
exhibit in our dealings with the world, and lo our intercourse with each other, an
abiding faith in that which we profess. We should be consistent. Of all the virtues
that adorn the human character, that of consistency is the most j>eantiful. ProfesBioos are easily made. It is what 11 man does that gives confidence and respect.
