We learn that in Pennsylvania a Lodge has no defined territorial jurisdiction.
An applicant for initiation and membership can present his petition to any Lodge
in the State; but if he does not apply to the nearest Lodge, the Lodge to which
he does apply cannot act upon the petition until after it has addreBSed an official
inquiry to the Lodge nearest the place of residence of the applicant. The Lodge
thus inquired of, after giving notice to its members, takes ·a ballot on the inquiry.
Thus virtually the Lodge nearest the applicant's residence has the power of determining his election or non-election. The plan does not strike 11.8 very favorably.
The Grand Master is of opinion that the system of Grand Representatives has
outlived its usefulness. Since communications passing between Grand Jurisdictions are through the office of Grand Master, it appears to us that the system
never had any usefulneBS. So far as ·our observation and experience extend we
have never known of any duties attaching to'the position, and we would not know
of the existence of such a position were it not for an occWlional mention in the
proceedings. We regard the recommendation of Grand Master Al!'BIOA, that the
practice be abolished, as a move in the right direction.
A number of decisions are re~rted, all of which are sound as viewed from the
Pennsylvania standpoint, but not in accord with those on similar questions of
Masonic law in our own jurisdiction.
Upon the "physical qualification " of candidates Penney1vania adheres, in
theory, to the principle that "a candidate must be without blemish;" in practice,
we presume, "he is almost the same as other Grand Jurisdictions ; otherwise we
must conclude that a great change has tak6n place in the physical nature of man
in that jurisdiction since we left there some forty odd years ago.
It is gratifying to see that' the Grand Lodge debt has very greatly decreased
during the last two years.
The Grand Lodge officers were duly installed; whereupon the Right Worshipful Grand Master delivered a brief and pointed Address, the chief topic being the
neceBSity for adherence to the Landmarks of the Fraternity. Pennsylvania is
exceedingly conservati \·e.

Craft. Bro. VAUX had just pasaed the fiftieth anniversary of his initiation into

Grand Master. On his retirement from the office of Grand Master he was appointed a member of the Committee on Appeals, and subsequently its chairman,
in which capacity he has served for many years. He has also served his Grand
Lodge as chairman of the Committee on Correspondence since December, 1875.
To this eminent brother, Masonry not only in his own, but also in sister Grand
Jurisdictions, owes a debt of gratitude. His Grand Lodge did well thus to honor
him. We unite with his brethren in the hope that he ma;t long live to enjoy hi&
well earned honors, and to give to all the benefit of his wise counsels.

In his introduction to the rep<irt, Bro. VAUX in a very forcible manner sets
forth his beliefs, or a few of the more important questions that have occnpied the
attention of the writers of these reports. Notwithstanding, however, the ability
with which he advocates his opinions, we are compelled to differ. We are not pre. pared to give our assent to the proposition that, when a Lodge rejects an applicant for initiation and membership, the person so rejected should not be made a
Mason while the rejection stands. It seems to us that the enforcement of such a
doctrine would be a clear violation of the plainest teachings of justice. The perpetual disqualification of which our brother speaks is not the result of the actipn
of the Grand Lodge, nor even of •the Lodge rejecting the applicant ; it is even
more frequently the result of Individual prejudice or animosity. The recognition
of the fact that any individual Mason by his vote can perpetually disqualify an
applicant is a wrong, a grievous wrong. If humanity were perfect, if men and
Masone would always act from pure motive and without liability to err in the
expression of disqualification, it might be different. The rejection of an applicant is by no means always an indication or expression by the Lodge that the
applicant is disqualified. It more frequently is either the result of individual
dislike, or an expression by the LodAe that the appijcant, in every way qualified
is not desired as a member by that particular Lodge. We think that the obeervation of every Mason will lead him to the belief that there ought to be a limit to
the time for which the rejection of an applicant will disqualify him for reapplication. We care not whether it be called perpetual disqualification or perpetuii.l
jurisdiction, the result is the same. We know nothing in Masonry that justifies
any Lodge or any Grand Lodge in declaring an edict of perpetual disqualification against any man.
We are in accord with our brother on the matter of Grand Representatives.
The inutility, say nothing of the fact that it is not recogniged by Masonic authority, ought to condemn the system. In all our experience and obeervation in our
own Grand Lodge we have not known a single instance in which it has been of
one iota of use.
We are also in accord with Bro. VAUX in his expression of opinion regarding
Masonic recognition of Grand Lodges by other Grand Lodges. No treaty recognition, but only a recol!'llition based upon proper investigation, can ever be justified. We therefore earnestly hope that the action of the Grand Lodge of Texas
in what is known as "The Treaty of Monterey," will be carefully scrutinized before any action looking to the recognition of the "Gran Dieta Simbolica of
Mexico."
Bro. VAUX discU88eS the matter of public installations, remarking that "it is
problematic at best if a Grand Lodge can consent to the performance of this ceremony in pnblic." Whilst we have seen no harm resulting from occasional public
installations in this jnrisdiction, we are inclined to the opinion that Bro. VAUX
reasons correctly in representing that " the official acts of Lodges, the performance of a ceremony that is exclusively Masonic, directly connected with the
business of the Lodge, which is in ·itself the perfecting of the election by the
Lodge of its officers, investing them by installation with the right and authority
belonging to their stations, and the undisputed discharge of their Masonic duties,
cannot, we believe, be isolated from the secret work and made a public spect:Mlle."
The Hubject is one worthy of very careful consideration.
We are not one who for a moment thinks that our able brother merits repressive criticism. We have always admired the frankness with which he gives
expression to bis views upon all Masonic questions; and while we may differ from

We are in full accord with him relative to "fraternal congresses" and uniformity of rit\lal. as proposed by the Alabama resolutions. All such attempts will

PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND .

An Emergent Communication of the Grand Lodge of Prince Edward Island was
held in Charlottetown, on the twenty-fourth day of May, 1892, for the purpose or
laying the corner-stone of the new Masonic Temple.
On this occasion the Past Grand Chaplain, the Rev. Bro. W.W. BRRWKB, delivered a very eloqnent addreBB, which, did space permit, we would be pleased to
transfer bodily to this report. We qnote the following as a specimen of the reverend
brother's eloquence, and excellence of Masonic teaohing:If we would preserve and beautify our ancient and illustrions Order, we must not
be satisfied with the name, parade, and mere outward trappings of the Craft. We
must live Masonry-if it be of any value to the world or onrselves. Wearing an
apron does not make a man a Mason, or even a correct knowledge of our working
tools and ritual-these are but the emblems of those grand principles which constitute Freemasonry. Applied Masonry is the need of the hour. Be it ours to imitate
our ancients, evidences or whose skill and faithfulness remain to the present day ht
those stately cathedrals which adorn and beautify the Fatherland. Examine them,
and in every perfectly finished arch, every quaint cnpital, every bit of carven satire,
you 'Will see evidences of the life and freedom of the workmen. Yon will find no
mechanical slave labor, no details careleBBly finished, no part, because it was unseen or inconspicuous, scamped or left bare and rough; but every niche or tracery
shows that the soul of the craftsman was in his work; there was principle In the
touch of his chisel, honor iu the stroke of his gavel, self-sacrifice In the nice adjustment of his compass. And shall we to whom the Great Architect has committed the
erection of a far more superb and majestic edifice, fall behind the operative m&l\Pn
in the quality of onr work? God forbid !

The selections from the sentiments expressed by others, and his own well expressed opinions, indicate that our brother has a purpose in his work-the edification of his brethren in all that appertains to our noble Fraternity. Not only to
this great purpose will hie work contribute; his brethren will find much to afford
real enjoyment as well as Masonic profit. What a desirable thing it would be
could the membership of our Order be made to know how much there is in the
writings of such reviewers as DRUMMOND, and VINOlL, and PARVIN, and CHAMBERS, and all of these devoted workers, which tends to the advancement of Masonry, and at the same time to the uplifting of humanity. If our brethren would
seek access to the volumes of proceedings of the several Grand Lodges their.ideas
of Masonry, its grandeur and its beneficent work, would be so enlarged as to lead
to a more faithful fulfillment of their duties both as men and Masons.
We entirely concur with Bro. CHAMBERS regarding the desirability and necessity of having the Masters of our Lodges thoroughly qualified. Califomia long
since took advance ground in requiring that before being installed the Master of a
Lodge must produce the certificate of the Inspector of his District, or of the Grand
Lecturer, that he is qualified not only so far as concerns the ritual, but also in
reference to the Constitution and By-fa\ws of the jurisdiction. It is in the in~rest
not only of the particular Lodge, but of Masonry in general, that the Grand
Lodges should req;nre of the Masters that they should qualify thepiselves to be in
fa.ct what their very name implies-Masters, teachers, who may go in and out before their brethren, bleBSing all with their intelligence and their fidelity to their
trusts. We never yet have seen a live, )ll'ogressive Lodge, when under the charge
of a Master ignorant of the work and of the modes of conducting the business of
the Lodge.
We have no disposition to quarrel with him who is addicted to the use of "the
weed," for we ourself contracted the habit when yet a. mere lad. We will second
Bro. CHAMBERS and every brother who will publicly and privately denounce the
abusive use of the weed in any form in our Lodge-rooms. Masons considerate of
the feelings of their brethren in the Lodge-room, will be governed by the same
principlett of action that would control their conduct i~ the drawing-room.
Bro. CHAMBlllBS is right in refusing to join any one in preaching Christianity in
the Lodge, whether as an officer or a private member. Masonry teaches a decent

respect to· the opinions of our bfi>thren, and should know no distinction but that of

The following does not meet with onr concurrence, because it appears to ns as a
violation of that principle which forms "the very cement and support of civil BO•
ciety":Onr Grand Lodge has always held to the doctrine of perpetual jurisdiction by reJection, and I think it is one of the wisest provisions of onr Constitution. If we know
JUBt cause why an applicant should be rejected and refuse to let him be made a Mason
in Texas, we think we should he permitted to exercise that right in any Grand Lodge
Jurisdiction to which he may move.
The doctrine of perpetual jurisdiction over rejected material is rapidly becoming
a thing of the past. If only bad material were that which is subjected to rejection,
there might he little cause for opposition to this teaching; but, nnfortnnately, it very
often happens that the most worthy, without any reason except personal bias, are
the sufferers. Harm to the Fraternity must al ways follow in the wake of injustice.
In Texas it appears that mere blemish. may be regarded SR a satisfactory reason
for rejection. We are rejoiced to know that in that large jurisdiction there are
nearly twenty-five thousand sonls-bodies-withont blemish. Oalifornia has not been
able to find so many; indeed, she has not found any.

The Board of Directors of the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home presented a
report which is placed as an addenda to the proceedings. From this report it appears that the Board have cash in hand $5, 777. 75, and loans to the amount of
$45,503.35, being an increase over last year of $10,935.04. The Home has now been
in contemplation for about eight years. One-half of the gross revenues of the Grand
Lodge are appropriated to the support of this institution. In December, 1885, the
fund amounted in ca~h and notes to $5 ,959. 75; in December, 1892, it amounted to
$51,281. 75. Ao early location of the Home is greatly desired by the Lodges, sod
the Directors are using their best efforts toward this end consistent with the establishment of the Home upon a healthy financial basis. In this respect the Board are
displaying excellent judgment. The proper founding of a Home is not the work of
a brief period; it is a great undertaking, and necessarily requires time.
Bro. THOMAS M. MATTHEWS presented an excellent Report on Correspondence.
He reviews the proceedings of fifty-six Grand Lodges in a manner worthy of the
great jurisdiction for which he writes. California for 1891 receives pleasant and fraternal notice. He quotes' from Grand Orator BoRUCK's eulogy upon the life and
character of our late Grand Secretary, and adds, "More could not truthfully be said
of soy man."
Bro. MATTHEWS believes that the matter of furnishing refreshments in the Lodge~
should be left to the discretion of the Lodges. We believe so, too, but a maximum
limit should be designated beyond which discretion should not be permitted to go.
Experience has fnlly demonstrated to ns that the custom of having some simple refreshment at the conferring of the third degree is a good one. We are not willing to
believe that the only avenue to a man's heart. is, as some assert, through his stomach;
but we do believe that for the members and visiting brethren of a Lodge, after work,
to sit around the board and enjoy a social honr is a means of bringing brethren into
a closer intimacy and friendship toward one another. Masonry is peculiarly a social
institution; but we regret to be compelled to chronicle the fact that in onr experience and observation there is great lack of attention to the social feature in most
of our Lodges.
He dissents in toto from the decision of Grand Master CONKLIN to the effect that
a Lodge cannot give any part of its funds for the relief of the widow of an Entered
Apprentice. We are not willing to say that a Lodge should be permitted to use its
. fnnds as It pleases, consonant with the teachings of Masonry. Wholesome restraint
exercised by the Grand Lodge is in many cases required. Let it be known that a
Lodge can thns use its funds, and we opine that in a brief time many of the Lodges

The views of the Grand Master on finances are eminently sonnd. There is no
better criterion by which to judge of the prosperity of either a Grand or a subordinate Lodge than is a well filled treasury.
One of the Lodges had raised the fees for the degrees lrom fifty to seventy-five
dollars. The Grand Master expresses doubts of the wisdom of raising fees or dues.
So do we. The surest way lo enable Lodges to reduce their dnes is, in our opinion
the placing of the fees for the degrees at snch a figure as will not make Rach fees ~
bar to the entrance of good men and true who happen not to be endowed with a
great abundance of worldly wealth. There is no gainsaying the fact that Masonry
is in these latter days heooming so expensive a bnrden that many who would be or-

The Grand Master, by timely letter of warning to the various subordinate Lodges,
pot a quletoe upon the efforts of certain parties who bad engaged in hawking the
muob questioned " Cernean degrees." In this connection he stated that, as this
matter had nothing to do with Ancient Craft Masonry, be did not deem it necese&ry

The Grand Master had, as Is generally the case, because o( the lack of proper
knowledge on the part of Masters of Lodges of the simplest regulations, been compelled to render many decisions. It seems to be a very general complaint in all
Jurisdictions tha't ignorance of fundamental laws and regulations exists. There can
be no reasonable excuse in these days for such ignorance of law and nsages, and
there would be much more of harmony and good work If Masters and other officers
of Lodges were half as eager to prepare themselves for the discharge of their
duties as they are to push tbeD18elves forward to positions for which they are not
qoalilied.
The Grand Master has a very correct appreciation of the Importance attaching to
the position of Grand Lecturer. He bolds, rightly, that it is an office that should be
ftlled by a bright and active man, and that to keep such a man, he should be paid in
some due proportion to his ability. It is good policy on the part of the Grand
Lodge, says the Grand Master, to secure good service; and when a Master Workman
is found to keep him at bis post, t.bougb expenses may have to be cnrtailed in other
directions. The Grand Lodge of Washington concurred in the views of the Grand
Kaster, and voted an allowance of Sl ,500 for the salary and SI,000 for the e~enees
of this officer. Well done l . We have no doubt that the benefits resulting from the
labors of the Grand Lecturer will amply oompensate the Grand Lodge forltbis outlay, even In the way of dollars and cents; and that ·Masonry in Washington will
lengthen ite cords and strengthen ite stakes mightily in consequence of the
liberality and good judgment of the Grand Lodge in providing proper serviee for
the Lodges.

Under California, our brother takes very grave exception to the decision rendered
by Grand Master OOMJa.11' regarding the requirement in onr joriedlctlon that a nonaffiliate muet pay eix moothe' doee on making applioation for aftlliation. Be characterizes the provision as" unftiet and unholy," and ciiee the.case of a brother, a member of a Lodge In Washington, who, being feeble In health, concluded to visit southern California for a few months in the hope that the change would be beneficial to
bis physical condition. This brother. is represented as a worthy and devoted Ma·
eon, but, b.;iilg a man of limited means, he thought it beet to dimit from hie Lodge
In Washington. After remaining in California for a abort time, fearing that hie stay
might be protracted for an indefinite period, he concluded to petition a Lodge for
affiliation, and was bewildered with astonishment upon being informed that he must
accompany bis petition with six months' back does.
We fear that Bro. RBED has misinterpreted the Grand Master's decision, or that
he le not aware of the provision in oar Conetitotion relative to non-affiliates. Our
Constitution contains a section which reads tboe:• It is the duty of every Mason. to be a member of Rome Lodge, and every non·
affiliate Muon who, having reeided six months within this Sta~, shall refuse or neglect to make application for membership to some Lodge there10, ebal! be deem!'d. unworthy of Masonic consideration, and sbal! not be entitled to, nor be the rec1p1ent
of, any of the rights, privileges or charities of the Order.

The language of Grand !rfaster CoNKLIN's decision leads us to the inference that
the brother alluded to therein was not in standing; that le, that he had been a nonaffiliated Mason for the period of six months, or more. a does not seem to oe a
very nnfuet or unholy thing that each .a Mason shall be required to put himself in
good standing in order to be privileged to apply for membership in one of oar
Lodges, more particularly when what he pays for this purpose keeps him in standing for six months. Under our law the non·affiliate of six months is out of standing,
and being so he could not apply for membership until he puts himself in standing.
Thie he does by the payment of six months' dues. The brother to whom Bro. RBBD
alludes must have been a non-aftlliate of six months or more; we presume that there
was no assumption about his standing, but that it appeared from the face of hie dimit
that he bad been a non-affiliate for six months. There was certainly no exaction of
money without corresponding privileges-the privilE>ge incident to good etandlng-of_
making application for membership.
Onr jorlsdiction, like most others, has always been afflicted by numbers of nonaffiliated Masone, and oar Grand Lodge thought proper to enact a provision that
wonld compel each Masone to do their duty, at leRBt so far 1u contributing to the
enpport of Masonry is concerned. The role formerly was that such Masons could
keep themselves in standing by contribotlng an amount equivalent to its does to
some Lodge. But it was thought advisable to repeal that law and enact the present
one- one which ·we do not regard as being either "unjust or unholy," and one
which our Grand Lodge bad perfect right to enact.

Oommenting opon the decisions of Grand Master Comi:.1:11, Bro. ATXIKSON thos

must)oin the Lod~e nearest to his residence. The Grand Lodge reversed him. Accordrng to oor law, the Grand Master is right. It seems clear to os that the nearest
Lodge to the applicant's home should have jurisdiction. This rule i• always applied
to a profane seeking admission, and should apply with equal force, and for the •ame
reasons, to the non-affilinte. One ma.v be worthy when he is initiated, and. v~ry soon
thereafter become in all respects very unworthy. When a brother takes a d1m1t, he assumes the risk of getting back into a Lodge again as a member. If he applies .tor
reinstatement, a ballot must be taken opon his application, and nnless it is found
clear, he is kept out. Now, i• it not plain that the Lodge nearest the applicant's
residence should have jurisdiction, because its members would know the weakness
of the applicant, if aoy existed, and could better jodge of his fitness for membership
than a Lodge remote from the applicant's home?
For the reason stated, i* is plainly right, to our minds at least, that jurisdiction
should be confined to the nearest Lodge.
We remark, for the information of our brother, that the Grand Lodge could not
do oth<lrwise than reverse the Grand Master, as it is a provision of oor Constitution
that a non-affiliated Mason may make application for affiliation to any Lodge in the
State. We recognize the force of what he says opon this.question, however, and in•
dividually we are of opinion he is about right.
He gives his opinion oo the question of suspension for non·payment of ddes, and
also upon that of the limit or time for which a dimitted Mason may remain in stand·
Ing, in full accord with California:We have always believed that a dimitted Mason, after six months' or a year's
duration, should be oot olf from all the benefits of Masonry. California fixes the
time at six months . This is about right. We never could see the fairness of placing
a brother who pays no annu11l does, alongside or another who holds his membership
In his Lodge, and giving to one all the rights and benefits that you give to the other.
It is unfair and irnjost, and therefore should not he tolerated.
For the same reason we hold th.at when a brother fails to pay his dues as required
by the by-laws of bis Lodge, unless good excuse can be assigned for such delinquency, he should be promptly suspended.
In the following, under Arizona, we folly concor:-

This Grand Lodge seems to have great difficulty in establishing a ooiform system
of work. There is but one way to do it, and that is to pay a competent Grand Lecturer, oot of Grand I.odge funds, to visit each Lodge and stay ·with the brethren
until they are thoroughly posted. No other plan will prove elfective.
Tbe following, from his reviQw of Canada, is too good to be omitted. We say
amen to every word of it:The lm-called right of burial, fashioned by those who manufacture landmarks for
every letter of the alphabet, is merely a regulation, not by any means universal. It
should not be enough that Masons before death, or their friends for them, request
Craft burial. Care should be exercised that those who are dead and gone are
worthy of the honor. It is an outrage on public sentiment, and a prostitution of our
ceremonies, to assemble at the grave of a brother, who perhaps wrecked his life by
indiscretions, which made his name a by-word, and whose daily life was so improper
that shame herself kept watch that even her sense of decency was not violated. To
cast the evergreen into the graves of men who lfave made their hearths and homes
desolate, whose wives and children have sought for happiness ooder the cold stars
of heaven rather than under the paternal roof, is sanctioning vice, and attempting to
use the broad mantle of a Ma9on's charity, with its ample salvage, as a cover for the
sins or a life that can best be crowned with forgetfulness.

applicant stands rejected for the period of one year, when he is at liberty to apply
again for advancement.

The Grand Master thus expresses himself on the matter of re-election of Grand
Masters:It bas for some years been my opinion that the Grand Master, except for some
special reason, should not be re-elected to succeed himself. He has bad th«: great
honor, and if only re-elected because it is the custom, no additional honor 1s conferred upon him. Our membership is now very large, among whom are many 1!ot
only well qualified, bot deserving of recognition, who stand a poor show of obtaining their deserts if the present custom is adhered to.

Here is a peculiar case, decided by Deputy Grand Master SWAIN:The facts, briefly stated, are as follows: HUGHES, claiming to be a me~be! of the
Lodge, objected to a candidate, who was initiated in the face of the obJect1on,_the
W.· •.M.·. claiming that HUGHES was not a member of the Lodge. Upon Investigation, I found that HUGHES applied for affiliation in October, 1891, and was afterwards
informed bv the Secretary that be had been elected; he freq,uently visited the Lodge
and paid some dues. After the objection above mentioned the discovery was made
that there was no record that he had ever been balloted for.
I rnled that if he bad been balloted for and elected he was a member of the
Lodge and his objection entitled to respect, notwithstanding the abse~ce of r~cord ;
bnt that if he bad not been balloted for he was not a member, notw1thstandmg he
had been informed he was elected. That if he was able to bring a single witness
who could remember a single ballot in the case, it would be sufficient. Bot as he.
was not able to do that, the records of the Lodge must govern, and be was not a
member of the Lodge, and consequently not entitled to have his objection impera·
tively considered.

In reference to the complaint of one Lodge against another for refusal to admit a
visiting brother, the Committee on Appeals, in their report, say that while such
refusal, without the assigning of reasons by an objectir:1g brother, may cause hardship to visiting brethren, they believed that a member had a perfect right to object
to any brother visiting his Lodge, without giving any reasons for the objection. The
Lodge, they say, being the Masonic home of its members, visitors are admitted as a
privilege and not upon any right they may possess. 'The adoption of the report was
deferred in the absence of the Lodge complained of.
Whilst we recognize the fact that visiting 11 Lodge cannot .be claimed as a right,
we think that the courtesy which shonld obtain among Lodges wonld dictate that
the privilege, on ordinary occasions at least, should not be subject to the whim of
any individual member. We think the Master of a Lodge shonld have the reason
for objecting to the admission of 11 brother presented io him, and that he should
dettirmine the matter upon reason presented. We do not think that the reason, or
the name of the party objecting, shonld be given to the brother seeking the.
privilege.
The Committee on Visiting Brethren in the Grand Lodge reported that they• had
found none in waiting, except"snch as were duly vouched for, and recommended
that all Master Masons in good standing sbonld be invited to attend, unless for good
and jnst reasons objected to .bY any member. The Grand Lodge adopted this
report. If visitors should not be refused admissfon to the Grand Lodge withoo t ·
good and jnst reasons, we are ·nnable to see why the same rule should not he
observed in subordinate Lodges.
The present copy of proceedings contains the Constitntion and By-Laws of the
Grand Lodge. A cnrsory examination of these impresses us favorably, though there
are some principles which do not meet our approval. A constitutional provision
authorizing the Grand Master to make Masons at sight does not seem to ns to be in
the interests of the Fraternity. Nor do we subscribe to the doctrine of perpetnal
jnrledictioo. We prefer the one ballot system, with the right of objection to
advancement after initiation.

Bro. FRANK MABION ANGELLO TTI, from the Committ ee "on Grievances, presente d the followin g reports :To the lrf. '. W. •• <hand Lodge of CaJ,ifrrrnia:.:....
In the case of WILLIAM HENBY MOBB!BBEY, suspended by Orland Lodge;
No.
265, on Septembe r 4th, 1893, your committee report as follows:There is no record of the meeting for the election of Trial Commissioners
nor
is there anv record of an announcem ent in the Lodge of the result of the trial,
~or
is
there any approval by the Master endorsett as required by the 26th Gen. Regulatio
n.
These omissions might be easily supplied, but an examinati on of the charges
and
apecifications and the testimony given satisfy us that. the rcood oi Masonry
would
not be subserved by an aflirmance of the verdict of the Trial Commissioners,
or by
any further proceedings under the charges ma.de. The charges, containing
nine
specifications, are all directed toward a statement made by the accused to
three or
four acquaintan ces, to the effect that he had found the accuser in a moat
comp:omising and disgusting position. One cannot read the transcript without
coming
to the conclusion that the statement of the accused was fully in accord with
the
facts; indeed, there is no pretense on the part of anybody, so far as the transcript
shows, that the statement was untrue, and th'lt it was true was distinctly
stated
by the accused on the trial in response to questions by one of the commissio
ners, in
the presence of the accuser. The position of the accuser seems to be that,
conceding the truth of the statement , the accused should have said nothing about
it.
But it appearB that the acts of the s.ccuaer spoken of were committed in
a public
.place, that the accused learned all he knew in regard thereto simply because
he
was passing the place, and that he afterward s spoke of the matter thoughtles
sly to
a group of three or four acquaintan ces when the name of the accuser was
mentioned, without any intent or desire to injure the accuser. Certainly the
conduct
of the accused, if the statement be true, was uot nearly as damaging to Masonry
as was the conduct of the accustir. No good can result from the further
prosecution of these charges. If the statement of the accused regarding the accuser
was
true, as the transcript herein seems to indicate, we have no hesitation in
saying
that charges should be preferred against tlie accuser. We therefore recommen
d
the following re.!Olution for adoption by the Grand Lodge:Ruolved, That the judgment of Orl,and Lodge, No. 265, in the ease
of Bro.
WILLIAM HENBY MORRISSEY, be and the .same is hereby reversed, and
that the
charges against said brother be and the same are hereby dismissed.

In the case of GEORGE HENRY GnAHAM, expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry by Murning Star Lodge, No. 68, on the 14th day of August,
1893,
your committee present the following report:The accused did not appeal, and his residence was unknown. The charge·
of
unmasonic conduct is based on two specifications. The only evidence introduced
to sustam the first specification, which was a charge of obtaining $41.7!\ from
the
Masonic Board of Relief of San Francisco by false and fraudulen t representa
tione,
was a letter from a Master Mason of San Francisco , Cal, together with two
other
letters written by Masons in Missouri and Minnesota . The Constituti on (Part
VI,
Art. IV, Sec. 5), provides a way by whi'ch the testimony of a witness, who
is a
Mason and who resides without the jurisdictio n of the Lodge in which the
trial is

196

[Oct. 11,

Proceedings of tl1e

had, and whose attendance cannot be procured, mBy be obtained, and the way
there provided is the only legal way to obtain such testimony. S~ch testimony
must be taken before the Master of a Lodge within whose jurisdiction the witness
resides, and "authenticated by the oertificate of the Master before whom it is taken,
under the seal of the Lodge. Under the Constitution and decisions of this Grand
Lodge, the letters introduced in evidence were inadmissible for any purpose, and
there is no other evidence to sustain °the fil'llt specification. The allegations of this
specification seem to be sufficient, if proved, as the letters indicate they can be, to
justify the expulsion of the accused, but they must be proved by competent testi· •
mony. The second specification is not sustained by competent testimony. Your
committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution :Reaol:1Jf.d, That the judgment of Mo'l'fling Sf,ar l..odge, No. 68, in the case of
GKOBGE HENRY GRAHAM, be and the same is hereby reversed, and the case is
hereby remanded to said J,Qdge with instructions to again try the accused for the
offense charged, in conformity with our provided mode of procedure.
All which is respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM THOMAS LUCAS,
FRANK MARION ANGBLLOTTr,

Bro. WILLIAM CALDWELL BELCHER, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports :To the M. '. W. •• GTand Lodge of Calif<YrnW. ;The Committee on Jurisprudence have carefully.con•idered the matters referred

to them, and respectfully report:I. Relative to disqualifications of I\ Master to preside at a trial.
During the year 1891 this case was pre•ented to Grand Master CoNKLIN: A
Junior Warden had, in the latter part of 1890, by direction of hie Lodge, preferred
charges against one of ib! members. Subsequently and before a trial could be had.
the annual election came on, at which this Junior Warden was elected Ma~ter
After his installation as Master, feeling."some doubt whether, undt>r the circum:
stances, he ought to preside at the trial, be wrote to the Grand Master, stating
that he, as Junior Warden, had preferred the charges, and that he would at the
trial be called as a witness to a matter which, in hie judgment, would not affect
the merit.s of the case; and further, that he had no prejudice or bias for or against
the accneed, and asked if he ought. or could properly preside at the trial. Grand
Master CO.lOUIN replied that "he was not disqualified to preside at the trial as

206

Proceedings of the

[OClt.12,

Master, by reason of having, as Junior Warden, preferred the charges, or by being
a witness, if he was not personally interested." (Proc. 1891, p. 16.)
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this ruling with others on questions
of Masonic law made by the Grand Master was referred, reported:Thi~ decision is in accord with the rule adopted by the Grand Lodge in 1885, in
approvmg a report of its Committee on Grieva.nces. In the case then before the
committee the Master had ~een called as a witness, and the objection was made
that ~eing a. witness he ought not to be allowed to preside at the trial; but the
•committee said that the objection was untenable; that he was not disqualified by
reason of that .fact. (Proceedin~s, Vol. XVII, p. 203.)
We are satisfied that the decision of the Grand Master was correct in the caee
~fore him. As Junior Warden he had preferred charges because his Lodge had
imposed that duty on him. He was called as a witness, but not to the merits of
the case, and was in no way personally interested in the prosecution or the defense. We are not, however, satisfi,ed with the rule adopted in 188!5, and to the
end that it may receive further and more careful considerl\tion we recommend that
it be referreJ to our succeasors with directions to report thereon at the next An·
nual Communication.
In 1892 the committee failed to report on this matter and it came to us as unfin.
ished business. After careful consideration our conclusion is that the Master of
a Lodge ought not to preside at the trial of a Mason, whether a member of his
Lodge or not, when it is known to him in advance of the trial that he is to be
called as a witness, or when he, as Junior Warden or otherwise, has preferred the
charges upon which the trial is to be had. It i.e very true that he might be a witness, and might, by direction uf his Lodge or of his own motion, as overseer of the
Craft, have preferred the charges and yet be so free from bias and prejudice that
he could preside at the trial and hear and determine all questions calling for his
determination with the utmost fairness. Our acquaintance with men satisfies us
that some could and would do this, but that the number who would is very small.
But if we were assured that the Master, in a particul&r case, could, would it be
just that we should ask him to occupy a position in which his integrity would very
surely be called in question ?
Our procedure is e..sentially a criminal procedure. The charges perform the
office of an indictment or information-the Master is the Judge-the Commissioners are the jury; and, as in prosecutions for crime the people are plaintiffs, so
with us the great body of Ma.sons is the real plaintiff and not the individual who
sets the procedure in motion by preferring charges.
The offenses ilognizable in the criminal courts of the State are offenses against
society, so the offenses cognizable in our courts are offenses against our society,
and our judgments when rendered against the accused are for punishment for the
public wrong, and not for redress of private grievances.
The Junior Warden of a. Lodge is the public prosecutor for the Fraternity,
much as a District Attorney of a county is for the State.
Our own idea of the duties of a District Attorney is, that he should examine
every case presented to him fully and thoroughly, and, if from such examination
he is convinced that the accnaed is guilty of the offense charged, should present the
case to the court fully a.nd fairly and use all honorable means to secure a conviction; but that, if satisfied from his examination of the case, or on its presentation at
the trial, that the accused is innooont of the offense charged, he ought not to urge
or in any way assent to a conviction. That is all that the public requires of him,
yllt we all know that very many, perhaps a large majority of District Attorneys,
become thoroughly partisan in the management and trial of cases, seeming to
think, and certainly acting, as though duty required of them to secure a convic·
tion, right or wrong. Henc:e, under our statute, a Judge who, as District Attor.

1893.J

(}rand Lodge of California.

207

· ney has appeared before a Grand Jury and secured an indictment, or has himself
prepared and presented an information, could not .preside at the trial of the party
thus indicted or accused. '.rhe language of the statute is: "A Judge cannot act
as such • • * when he has been attorney or counsel for either party in the
action or proceeding."
We should certainly be quite as careful as is the State to avoid the probability
or even the suspicion of partiality. The Junior Warden in his examination and
preparation of 11 case, should, and we · must presume does, aoquaint himself thoroughly with the evidence on the part of the prosecution, and we may reaRonably
oonclude that he would have.formed decided opinions as to what ought to be the
result of the trial else he would not, even under the direction of his Lodge; have.
preferred charges', and that he could not preside at the trial with such exact im·
partiality as, in theory at least, we demand. Our opinion is that the Judge whq
presides at 11 trial ought to be as free from bias and preconceived opinion as
juror or trial commissioner, and that we ought not to require or permit a Master
to preside at 11 trial when he, as Junior Warden or otherwise, has preferred the
charges.
·
Our Codes provide that the Judge may be called as a witness in a case on trial
before him and leave it to his discretion to determine whether the trial shall proceed or be suspended and tried before another Judge. In cases before our courts,
if the Judge is called as a witness, it is usually to some collateral matter, as i:ir•of
of a signature to which he was a subscribing witness, and we should consider it a
gross abuse of discretion if he allowed a trial to proceed when he had been called
to testify as to the merits of the case. In Masonic trials it is very rare that a wit·
ness is called to testify except as to the merits of the case, and we think the safe
rule for us is to provide that the Master shall be disqualified to preside in any case
when he is advised, in advance of the trial, that he will be called as a witnllBl!~ and
that whenever during the progress of a t~ial he is called to testify, unless upon a
purely collateral matter, he should suspend the trial and repo~ to the 1Grand
Master.

Rhall have received the first degree or the first and second degrees in one Lodge.
and shall, at the request of such Lodge and on its behalf, receive the remaining
degrees or degree in another Lodge, no petition, reference, or ballot shall be necessary in the last named Lodge, as the work will be done for the first, of which he

receh·ed the degree of Master Mason.
Whenev1>r a petition is presented, whether for one, two or three degrees, the
proper fee must, in all cases, accompany the petition (Section 8, Article III, Part
III). In the case stated, Hro. DODSON says the third degree was conferred by

the first and second degrees in another Lodge, the fee to accompany his application
for the remaiuing degrees or degree shall be such proportion of the fee for all the
degrees as the by-laws of the Lodga may prescribe." Thie section, as it now stands,
was adopted in 1873 (Proc. 1873, page 2.57). Prior to that time the provision had
been that "the fee for each or all the degraes, as may be regulated by the
J...odge, shall accompany the application." At that time each Lodge, by its bylaws and for itself only, determined whether it would have a ballot for each degree
or one for the three (Proc. 1873, page 256), and not u~il 1883 was the present rule
of one ballot for the three degrees adopted (Proc. 1883. page 263).
Under that rule, and the other raquiring the fee to accompany the petition, if
the applicant is elected the fee becomes the property of the Lodge absolutely, and

limited by the Uniform Code of By-Laws, unless the Lodge otherwise direct.

The Grand Master thinks our law lame with reference to non-affiliates, giving

213

applicant is known to be nnworthy to be received as a member, to cause charges.. to
be preferred against him.
It is true that the law has not declared these duties bot they follow as necessary
corrollaries of that which is declared. Duties and obligations are never all on one
side. All of us owe to the Oivil Government under which we live, loyality and obedi·
ence to its laws, but that Government also owes to us the duty of protection in the
enjoyment of life, liberty and property. So every Master Mason owes to the
Masonic Government under which he lives the duty of loyalty and obedience to its
laws, and, upon the performance of such dnty the reciprocal duty of protection in
the enjoyment of all hie Masonic rights and privileges is eqnally incumbent npon the
Masonic Government. We enjoin upon the non-affiliate the duty of being a mem·
ber of some Lodge and, to that end, of making hie application for membership within six months from the date of withdrawal from a Lodge here, and within six months
from the date of fixing hie residence here, ifhe comes from another jurisdiction; and
when he has made the application he has performed the duty, so far as he then can
perform it-has performed hie part.
We say to him, here is a plain duty for you, if you neglect it for six months the
penalty will be suspension, and there is one way and only one in which you can per·
form that duty. Do what.is required of you, and if, for any reason, your application
is rejeoted, your term of grace shall be extended for another term of six months,
and you can during that term make still another or other applications. If these are
rejected the term will be still extended from each rejection in recognition of your
endeavor to do the duty enjoined.
It is true, therefore, that one might, as the Grand Master says, if rejected, keep
himself in good standing many years by making a new application every six months,
and so it ought to be, because he is striving to do what the law requires of him, and
the Loclg~ or Lodges rejecting are not doing what they ought to do, which is to receive him, if worthy to be received, and to prefer charges against him if he is unworthy to be received.
In such cases it might quite as properly be said that the Lodges have "the advantage'' over the non-affiliate, because they may thus keep him manylyears struggling to secure the recognition to which he is presumptively entitled and the means
of enjoying all the privileges of a Mason as well as performing all his duties.
The law as it now stands is plain and affords ample protection for the rights of
non-alliliates and of the Lodges, and in our judgment needs no revision.
·

6. No Lodge in this State has authority to waive jurisdiction over an applicaut
for degrees whose application has been rt>jected by it.
Under our law, the Lodge, whether~ this State or elsewhere, acquires, by re·
ceiving and rejecting his application for degrees, exclusive jurisdiction over the
applicant for the period of twelve months from the dnte of rejection, and no other
Lodge can lawfully, within that period, receive an application from him. When
that period has expired, its jurisdiction is gone, and the party i11 as free to make
another application as he would be if he had never made one.
The case calling for the Grand Master's decision arose in St. Hdena Lodge, No.
93, and from the statement presented it appears that a party living at or near St.
Helena made application to the Lodge for the degrees and had been rejected.
Subeequently he moved to and established his residence within the jurisdiction of
Cori.nm Lodge, No. 6, in Utah, and after living there sufficiently long to gi7e that
Lodge jurisdiction to receive his application, and more than twelve months after
his rejection, he applied to Corinm Lodge. The Lodge, having learned of the rejection, asked of &. Helena Lodge a waiver of jurisdiction. The Master replied
that by lapse of time his Lodge had lost jurisdiction and, therefore, could not
waive it.
We recognize perpetual jurisdiction only when an applicant has been elected
and initiated by the Lodge to which he applies. In such a case our law is so general, and yet so precise, as to leave no room for doubt. The language is: "No Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft shall be advanced to a higher degree in any Lodge
other than that in which he shall have received those or either of thoSI' degrees,
unless by the official consent of such Lodge, if it be then in existence and he within
the United States of America or the Dominion of Canada." The policy of this
prohibition might be doub~, if it were open to question. If it were a matter of
absolute right t\lere should be no limitation to particular countries. But we accept it as our written law.
We also recognize a jurisdiction of one year over a rejected candidate. During
that time the rejecting Lodge may, by dispensation from the Grand Master,
• receive from him a second application, but no other Lodge can. When the full
year after a rejection has elapsecl, tbe jurisdiction has l.apaed, and we recognize no

18 When a. cause baa been transferred from the Lodge in which the chq.rges
were presented to another for trial, the accused is no~ e!'.ltitled, as a matter of right,
to notice of the time fixed for the election of Comm1BS1one~.
The provisions of our Constitution (Art. IV, Part IV) a.re that when any member of o. Lodge, except its Master or the Grand Master, or any Mason residing
within its jurisdiction, shall be accused of unmasonic conduct, charges in w_riting
may be presented to the Master, who, if he judge the charges sufficient in form
and substance, must, unless the case is transferred to another Lodge for trial, by
due notification call a special meeting of his Lodge for the election of Commissioners.
Of this special meeting the accused, if a member of the Lodge, would receive
notice and could attend. If not a member of the Lodge, he would not be entitled
to notice. The. Commissioners are, in fact, jurors, and we think the accused should
be notified of the time and place of election, and have the right to attend and canvass the qualifications of every one nominated for election. As no provision is
made in the Constitution for the exercise of this right, it hBB been held that the
accused may, at any time before the commencement of the trial, interpose an objection to any one of the CommiBBioners elected on the ground of bias or prejudice.
It is plain that both the accused and the o.ccuser should have the right to attend
at the time Commissioners are selected, and in a proper manner to canvaBB the fitness of each one named as a Comlllissioner before he is selected. In our courts,
Sto.te and Federal, the accused is advised of the offense charged by having the indictment or information read to him at least some days before the trial, and it is
his privilege to be present with his counsel at the impaneling of a jnry and to can.vaBB the qualifications of every one called as a juror before he is selected. We
think a like practice should prevail in Masonic trials, and that specific provision
therefor should be made in our Constitution.
Under the law, as it now stands, the decision seems to us correct; but believing
that further and specific provision in regard to the matters referred to in this report, and perhaps to other matters relating to trials, ought to be made, we recommend that this decision be referred to our successors, with directions to prepare
and at our next Annual Commnnication present such amendments, relative to
trials, as they deem proper.

The occurrence and recurrence of this violation of the sacred obligationa of the
Craft is so frequent, I regret to confess, that the conduct referred to must be
bright in recollection, at one time or another, to every member of this Institution.
At the very threshold of the Craft, as an Entered Apprentice, the lessons are impressed that the three principal tenets of Masonry are brotherly love, relief and
truth, and that brotherly love causes true friendship to exist among those who
might otherwise remain at a perpetual distance. That by reli,ef we are linked together with an indissoluble chain of sinC6re affection, and on this basis form our
friendships and establish our connections; and that by flruJ;h, that sincerity and
plain dealing distinguish us. That with heart and being we join in promoting
each other's welfare and rejoice in promotin~ each other's prosperity. We are
charged to learn the important duties which we owe to God, our neighbor and ourselves. To God, by a.we and reverence; to our neighbor, by acting on the aquare,
by rendering him every kind office .and doing unto him as we would be done by.
As a citizen we are enjoined to be exemplary in the dispatch of civil duties and
never to lose sight of the allegianoe due to our country. As individuals w~ are
trusted to practice domestic and public virtues, that temperance may chasten, fortitude support, prudence direct, and justice be the guide of all .onr actions.
As Fellow Crafts we are advised that Masonry is a progressive moral science•
that we are not to aggravate the offenses of the brethren, but judge ~ith candor'
admonish with judgment, reprimand with justice. When the crowning glory of ~
Master Mason is arrived at and we are raised to that degree, then we are instr'1cted
that we are authorized to correct the irregularities of our individual brethren and
guard them against every allurement and vicious practice, and to preserve unaullied the reputation of the Fraternity. Finally we a.re apprised that we are to
let no motive make us swerve from duty, violate our vows, or betray our trust.
With such lessons before ua for our discipline and guidance, can there be any
excuse for secret revilings of one brother against another? It ia the duty of the
members of the Order, when they discover or hear from others that unpleasant
criticism or hostile comment is being made against a fellow member, that he should
warn the one so assailed. If it should be discovered that the brother assailed is in
truth unwcuthy of association with those who hold in high esteem all the principles of F.reemasonry, and who are closely bound by the pure and sacred obligations
of the Order, then proper charges should be presented against the accused person,
and either vindication be had or punishment visited upon the offending brother.
Ever bear before our mental eye a banner inscribed:" The purest treasure mortal times afford
Is spotless reputation; that away,
Men are but gilded loam or painted clay."
If there is one pos80B8ion given hy the Almighty Father to weak mankind, it is
a good name, a pure reputation, the value of which is so forcibly pictured by the
.
immortal bard in the lines:-

" Good name in man and woman is the immediate jewel of their souls.
Who steals my purse, steals trash; 'tis something, nothing;
'Twas mine, 'tis his, and has been slave to thousands;
But he who filches from me my good name,
Robs me of that which not enriches him,
And makes me poor indeed." .
It is my earnest belief that frequently the fault of dealing unkindly with a
brother's character, or uttering some tainted word against his fair name, arises
from carelessness which is a.a inexcusable as it is horrible. I would impreBB upon

COMPETENT OFFIOEBS.

We can well agree with the claim made a year ~o, th:i.t in order to accomplish
intimate social communion among the members, the meetings of the Lodges must
he made both pleasant and attractive. While lectures and gatherings around the
banquet board can in a very large measure assist in bringing about that which is
attractive to all the inembership, there appears to me to be even a more vital
measure which can he adopted to secure the need, and which we all eagerly seek
to have done. It is that the men who are selected as the officers of the Lodges ·
should J;iave the highest qualifications to be found within the Lodge membership.
My contention is that the qualifications should be, so far as can be procured, a
widely developed mind, whether gained by education or self investigation or
eelf improvement. A man to hold official station in a Lodge should be poeseesed of a disposition to be just, to be ddcrmined, to be gentle, to be kind, to
be patient; slow to form final opinions of a brother's worth or weaknese; ready
at· all times to be fair and considerate. He should he a student of the Masonic law, a student of the ritual, a student of the beet interests of the Lodge,
a student of the direct welfare of those who may be brought in closest contact with the direct membership, of which he is one. He should be able to
acquire and retain both the eecret and the writteµ work, and tn,ke e;are that
when the occasion requirfie to so deliver the work that not only the person to
whom he addresses himself gives attention, but that all who may be present
to see and hear shall do the same. Tliis is notably demanded in all of the degree work. It is not my claim that theae qualifications should rest with the
Worshipful Master of the Lodge al.one, but that they should exist to an eminent
degree in the Junior and Senior Wardens and Junior and Senior Deacons, as well
as in the Master. The chairs all properly equipped with the best capability, no
danger will be present .upon questions of promotion.
Give to me impreesive and complete work in a Lodge-room and I will assure
and guar11ontee yon filled benche.a and filled seats, a crowded Lodge-room with an
interested, entertained and loyal membership. Present me with poor work, slack
attention to duty, carelessness to the interest of those who are the members of the
subordinate body, and I will point out to your gaze a decreaBilng membership, a
di3gulted circle of brothers, and a Lodge well on the way to decay and in position
for the foneiture of ite charter.
You may answer that these suggestions are Utopian, too ideal, that it is not
possible in all Lodges to obtain the material asked for. But pause a moment, and
consider whether it is a fact that there is any Lodge in the State of California
which has not able and learned men of capacity and of willingnese to do their

THE BLAOKBALL.

Information has from time to time been brought to my hearing of the abuse of
the black cube and sphere. Abuse in this, that the deposit of the symbol of rejection was not against the candidate, but to serve an untoward feeling to a brother
or against several brethren of a subordinate body. No greater protecting shield
could be afforded our Fraternity to exclude improper characters among men from
associatioi;i with the Craft than the use of the ball or cube of objection. It should
be used with fine judgment, after full deliberation, with a deep seated affection for
the Order and a sense of justice to the applicant. It is unmasonic conduct, it is a
cruel blow to an innocent person. to cast the negative sphere or cube against one
who is in every way worthy, simply for the rea..•on that he is proposed by, or is on
terms of friendship with, a member who has in some wiee engendered the ill will
of the brother using the black. Wounded feelings have resulted to an unoffending
man; character has suffered a stroke; bitter prejudice age.inst Masonry has found
a resting place in a stranger's breast. 'l'he wrong thus done cannot be requited.
Do not commit this crime against fraternity, against manhood; against right,
against every propriety of life. Do your duty, my brother, against the unworthy,
but do not injure Masonry, or bruise the finer feelingit of man, by lack of deliberation or the expression of malice against a brother or brethren.

Another subject has vividly introduced itself to my observation, which, if properly and with due caution should be developed, might, to a very material degree,
give push and impart interest to the membership, and at the ~ame time permit the
members of our families and those who will be desirable men to become Masons, to

the Craft ; that is to have, as far as feasible, the installation of officers public.
Wives, •isters, daughters and their beet acquaintanceship would by this means, in
my estimation, be attracted to thP tenets of the Order and the principles' and doctrines which guide us.
WILLIAM JAMES HUGHA.M, the distinguished Masonic author, is accredited
with the statements that :"Though in one sense we are a secret society, yet strictly speaking we are not
really a secret society. We have no secret aims or constitutions; the objects we
have in view are open to the world ; our regulations may be obtained by anyone,
and all our members are as free to leave as they must be to join. There has been
too much mystery made over the cemmunity, for, unleBS it is directlv or indirectly
with the way we know each other in any part of the irlobe, by night or by day,
knowing or not knowing the languagll, and when meeting utter strangers, we have
no secrets. In fact, it might almost be said that the actual secret of our Freemasonry is that there is none."
Now, is there, as a matter of fact, anything in our ceremony of installing officers that demands secrecy? If the opportunity is given, once in a while, to permit
our families to know that we are engaged only in laudable work and for laudable
ends, the interest in the home circle will be mutual, as to the calling the attention
of the one who is a brother in that' family to the Lodge night and a request of his
attention to the Lodge dubies. Are we not justified in believing that much of the
objection that we hear from good. wives and daughters to husbands and brothers
attending Lodge assemblies arises from the fact that they have neither knowledge
nor information of the noble deeds for which the Masonic Craft is banded together?

Masonry has progressed. Lodges long dorma!lt have been aroueed and the general

We are convinced that this condition of alfairs should uo longer exist, and that

a be'nellt and obtain the good results of a visit and instruction from a Grand.Officer.

necessary, and to visit each Lodge in the j orisdiction at least once in two years ; sud

Bro. WILLIAx CALDWJllLL Bl!ILCHEB, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following rep<?rts:To the M.·. W. •• Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :. Relative to a communication from the Grand Master of Pennsylvania, announcmg his withdrawal of his Representative near this Grand Lodge.
Bro. ATKINSON, a member of this committee and a Past Grand Maeter of this
Grand Lodge, has been received by us and reported in our proceedings, since ,tbe
date of his appointment in 1889, as the Representative of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, and not until this communication, addressed tQ our Grand Master was
placed in our hands, had we the slightest suspicion that he was, in fact, onl; the
'
·
Representative of a Grand Master.
We have before us the printed proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania
for 1891, and on page 67 we find that at the Annual Communication, held on the
28th of December of that year, the following Pa•t Grand Mast_ers of Pennsylvania
are reported present as Grand Representatives of oth6' Grand Lodges: SAMUEL
C. PBIUilNS of :he Grand Lodge of Canada, M!CHAl!'L NISBET of the Grand Lodge
of North Carolma, CONRAD P. DAY of the Grand Lodge of Ohio, Jo@EPH ErnHliAUlll
of the Grand Lodge of New Brunswick, and CLIFFORD P. MAoCALiiA of the Grand
Lodge of Michigan; and that the Grand Maeter, his Deputy, Wardens and Treae.
urer were also reported present as Grand Representatives-the Grand Master, Bro.
J. i'IIMPSON Al'RIOA, of Missouri and New Hampshire, the Deputy, Mrna:All:L
ARNOLD, of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas, the 8enior Grand Warden, MAl'l'mAS H.
HBNDBRSON, of the Grand Lodge of Indiana, the Junior Grand Warden, WILiiIAM
J. KuLY, of the Grand Lodge of Arizona, and the Grand Treasurer, Ta:OMAS R.
PA~N, of the Grand Lodge of England. And in the same volume, at page 129,
we find the name of our Bro. ATKINSON given as the Representative of the Grand
Lodge of Pennsylvania to the Grand Lodge of California. We have also before us
the proceedings of that Grand Lodge for 1889. In his Address for that year (page
111) Grand Master MAOCALLAsaid: "During the past year I have commiBSioned
the following named brethren ae Representatives of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania near other Grand Lodges: Bro. EDMUND CLBlllENT ATIONSON near the
Grand Lodge of California," and fourteen others near other Grand Lodges. At
that Annual Communication the four Past Grand Masters present were reported
ae Grand Representatives, Past Grand Master VAUX heading the list as Representative of New York.
We do not kuow, nor do we at this time care to inquire, for what reason the
system of Represent;i.tives was adopted, but we do kuow that it bas been very generallv adopted and hae been in use for more than thirty years. In the revision of
our own Constitution, proposed in 1857 and adopted in 1859, among the enumerated r><>~ers ~nd duties of t~e Grand MO:Ster we find this: "9th. To appoint Representatives ID other recogmzed Grand Lodlfes, and to receive and accredit .such
Representatives from them." In the last revision this provision reads: "To ap-

1893.J

Grand, Lodge of California.

237

point Representatives near other recognized Grand Lodges, and to receive and
accredit Representatives from them." From this it is apparent that, in California
at least, t-he power to appoint and receive Representatifes bas been vested in our
Grand Master, but that his appointees are Representatives of the Grand Lodge
and not of the Grand Maeter, and that bis authority to receive and accredit is
limited to the Representatives from other Grand Lodges.
Grand Master ARNOLD, in hie communication, gives as a reason for withdrawing his Representatives near other Grand ·Maeters that "official communication
between the several Grand Masters is carried on directly with each other, under
their private seals or by and through the Grand Secretaries under the seal of the
Grand Lodge; and the promptness of such communication is so well secured by
railroads, posts and telegraphs, that the Representative of the Grand Master has
no official duty to perform.'' ·
Our government bae an Ambassador at the Court of St. James, and .the British
government also keeps its Ambaesador near our government, and through these
Ambassadors the official correspondence of the two governments is conducted. Our
President might, under bis private seal, communicate directly with Queen VIOTORIA,
and it is probable that his communications by mail or telegraph would reach her
quite as promptly ae if made through the proper representative of our govemment
at the Queen's Court. Yet the fact that the President could communicate directly
with the Queen bas not been considered by Congress or by the President a good
reason for withdrawing our Ambassador from the English Court. Every political
government is careful that all its "official correspond_enoe" be transmitted through
ts accredited representatives, and not directly by its executive head.
Grand Master ARNOLD finds that bis Representatives have become "auperftuous and unnecessary," and we imagine that the reaeon is -that he, and perhaps
hie predecessors as the chief executive officers of the Grand Lodge, have practically
ianored the existence of these Representatives and have, in the face of the custom
prevailing in all political governments, assumed to themselves the right to carry
on all <ffficial correspondence with other Grand Bodies and their officers by direct
communication by telegraph, express or mail. The fault is not with the Representatives, who are ready, willing and competent to attend to the proper duties of
their office1 but is and has been with Grand Masters who, like our dietin1,'1lished
brother of Pennsylvania, seem to think that they can not only conduct and trans·
mit official correspondence more satisfactorily, but can manage negotiatiQDe, involving even the most delicate matters, with better results than anybody else
could.
The system of appointing Representatives has been adopted by all the Grand
Lodges of the world, so far as we are advised, and has been recognized by all for
more than a third of a century; hence, when it is proposed to abolish this eatablished svat.em, we do not so much consider what good it has accomplished as what
it might do under different conditions. Referring our Most Worshipful brother to
the parable of the fig tree, we would say to him, give these Representatives a
chance to do the work appropriate t o their office before abOlishing the office.
In reply to the communication, we would say our Bro. ATKINSON wae received
by us ae the Representative of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, with which we
have maintained, and hope ever to maintain, the closest relations of amity. While
we recognize the fact that communication is well secured and reasonably prompt
by railroad; poet and telegraph; and that official communications between Grand
Lodges are and have been very largely carried on by the Grand Masters and tr1111&mitted directl;y, we are of opinion that there are appropriate duties to be performed

To the M. •. W. •. Grand. Lodge of California :your Committee on Finances, to whom was referred the resolution offered by
Past Grand Master RuoKEB, that the Grand Lodge appropriate one thousand dollars to aid in the construction ot a. monument to our deceased brother, Past Grand
Master LEONIDAS E. PRATT, have considered the same, and beg leave to report
that through the liberality of the subordinate Lodges and individual brethren, a
fund for this purpose has been raised, which now amounts to the sum of $fl03.
While we deem this amount insufficient to erect a very elaborate or imposing monument, we yet are inclined to believe that the sum can be increased sufficiently to
accomplish the object desired without intrenching upon the treasury of the Grand

Lodie.

We yield to no one the high estimate of the character, the ability and the valuable and distinguished service which our deceased brother poBBessed and rendered
to this Grand Body and to the world at large, yet we cannot consent to the finances
of the Grand Lodge being perverted from their legitimate purpose of extending
charity to the Iivin~ to attest our admiration for the dead. Past Grand Master
PRATT has builded his own monument in the love which hie Masonic brethren had
for him while Iiving, and dying he has left to us a rich heritage of the great work
which he did, and the appreciation of which is so thoroughly imbued in the mind
of his brethren that the memory of his great works, and the affection which they
entertain for him, will live long after any monument which we might rear over hie
remains shall have crumbled to duet. We therefore offer the following resolution:Ruolved, That the Grand Secretary be requested to again appeal, through the
subordinate Lodges of the jurisdiction, to the individuals composing their membership to exert their liberality, by making such contributions as they may be able
to give in increaeinir the "Pratt Monument Fund;" and that all donations be forwarded to the Grand Secretary.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Your committee have considered the action recommended by the Committee
on Report of Grand Lecturer, heretofore referred to this committee, and, while
in full sympathy .with the opinidne expressed therein as to the good results to flow
from a more active and constant supervision of the ritualistic work of our jurisdiction by that officer, respectfully submit that the adoption of the resolution referred to them is, in the opinion of the Finance Committee, impracticable in the
present state of the treasury with the accepted demands of the ensuing year.
We refer to the fact that while the adoption of our system of inspection was
euppoeed to be a succel!llful attempt to eo divide the expenses of a complete supervision of the work that the burden thereof would be but a moderate tax upon our
resources, your committee experience a constantly increasing pressure to add to
the expense of continuing the system. We fully appreciate the necessity of keeping our work in full accord with the adopted method, but we submit to the Grand
Lodge that we see no neceBBity for a constant.Iy increasing tax for ite support, We
believe the Grand Lecturer receives at present, from the several sources in which
hie services are made available by the Grand Lodge, Huch compensation as it can

1893.]

afford to appropriate for that purpose, and we recommend that the present compensation of the Grand Lecturer be continued for the coming year, and that he be
required to present with his report to the next Grand Lodge an itemized account
of his expenses.
We therefore recommend that the resolution submitted by the Committee of
Inspectors on the Rewrt of the Grand Lecturer, fixing the salary of that officer
for the coming year at $2,500, be not adopted.
Your committee have examined the report of the Masonic Board of Relief of
San Jose, California, and find they have expended for the relief of destitute
brethren the sum of $207.30. We also find that in the year 1883, Bro, JOHN
CHAPMAN, a member of Eacurfai Lodge, No. 7, F. and A. M., Virginia City, Nevada, removed to San Jose with hie family, consisting of his wife and two children.
That Bro. CHAPMAN was seriously injured by an accident in a mine in Virginia
City, Nevada, which incapacitated him from doing any labor. That said Eacuriai
Lodge, No. 7, F. and A. M., dimitted Bro. CHAPHAN, soon After his removal irom
the jurisdiction of Eacuriai Lodge, whether upon his own request or not we are
not informed. That since the year 1883, he and his family have been a charge
upon the Board of Relief of San Jose, and that up to the present time the Board
ot Relief have contributed to his widow and orphans, he havi!lg died some time
since, the sum of Sl,752.00, and at the present time the widow and the two orphan
children being in delicate health, are yet a charge upon the Board of Relief of San
Jose. That in consequence of the · numerous calls for charity upon said Board,
thev are unable to continue their contributions without &SBietance from this Grand
Lodge. Your committee therefore offer the following resolution and recommend
its adoption:.Ruolved, That the sum of one hundred and eighty dollars be and the same is
hereby appropriated from the general fund of this Grand Lodge to the Masonic
Board of Relief of San Jose, California, to enable them to continue their contributions for the relief of the said widow and orphans.
