Bro. WILLIAM C. BELOBEB, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following report:To the M. '. W. '. Grana Lodge of Calijwnia :Relative to an amendment to the Constitution prohibiting electioneering for
office and the sending out of circulars intended to secure influence in favor of or
against measures or matters to b& brought before the Grand Lodge.
Bro. JAMES WRIGHT ANDERSON proposes a new regulation, intended to preserve
the purity of our elections and the integrity of our legislation, and asks the Grand
Lodge to declare, as a part of its fundamental law, that the sending out of circulars, with the purpose of soliciting and securing votes in favor of or a~ainst any
proposition or measure to be brought before the Grand Lodge for action, and electioneering for office in any way, are improper and unmasonic, and that any persou
found guilty of electioneering in Grand Lodge or a subordinate Lodge shall be
removed from office if be bold one and shall be ineligible to any office in the future.
There is no recital, by way of preamble, to this new regulation that any Lodge
or Mason within the jurisdiction bas resorted to improper solicitations to secure
votes for office or to Influence the action of tbill body upon any matter, yet we are
advised by the Grand Master that some one of our Lodges bas, during the last
year, sent out circulars to the other Lodges, soliciting their influence in favor of
the adoption of a resolution to be introduced, and which bas been, in fact, introduced at this session, permitting Lodges to use a part of their revenue for "social
purposes.,,
.
And it is fresh in the recollection of many of those present that on the first day
of the session in 1889 the members found in their chairs and on their tabl09 a circular soliciting their votes in favor of a resolution to be proposed at that session.
This year the resolution was offered on behalf of Tuolumne Lodge, No. 8, and
we are advised that the.circular referred to by the Grand Master was issued and
circulated by that Lodge. It was in regard to the use of the Lodge funds for
social purposes, that i11, for refreshments and entertainments-a subj~t upon
which the Grand Lodge, directly and indirectly, has many times taken action, and
always adverse to such nse, or to any use, except for payment of the legitimate
expenses of the Lodge and for calls of charity,
In 1853 the expenditure complained of was for jewels to be presented to retiring officers. In 1872 it was, in one case, for the expenses of organizing a Chapter
or Lodge of 1ome side degree; in another, for hiring carriages to take members
and their families to a plaee of entertainment; and in still another, foi:: a supper
or entertainment to retiring and newly installed officers. These were brought to
the attention of the Grand Lodge by Grand Master P!IATT in his Address. In

252

Procoodin<JB of the

[Oct. 13,

1876 it was for an entertainment to newly installed officers, by Woodb~e Lodge,
~o. 131, and the matter was brought to the attention of Grand Lodge by the proteet of a member of that Lodge. In 1887 it was for an entertainment to newi'Y in.
stalled officers and their friends, by <Jl,ay Lodge, No. 101, and was brought to the
attention of Grand Lodge in the Addrees of Grand Master RUCKER, who had arrested the charter of that Lodge for a willful attempt to evade and disregard the
rule adopted by Grand Lodge, by inducing the Senior Warden to pay the bill and
afterwards voting to bestow the same amount upon him as a charity. And again
in 1892 upon a reeolution introduced to authorize Lodges to use five per cent. of
th!lir revenue for refreshments. We caBnot therefore even suggest as an excuse
that this circular was sent out for the purpose of beinging a new matter to the
attention of the Lodges. We can understand that it may be important to advise
the Lodges of some new matter, to give them an opportunity to consider it ; but
whenever this shall become necessary or proper the information should be given
by direction of the Grand Master or Grand' Lodge and through the Grand Secretary.
Our proceedings show that as long ago as 1868 these evils had appeared in our
midst, for in that year Bro. MELVIN J. GILKICY proposed, and the Grand Lodge
adopted, the following resolution :Reaolved, That it is the opinion of this Grand Lodge that cauCUBill/t or electioneerina- to_influence the votes of membef!l !>f Grand Lodge In the elect1on of Grand
Officers._ 1s contrary to the letter !"nd spmt <?f M_asonry, and that we disapprove of
conventions or other local or sect1onal combmat10ne to affect the legislation of the
Grand Lodge or to secure election to office.

This was an expression of opinion, but it was doubtless thought to be, and
ought to have been, sufficient to have ' prevented any further offending. That
opinion has been many time11 disregarded since that date, and we fear that some of
our brethren have learned the ways of politicians and would introduce those ways
into our Order, and if thev can be persuaded to desist only by the strong hand of
penal statutes, then we must Invoke the aid of such statutes. The evil is intolerable and, if wholesome advice is not heeded, we must have recourse to something
more efficient, something that will be efficient.
In the Grand Lodge of England a decided expression of opinion seems to have
been sufficient. There, in 1888, the Board of General Purposes was informed that
a candidate for Grand Treasurer who was, at the time of the meeting of Grand
Lodge, sick and unable to leave hie house, had sent invitations to members to call
and take luncheon w.ith him. The Board reported the matter to Grand Lodge,
which unanimously adopted this resolution :That t~ Gran~ Lodge emphatically condemns any entertainment or other inducement given to mfluence membera by any candidate in Grand Lodge.
A like resolution was adopted by the Grand Lodge of MiBBouri in 1877, with
like effect. It is plain, however, that with us, as with our friends in Kentucky,
resolutions of condemnation have not proved effectual, and that it is incumbent
upon us to make such a new regulation as will immediately stop these disreputable
practices. We call them disreputable advisedly, because to us it seems disreput able for an aspirant for office in an Order like ours, by circulars or personal can.
vass, to publish his own peculiar qualifications and fitness for office and solicit the
influence or votes of others to secure office for him, even if, in such circulars and
such canvass, he avoids villifying the character of hie competitors. The practice,
if permitted, will surely lead to serious trouble, and it ought not to be permitted
at all We thoroughly approve the purpose of the new regulation proposed by
Bro. ANDERSON, but think that the penal provisions should be still more stringent

just how much more. We therefore recommend that the matter be referred to our
successors, to be reported upon at the next Annual Communi~tion of the Grand
Lodge.

Bro. Emnnro CLEMENT ATXINSON, froni the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following report :To the M. •• W. •• Grand Lodge of CuJ,iflYl'iiW. :-

Bro. HENBY .A KELLEB, of P~ Lodge, No. 178, presented a resolution at the
last Annual Communication proposing to amend Section 8, Article III, Part III,
of the Constitution, by striking out the word "fifty," in the second line of said
section, and inserting in its stead the word "thirty." If it should be so amended,
the fil'llt clause of that section would read as follows :Section 8. No Lodge within this juriediction shall confer the three deg~ of
Masonry for a lees sum than thirty dollars (instead of fifty).
Similar amendments to this section of the Constitution have been offered at
different times since the Communication of 1878, when ~ro. NELSON R. SHAW
proposed an amendment fixing the minimum fee at thirty dollars. Thia amendment was rejeeted in the succeeding year. At the Annual. Communication of
1879 Bro. FRANOIS E. BAKER propoeed a similar amendment, which was rejected
in the following year. In 1886 Bro. SAMUEL GUTHRIE proposed an amendment
fixing the minimum fee at fwty doll.ara, which amendment was also rejected. In
1890 an amendment fixing the minimum fee at thirty dollars was offered, and again
the Grand Lodge rejected the proposed reduction. Notwithstanding the repeated
action of the Grand Lodge on this same proposition, the committee a.re again asked
to take the matter under consideration. We have done so, but fa.ii to find in the
arguments of those who have favored this constantly recurring proposition anything which convinces us that it would be wise to favor the proposed reduction
of feee, It has been claimed that as the section now reads, the fee is beyond the
means of many who desire to receive the degrees of Masonry. Would it not be as
reasonable to suppose that the ea.me· persons would find, after having received the
degrees, that the Lodge dues were also above and beyond their means? We fear
that such would be the case. We observe that the champions of this standing
reaolution are usually anxious to reduce Lodge dues, and also to appropriate the
funds of the Lodge for purposes of refreshment. Your committee believe that the
sacred fund which is devoted to charitable purposes should be most carefully
guarded. We therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
All which Is respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM CALDWELL BELCHER,
EDMUND CLEHRNT ATKTNBON,

AMENDMENT
TO THE

CONSTITUTION OF THE GRAND LODGE.
Adopted l~th October, 1893.
ARTICLE III.
OF THE GRAND TBll:ASUBll:B,

SJ«JTION L It shall be the duty of the Grand Treasurer:
let. To receive all moneys belonging to the Grand Lodge from the Grand
Secretary; to give him duplicate receipts therefor; and to keep in proper books a
just account thereof; and, from time to time, immediately upon the receipt of said
moneys, to deposit the same to the credit of the Grand Lodge, in some hank or
hanks selected by the first three officers of this Grand Lodge. When a depol!it is
so made, a duplicate deposit tag shall be immediately transmitted by the Grand
Treasurer to the Grand Maater. The money shall be withdrawn from the bank
only on checks, drafts, or orders signed by the Grand Master (or Deputy Grand
Master) and Grand Treasurer.
2d. To take charge of all other property of the Grand Lodge, except as provided in Sec. 1, Art. IV, of this Part, and keep an accurate account thereof; whenever any such property coneiete of bonds, or other evidences or securities for debt,
the same shall be deposited in some bank or Safe Deposit Company's vaults selected, as provided in subdivision one of thi11 section; and shall only be withdrawn
from such depository on the written order of the Grand Master and Grand
Treasurer.
Amend subdivision 4th of Section 1, Article IV, so that the same shall read as
follows:4th. To collect all moneys due to the Grand Lodge, keep a correct account
thereof in proper books, and pay the said money within ten days after ite receipt
to the Grand Treasurer.

The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge, as follows:BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE : -

Jn the revolving year the day has again arrived for the stated Communication
of our Grand Lodge, and I greet you at its forty-fifth occurrence, to measure the
progress of the past year and to deliberate upon the present condition and needs
of our jurisdiction.
In performinjl' this duty we but continue the lessons of the past and but emulate
tho example 'of the teachers whom .:e have succeeded. Men die, but human life
flows on like a river, as it has in ages jl'One by and will continue during the brief
term of our existence. Let us then faithfully perform the duties of life and ask of
our Heavenly l<'ather such strength as shall enable us to do His work to the end.
Organized as was our Grand Lodge in the pioneer year of the history of our
State, our Body is coeval with the present epoch, and we may confidently expect
its progress to be parallel with the destiny of the commonwealth.
It is a subject for congratulation that, thoUfl'h the business interests of California have suffered a great depression during the past year, our Order has maintained
its general prosperity, not having been involved in the political and industrial
questions which have agitated the public. By a strict adherence to the ancient
landmarks and the established tenets of our profession we avoid the storms which
wreck other societies, and continue unabated our works of benevolrnce.
We should not be unmindful that ambitious men in certain foreign countries
have heretofore sought to pervert our Order from its legitimate purposes of social
brotherhood and charity, to political intrigue, and that the result has always been
disastrous to Freemasonry.

530

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 9,

In religion we have always refused to be sectarian, and religious zealots have
charged us with being irreligious. No accusation could be more unjust, as numerous devout men of various creeds who are found among us can testify, and the open
Bible upon the altar of every Lodge, and the invocation to Peity in our ceremonies
Bil\'Dify the religious spirit which animates the Fraternity of Free and Accepted
Masons.
I have alluded to the fact that this Grand Lodge is coeval with our State in
organization. It is historical that Freemasonry was established .in this country
early in the Colonial period. Most cif the noted personages in the great events of
our country's history, up to the present time, have been members of our Society.
Let it not be forgotten that Masonry, while it is the most ancient of the social
organizations of mankind and the most influential, is qualified by the distinctiv!l
word "Free," and stands for toleration in the great questions which divide the
minds of men. It aims not to govern opinion, and it steadfastly resU.ts coercion
on all Rides. On the other band, it professes and enforces adherence to the moral
law, which binds civilized mankind in a common brotherhood. We stand, therefore, on a platform broad enough to. hold all good men, but let us remember that
those who are to be of us must come of their own accord and not by our solicitation. Our precepts are not proclaimed from the rostrum, pulpit, housetops or
streets, but should be exemplified in our daily life and conduct according to the
words of Holy Writ: "Behold bow good and bow pleasant it is for brethren to
dwell together in unity."
Trusting that the proceedings of this Commnuication, now opening, may be guided
and governed by the familiar principles of our Order, I will now call your attention
to the various topics connected with the discharge of the duties of my office during
the past year. It is with much satisfaCtion that I.am enabled to report to you the
healthy condition of the jurisdiction. From all reports received by me I am able
to assure you that harmony prevails among the Craft, and that no contention exists
among our households, except the creditable rivalry-in striving to exemplify, by a
faithful and efficient performance of duty, the sublime tenets of Freemasonry.
The reports of our Inspectors, while not showing a rapid increase of membership, as was the case in former days, clearly establish the fact that no baiting steps
are impeding the thorough e&tablishment and onward marcli of this great Fraternity. This fact is shown in an increased interest, by our Inspectors, in those
matters, which it has been alleged obstruct 'ts growth and binder its prosperity.
It is true that.the net increase of the last is less than that of preceding years, and
as a reason it bas been suggested to me that our lines of legislation were perhaps
too consehative, and that we adhere to the stringent laws and regulations of our
earlier years with perhaps more zeal than wisdom. It has been suggested to me
that to deserve prosperity a more' liberal policy should prevail.
The exaction of an affiliation fee is thought by many to be a principal factor in
causing the great evil of non-affiliation, as not only contrary to the spirit and pros·
parity of the iustitution, but a direct incentive to non-affiliation. We recognize
the duty of affiliation, but we refuse to grant membership except by the same
method that we obtained admission to the Fraternity. An unaffiliated brother
stands in precisely the same position as the profane, so far as the rights and
benefits of Lodge membership are concerned. It is proper that a brother who bas
once passed the ballot should never again be subjected to its ordeal, unleBB be
bas been suspended or expelled for unmasonic conduct. I know of several good
and true Masons who are non·alfiliated because of repeated rejections. This
ought not to be. Any Mason of go.od report, and coming well recommended,

should be permitted to affiliate with the Lodge of bis choice, or charges should
be preferred against him and bis status determined on a trial by bis brethren.
Another suggestion in the same line is the abolition of any regulation which bas
been enacted, restricting the Lodges from using their funds in such manner as they
may determine, after performing their duties of charity and all payments to
Grand Lodge, and incidental Lodge expenses for salaries, etc. Thia opens up the
matter of refreshments, incidentally, and more directly the important question of
what is the source of life and power in our beloved institution : ·the Grand Lodge,
or individual membership, as expreBSed through the constituent Lodges. When a
government becomes a burden, a people do not hesitate to throw it off.
The Master and officers of a Lodge ought to be personally acquainted with
every member of the Lodge. In some countries, I understand, the Lodges are
limited to a membership of one hundred, and they are allowed by their by-laws to
expend a certain amount of their funds at stated times for refreshments and social
purpoSeB. One Inspector in this State, in his report, says "that he cannot dwell
too strongly upon the absolute neceBSity of each Lodge having the power to expend
a portion of its funds for social purposes." From close observation in bis own dis.
trict, be is certain that the noticeable lack of interest in Lodge affairs displayed by
the members, is due solely to the absence of sociability. Each Lodge should be.
permitted to expend a certain per cent. of its income for social purposes; first,
however, deducting the amount of the running expenses, including the demands of
charity. A gradual maximum amount could be established so as to cover the
different grades of Lodges, which would serve to prevent the jeopardizing of the
Charity Fund.
He added, it is ~ell known that there are Lodges in thiij State which are yearly
accumulating wealth to the amount of thousands of dollars, who are talcing generous care of their widows and orphans, but ·the members of which are only
represented to the extent of thirteen per ctmt. at the degree meetings.
If a portion of this money could ~ expended for entertainment, not necessarily eating and drinking, but musical entertainments, lectures on Masonic and
scientific subjects, art and the topics of the day, intereat in the Order would, I
think, be enhanced, and our officers would not be neglecting their Masonic duties
for those of other orders, Rimply because the latter offer more entertainment.
This is a serious point, and I hope the Grand Lodge will give it very careful
attention and study, for during my term of office the matter bas come before me
from nearly every section of the State.

Since our last annual session the Masone of California have experienced a double
sorrow in the loss, by death, of their oldest and youngest Past Grand Masters.
Of the elder, Bro. JONATHAN D. STBVBNSON, who was witness of the creation
of this Grand Lodge, and who was chosen by his brethren as their firat Grand
Master in the year 181l0, we need only say here that, ae it pleased the Great Creator
to grant our brother a length of days reached by few, we record our teetimonv that
be was faithful to the trusts reposed in him in all the years uf hie eventful life.
Bro. STBVBNSON was born on the first day of January, 1800, and died at his
home in this city, February 14, 1894. He was made a Mason in Plu1miz Lodge,
New York City, in the year 1821. Hie Masonic age at the time of his death was
seventy-two years and three months.
Bro. EDWIN A. SHERMAN, Secretary of the Masonic Veteran Association of the
Pacific Coast, in writing a sketch of the life of Bro. STKVBNSON for the "Trestle
Board" of this city, says:-

•

To attempt to write the biography of California's first Grand Master of Masons
would require volumes, because it would embrace the history of the United States
for the period of a century, for the story of his life is so interwoven with that of
our common country and its most distinguished men and statesmen, that in a brief
sketch it would be utterly impossible to telescope or condense the history of eo remarkable and well knqwn character as that of Colonel JONATHAN DRAKE STEVBNBON.

In entire acc9rd with this opinion of Bro. BHBBMAN, I am content with this
simple announcement of the death of our venerable brother, leaving the biograph·
ical sketch of his eventful and useful life for the Committee on Necrology to present
for your consideration.
Of bis funeral, the same brother says :It was worthy of the man and the occasion, and the group of nearly one bundi;ed silver-haired members of the Masonic Veteran's Association of the Pacific
Coast, as they gathered around the Grand Master on that memora.ble d:oy, attested
their regard for the memory and history of nearly a hundred years that bad been
bound up in his life, nearly four-.fiftbs of which had been spent among the Craft,
and whose civil and military character was so eloquently portrayed by the Grand
Orator of the occ:!asion, Bro. WILLIAM H. L. BABNBB, who was lost in bis theme,
captivating all who listened to his matchless paneicyric and eulogy of the Masonic,
civil and military life of this eminent America~ citizen.

Brother GRITMAN was born in Providence, Rhode Island, in 1838. He was a
graduate of Yale College, a veteran of the civil war, and since that period a banker
by profession, being at the time of his death Cashier or the Bank of Napa.
Brother GRITHAN was made a Mason In 1865, in Manhattan Lodge, of New York
City. He was a member of the Finance Committee, and its Chairman, in Grand
Lodge, from 1866 to 1839. After serving as Senior Grand Warden and Depnty Grand
Master, he was elected Grand Master In 1892.

no trials or sorrows. Until then, dear brother, good·by."

DECISIONS,
Nearly every principle of Masonic law, simple as well 11a abstruse, haa come before
me for adjudication. The greater number of the qnestions raised are folly answered
in ANDEBSON's Digest, and I shall malr:e no fnrther reference to them. If that nsefnl •
work were oftener consulted by the Lodge officers, the standard of Masonie intelli·
gence would be measurably increased, and the rontine labors of the Grand Master
greatly lessened.
Not long ago the Grand Mast.er of a sister jnrisdiction facetiously remarked that,
jndglng from the great number of simple qnestlons that were asked him, he came to
the conclusion that many of them were prompted by a desire to obtain the Grand
Master's autograph. My own experience teaches me that in Oalifornia many of the
Lodges are affiicted with the same disease, for the slightest familiarity witli Masonic
law or practice wonld, in most cases, make the qnestions nnnecessary.

Question. Please inform me of my duty in regard to a non-affiliate who took
his dimit from this Lodge some four years ago, has not paid dues for more than a
year, is living in this jurisdiction and was present at the conferring of the third
degree?
Answer. On the broad ground of Masonic charity, without evidence to the
contrary, I shall assume that the brother had made some proper effort to affiliate·
with some Lodge and had been rejected. If he had ma.de such effort within six
months, it would operate to keep him in good standing, and while in good standing
he is of course entitled to the privileges of the Order. But, on the other hand, if
he h118 not made a proper effort to affiliate with some Lodge, within six months
previous to his visiting a Lodge, he is by operation of law in the same position as
a Mason suspended for non.payment of dues, and is not entitled to "any of the
rights and J>rivileges or charities of the Order." If, while in this 'COndition, he
visits a Lodge, he lays himself liable to have charges preferred against him. for
visiting a Lodl!'e while he was under Masonic disability. You must not permit
any Mason to visit your Lodge who is not in "good standing."

In Oriental Lodge, No. l«, objection was made to the advancement of an Entered
Apprentice. Under Section 6, .Article HI, Part III, of the Constitution, the Master
appointed a committee to investigate the cause of the objeotion. At the next
stated meeting tht> committee reported that the cu.nee of objection was alleged
membership in a certain church, and that the objection was not a valid Me.sonic one.
The evidence taken by the committee appeared in the report. The Master pr0
tem. ordered a ballot taken upon the report, which ballot resnlted in the rejeo·
tion of the report. The Master then ruled that the objection was sustained, and
ordered the fee for the remaining degrees to be returned to the brother. From this
ruling, e.nd from the action of the Master in ordering a ballot upon the report, the
committee appealed.
Decision. I hold that, upon the reading of the committee's report to the Lodge,
disclosing as ii does the nature of the objection and the testimony taken, the Master
sbonld have confirmed the findings of the committee, and if no other objections
were offered, he should have proceeded with the examination and passing of the
brother. It therefore follows that the ordering-of a ballot upon the question ofadopting
or rejecting the committee's report was unwarranted, and the action or the Lodge
in snstaining the objection to the advancement or the brother is null and void, and
for these reasons: The report of the committee shows very clearly that the sole ob•
jeotion to the advancement of the brother is his alleged membership in a particular
religious denomination. Now, other than a belief in a Snpreme Being, there is no
religious qualll!cat!ous for 'membership In the Me.sonic Order. An objection to ad·
vancement, based on a brother's religious afllliatlon, is therefore not a. valid objec·
tion, and is not such a.n objection a.sis to be determined by the Lodge under Section
6, Article III, Part III, of the Constitution.
It is not an objection that a Lodge can entertain in any form, and no ballot of
any kind should be ta.ken upon it. Buch an objection is oontrary to, and is forbidden
by the ancient landmarks of the Craft, and also by Section 1166 of the lJecisions of
the Grand Lodge.
Unless objections of a different character be established, the brother Is entitled
to be passed a.nd raised.

DIBTBIOTING THE STATE.
California is a large State. My experience during my term of office has convinced me that if all the Lodges within its boundaries should receive from the
Grand Master the attention they require, more time would bei:onsumed than most
men can give. I· would, therefore, recommend that, without disturbing the present
division of the State into districts, or diminishing the duties or the number of the
present Inspectors, the Deputy Grand Master and the Grand Wardens should be
required to visit the Lodges in those sections of the State where they reside, and
report to the Grand Master any recommendations they see proper. This would
take some of the burden from the shoulders of the Grand Master ; it would also
familiarize the Grand Officers with the workings of the different Lodges, and the
experience so obtained would be of great assistance to them afterwards, should
they themselves become Grand Masters.

PBYBIOAL DBFEOTS.
The question of physical defect that is now agitating so many of our sister jnris·
dictions keeps coming to the front in California. There have been many appllca·
tions where the defect bas been slight, and the applicants would have been a credit
and an honor to the Craft, yet 1 have not felt that I could construe the law so as to
admit them. I have in every snob case held that an applicant must he physically
perfect to entitle him to the degrees. In some cases the defect has been so slight
that it bas seemed hardly to be a defect at all, and I refused with reluctance, bnt
my understanding of the law left me no other course. Onr law Is positive, and will
admit of but one construction,

THE NATIONAL HOME FOR CoNSUHPTIVES.
In May I received a "Memorial to the Masonic Brethren in the United States
of America and Canad&," from Montezuma Lodge, No. 1. at Santa Fe, New Mexico,
under the sanction of the Grand Master of New Mexico, in regard to the establishment of a "National Masonic Home for Consumptives" at Santa Fe, requesting
my approval of the undertaking, and asking permission to lay the plans before the
subordinate Lodges of the Order in California for subscription. It is intended
that the Home, when completed, shall be managed and controlled by Masons, and
that, whenever practicable, Masone only shall he employed in every position connected with the institution. It is estimated that the number of consumptives
seeking Santa Fe in search of health is about 2,500, and the number is every year
increasing, and that many of them.are members of our Fraternity. The citizens
of Santa Fe have pledged themselves to donate one hundred acres of land, and
more if required.
I replied that, as a medical man and a Mason, I was in favor of the movement
and would bring the subject before our Grand Lodge. for such action as it might
see proper to take; bot as Grand Master at this time I could not consent that appJi.
cation be made to our Lodges for subscriptions, for the reason that we are now
severely taxing them ourselves to establish in California a "Masonic Widows' and
Orphans' Home," and that the officers c;>f our Grand Lodge would discountenance
the aubacribinll' of any money by our subordinate Lodges as proposed, until our
own Home shall be completed and paid for. It is a worthy project, and I submit
the matter for any action you may deem proper.

total sum of $39,315.08. Of this sum, from the date of our first organization in
1891 up to the present time, we have expended the following amounts:·

The tract of land at Decoto, consisting of 267.46 acres, has been fully paid for
and deeded to the Trustees. The deed has been recorded and filed with the Treasurer of this Board.
Owing to the financial depression now prevailing over the country, and other
important reasons, this Board has refrained from making any further improvements or expenditures than were necessary to meeto the obligations that were
incurred previous to our last annual report, and the payment of the incidental
expenses of the Board. A question having arisen as to the availability of the
present site for the Home, in consequence of the lack of adequate water supply,
and for other reasons, the Board has now under consideration the advisability of
selling the present site and purchasing a more suitable one.
With returning business prosperity, and after the payment of the balance of
the subscriptions, your Board of Trustees hope to be able to p~secute their work
vigorously, and eventually to erect a Home which shall be a blessing to its inmates
and a credit to Masonic liberality.
All which is respectfully submitted.
E. M. PRESTON, President.

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to Grand Lodge,
as follows :- '
To the M. '. W. •• Grand Lodge of Oalijurnia:In accordance with a regulation of the Grand Lodge, I herewith submit a
report of my official acts as Grand Lecturer during the past year.
Immediately after my installation in October last, I commenced the instruction
of Inspectors and officers of the different Lodges who applied to me for that
purpose•
I have also visited a number of Masonic Districts, examined the Inspectors, and
given instruction to the officers therein. In every instance my reception was
kind, courteous and fraternal.
On November 19th, 1893, I visited Mil.si.on Lodge, No. 169. The third degree
was conferred in an able manner by the officers of that Lodge.
On November.21st, 1893, I visited Ori,ent,al Lodge, No. 144. The third degree
was conferred, and the work executed in a most satisfactory manner.
·

wa~ conferred in a most commendable manner.

In addition to the visits already chronicled, I have given instruction to the
Inspectors of the several Districts, and officers of different Lodges, who have
called upon me for that purpose.
I have received reports from Inapectors within the Jurisdiction as follows:Inspector JoHl!I MARVIN MELENDY, of the First District, reports the five
Lodges therein to be so nearly correct in rendering the work that there is very
little occasion for complaint. All of the Lodges are in a healthy condition, financially and otherwise. The books are neatly and accurately kept, and peace and
harmony prevail among the brethren.
Inspector CHARLES WILBUR NUTTING, of the Second District, reports all the
Lodges in that District to be in a healthy condition, financially and otherwise.
While there have been few accessions, there has been no diminution in the membership. The work throughout the District is performed in a very creditable
manner, and the brethren cherish a true fraternal spirit.

SAN FRANCISOO.
To the M. ·• W. •• (}rand Lodge of California and the Officers and Members of thr
Si:r:teen Lodges of San Fraflcisoo, parties to the Oompact :The undersigned beg leave to present their annual report or the Masonic Board
or Relief of the City of San Francisco for the year commencing on the first day of
October, 1893, and ending on the thirtieth day of September, 1894.
The co.Us for aid npon this Boa.rd of Relief daring the past year have been unprecedented, owing to two cause~. The mercantile and industrial depression, commencing a.boat J'nly, 1893, has thrown thousands in this city oat of employment, and
brought untold misery and distress into famili es which had hitherto never known
wRnt. Our city Lodges have felt the strain, and have nobly responded to calls from
their own members. Tbe gathering of people from all po.rte of the world, expecting
to benefit themselves from oar .Midwinter Fair, an d who failed in their expectations,
bas thrown an unusual number or distressed Masonic brethren upon our hands.
Quite a number have been aided to return to their homes- Egyptia.n and Syrian
brethren among the number. Prior to the industrial depression onr Employment

The demands upon us during the year just pased have been unprecedent in the
history of the Board. Notwithstanding the fact that Lodges, as a rule have stood
loyally by us, and in a isreater measure than ever before returned to us the monies
expended in their behalf, it was found necessary for the Board to either negotiate
a loan of monev or close their work for lack of funds. After due consideration
the Board on June 3d, passed a resolution authorizing the President and Secretary
to negotiate a loan of money on the best terms procurable, of not to exceed
$500.00. Pursuant to this resolution those officers obtained loans aggregating the
sum of $400.00, for which they hold themselves responsible. In view of the above
and also of the constantly increasing size of the City of Los Angeles, as well
as the almoet absolute certainty, that the demands upon us for this coming year
will exceed those of last, the Board would respectfully ask that the Grand Lodge
appropriation to be placed at their disposal be increased to as great an extent as
the funds in the hands of the Grand Lodge and the urgencies of the case will
justify.
We would also report that in the matter of the $73.50 due to the Board from
Mt. Olivet Lodge; No. 3, Parkerkburg, West Virginia, twioe reported to this Grand
Lodge, no further action bas been had.
All which is reapectfully submitted.
T. H. WARD, Pruident.
C. W. BLAKE, Secretwry.

ALA,BAMA.
The Grand Lodge of Alabama held its seventy-third Annual Communication
in the city of Montgomery, December fifth, 1893,-the M. ', W. '. FRANCIS L.
PETTUS, Grand Master, the R. '. W. ', HENRY CLAY ARHSTRONG being Grand
Secretary. There were present five Past Grand Masters, the representatives of
sixteen sister jurisdictions, and the repres~tatives of two hundred and thirty.
seven chartered Lodges.
The Grand Lodge was opened with prayer by the Grand Chaplain, and the
Grand Master delivered bis Annual Address, a very able and elaborate report of
the condition of Masonry in Alabama, which bears conclusive evidence of the
orator's ability not.only to understand and explain the needs of hie jurisdiction,
but records bis able decisions on questions submitted during the recess of the
Grand Lodge. He makes sorrowful reference to the univereal.bueinese depression, but cheers his brethren witli the assurance that as sun follows sun, so must
prosperity succeed adversity. To which we will all respond-so mote it be.
The Grand Master reports the death of three veterans of Masonry in Ala.
bama: Past Grand Masters WILLIAM H. NORRIS and JOSEPH HENRY JOHNSON,
and Worshipful Brother HBNRY CLAY WILEY. Bro. NORRIS (like our Past Grand
Master STJITBNSON) was born in the year 1800, dying, as did our Brother STB·
·vENSON, at the age of 93.

The Grand Master recommended that suitable action be bad to perpetuate the ·

The decisions rendered by the Grand Master are models in their analysis of
the subject considered, and his conclusion (No. 10) we quote a.s an illustration :(10.) The queiltiori wa.s asked me by several different M8sons: "Can a man
who · ha.s lost one arm, and who ba.s been elected Ma.star of ·his Lodge, be legally
installed ? " M.y. answer . to the question wa.s that be could. .How he became a

Master's office which cannot be properly performed by a man who has lost one of
bis arms, but still he is a mPmber of the Lodge in good standing ; he is on a level
with every other member of the Lodge, and I decided that the reasons for not
electing him should address tbemsel ves to the subordinate LoJge before the election. Having been elected and being otherwise qualified, I do not see how he can
be prevented from being installed. This decision was made with much doubt as
to its correctness, and is, so far as my information goes, entirely a novel one; but
I can see no escape from the proposition. How such a man was made a Mason, I
am unable to conceive; and how, having been made a Mason, the Lodge should
have seen fit to elect him a Master, I do not know; but a right of membership
certainly carries with it t.he right to bold office. The attention of the Committee
of Masonic J nrisprudence is respectfully called to this matter.

The Report on Correspondence is by Past Grand Master PALMER J. PILLANS,
Chairman, and is a paper which reftects no discredit upon his distinguished reputation. Bro. PILLANB chronicles a steady progressive growth in the organizations
of the Fraternity, with an increased attention to its principal tenets, manifested
in the erection of homes for the widow and the orphan and organized charity in
general. He gives a review of forty-one Grand Bodies, with the benefit of bis
matured judgment upon their action.
He finds nothing in the proceedings of California to diaapprove, and compliments our Grand Orator, Bro. REUBEN H. LLoYD, on the sentiments expressed
in hie addres•. He quotes liberally therefrom. Bro. PILLANB says "it baa the
true ring," and he selected the following portion which seemed to impress him
with its inftuence upon the welfare and prosperity of the Lodge:On our continent, in the slow progress of time, moralists of a higher pl,.ne
have gradually taken possession of the Order. Under their guidance the social
feature has gradually and slowly been expunged. No more are social dinners and
festivals .Permitted at th!" expense of the Lodge. No more do the Stewards perfol"!D their olden duty ; they go through a recital of what their duties are. but the
mam duty, which brought them into existence, is now considered but rudimentary
and useless, and when the Lodge is called from labor to refreshment, the word
"refreshmen~" is a misnomer.

[Oct. 10,

The idealists have declared the moral principles are too pure to be mingled
or debased by fellowship with the sentiments of the stomach. They do not
believe the feast of reason or the flow of soul brought into play around the dining
table, is anything but an indication of the gratification of the animal part, and,
they_ cry, cannot at all tend to uphold, cement or strengthen any idea of mora.lit:y.
They declare the funds of the Lodge shall not be used for L odge expenses, if
such expenses include any refreshments, however frugal those refreshments may be;
that iluch things have generally a demoralizing effect, and should not be favored,
but, if countenanced at all, the members alone who desire them must pay the
caterer.
They believe a recitation of the tenets and principles of their Order, as found
in the ritual, and the grand descriptive and explanatory addresses, should have
attractive force enough to draw men from pursuits of pleasure or business to listen
to their repetition fifty.two times a year, and that, too, though these same men
may have heard the same thing over a hundred times, delivered with all the grace
and charm which an eloque1;t and instructive speaker could give it.
They in effect declare all that is necessary to make men fast friends is to bring
them together in the Lodge-room while the sublime principles of our Order are
being enunciated for the gratification of the hearers and the mystification of the
candidate.
Is this not asking too much of human natnre 7 Is it not expecting too much
of the average mortal 1
We agree with you, Bro. PILLANS, and believe that in the excerpt made by
you, and which we emphasize by quoting above, lies the true remedy for the many
feeble and inert Lodges of to-day.
The close attention demanded, with the entire absence of any social features
in our Lodge meetings, as Bro. LLOYD says, is asking too much of poor human
nature, besides being a direct and radical departure from the customs and practice
of the architects who planned and designed this famous fabric of ours.
Brother .l::'ILLANB has grave doubts about the usefulness of the representative
system. Well, Brother P., we are waiting to hear urged some valid objection to
the system: the usual one, "that because A. B. paid no attention to the duties of
the position with which he had been honored," therefore the office should be abolished, is, we think, without merit. Why not try the plan of abolishing the repre·
sentati ve in lieu of the office and see how that would work?
Under the head of "Kentucky," Bro. PILLANS says this on the question of
"Perpetual Jurisdiction:"Some little friction occurred between this Grand Lodge and that of P ennsylvania, in consequence of a Lodge of this jurisdiction having received the petition
of, and having conferred the degrees on, one who had been rejected by a Lodge of
Pennsylvania. The position of the Grand Master of Pennsylvania is, that an
applicant for initiation and membership once rejected by a Lodge, is forever
debarred from applying elsewhere, without the consent of the Lodge. which
rejected him. That of Kentucky, "that while P ennsylvania Grand Lodll'e has
an unquestionable right to enforce such a regulation within its own jurisdiction,
·it cannot have any extra territorial force, nor control the action of the Masonic
L odges in other States." This position was sustained by the Grand Lodge of
Kentucky.
And we of California are with Kentucky on that question. Life is too short
to entertain the proposition of perpetual jurisdiction. We believe in the supremacy of the Grand Lodge, and that its right to enact laws for its protection and for
the advancement of its interests within its jurisdiction must be unquestioned.
Our Grand Lodge has ex.ercised its authority in that regard and declared what the
prerequisites for admission to Lodges of its obedience shall be; and while we
would not give cause for offence by questioning the judgment of a sister jurisdiction in its rejection of material presented for its use, we will always insist upon
our right to review such ca.see as are presented to us, and exercise, under our Constitution, the right to correct possible errors.

. The Grand Master speaks of a prosperous Masonic year, althoilgh one of great
financial unrest and disturbance. He announced the painful intelligence of the
deaths of the Grand Chaplain and the Senior Grand Deacon, and, after an affectionate tribute to their memories, concludes his notice with these loving lines:"They have passed away like a gentle breath, .
And their eyes are closed with the sleep of death;
The leaves of the trees will flutter and fall,
And the drifting snow will cover all,
But they will peacefully, calmly rest,
Forever happy, by angels bleat." ·

Grand MMter ORMSBY seems to have given the brethren of Arizona "a live

wholesome advice to the membership. He is decided in hie condemnation of
the use of ciphers, and counsels temperance among the brotherhood as the great

hie adhesion to the principle that "no member shall be permitted to dimit from a
Lodge of which he is a member until he shall present a certificate from some warranted Lodl!'e that he has petitioned for membership, and has been elected
therein." We believe the same doctrine regarding dimitting and subsequent affiliation prevailed in Rhode Island many years ago and was regarded as a preventive
of the evil complained of.
In reference to temperance legislation and'the ea.loon question, the Grand Master says:I would not go as far as some jurisdictions have done-expel those al~dr inbut I would make the withdrawal of those in who should hereafter engage in the
selling of intoxicants compulsory. It ie hnmiliating enough to see a brother eittin~ in a Lodge soaked with liquor, but it is infinitely more so to see the producer
of that condition received on equal ternie with the beet of Masone. I am no temperance fanatic, but I have seen in my visits durimc the past year enough to m.ake
one wish, at times, that he were not a Mason. If Masonry stands for anything,
it stands for all that is good, moral and temperate. I for one am ready to pro·
claim t o the world that Arizona is in the front ranks, seeking to bring about the
millennium in this direction.

We are taught, aa Masons, to be true to the government of the country under
which we live: and in a broader sense than mere loyalty, we should be true to the
principles which underlie its system. These principles were instilled into the
American heart by fortituile, prudence, justice, hardship, adversity, perserverance,
unselfishness and toil, and the best manhood to-day comes from the same sources
of strength. As citizens, we cannot too often present this truth to those who are
striving for fame and influence through paths which are less noble; and we cannot .
present it through a P.ander character than that Master Mason on whom waa bestowed the loving title of "First in War, First in Peace and First in the Hearts
of his Countrymen."
Tens of thousands of good men had their favorable attention directed to
Masonry, because it embraced principles and truths which were deemed worthy of
the loyalty of GEORGE WASHINGTON, and we are proud that it waa so in hie day
and is so still.

Tho following is a complete and correot statement of the conclnsions of the
Oongresa, as compiled by its Secretary, and read at the closing of the Congress,
and approved by the same :-

I. GRAND LoDGE SOVEREIGNTY.
The conclusion of the Congress is that a Grand I.odge, duly organized in a State
or other autonomous territory, is rightfully possessed of absolute Masonio sovereignty
therein.
II. A PLEA FOR IMPROVED PROCEEDINGS.
The conclusion of the Congress is that the formation of Masonic libraries should
be encouraged and fostered; and, inasmncb as the published prooeedings of our
Grand Lodges and other Grand Ma.sonic Bodies do and ever will constitute the larger
part of snob libraries, greater care and more pains should be bestowed upon the
preparation 11nd publication of sdch proceedings, to the end that they may have
greater value In every Masonic collection; and that there should be a freer and more
generous distribution of proceedings among the brethren, to the end that Masonic
light may be more generally dl_tfused.
III. GRAND RXPRESENTATIVEB.
It is the conclusion of the Congress that, under the changed condition of selecting
Grand Representatives, too little time has elapsed to give opportunity for definite
judgment as to the nsefnlneas of the system, and it should therefore be conti!lned.
IV. THE PREROGATIVES OF GR.AND MASTER.
It is the conclusion of the Congress that the dispenslnir power recognized by ihe
old regulation, as residing in the person and office of the Grand Master, has been so
generally exercised by that officer from the organizat ion of Masonry on the Grand
Lodge system down to the present time that its existence cannot be successfully
denied; but that there are no dispensing powers so residing that may not be limited
or wholly denied by the Grand Lodge, save each as inhere in thai offioe nnder the
sanctions of the ancient landmarks.

'

v. THE ANCIENT LAND.MARKS.

The ooncbi.sloh of the Congress is that the ancient landmarll:s are those funda•
mental principles which characterize Muonry as defined by the charges of a Free
Ma.son, a~d without which the Institution cannoi be identified a.a Muonry.

VI. THB CRBBD 011' A. MAsoN.
An nneqnlvocal belief and trust In God ls the fundamental principle upon which
the Institution of Free Masonry was founded and mnst forever rest.
VII. APPBALS FOR AID.
The conclusion of the Congress Is that worthy Masons are entitled to relief from
brethren and Lodges wheresoever they may be found In need of relief, and that the
brethren or Lodges granting snob aid are not eutltled to demand reimbursement from
the Lo~ges In which they hold their membership ; but that when a member of one
Lodge Is relieved by another, aud the financial situation of his Lodge is such as to
permit, common courtesy and duty alike demand that it should reimburse a poorer
Lodite relieving Its members. Written or printed appeals for aid which do not secure
the mdorsement of the Grand Master of the jurisdiction from which they emanate
should be discountenanced.

VIII.

NON·AnILl.6.TES.

The oonclusion of the Congress Is that every Masou ongbt to be a member of some
regular Lodge, attend Its meetings and share its burdens.

IX.

PHYSICAL QUALill'JC.6.TION.

It is the oonclusion of the Congress lhat absolute comfetency to couform literally
to all the requirements of the ceremonies of the severa degrees of Ancient Craft
Masonry fulfills the requirement of physical perfection In a candidate.

The Oommittee on Appeals and Grievances gi'l'e the following as the true mode
of prooedure, under the law of Georgia, in the matter of the non-payment of dues.
We quote it for the benefit of those brethren in California who think our law In regard
to non-payment of dues uncharitable and too exacting:When a member fails to pay his dues for the period of twelve months,.it is the
right of the Lodge to bring him to trial for the grave Masonic offense.
The Secretary should issue a notice, when ordered by the Master or the Lodge,
and serve It on the brother, requiring him to appear at a certain time to show cause
why he should not pay his dues. If the brother falls to appear, or If he· fails to
answer the notice, or if be appears, or answers the notice without appearing, and
his appearance and auswer is unsatisfactory to the Lodge, then the Lodge may prefer
.
charges in the same manner as for other offenses.
U the auswer of the brother Is satisfactory, then the Lodge may granl further
time for the payment of the dues, or remit them for good cause shown, or grant such
relief as may seem meet and proper.
When the Lodge orders that oharges be preferred, the Juuior Warden should
prefer them, and the delinquent should be served, as In other cases, with a copy
thereof, as provided by the regulations or the Grand Lodge, for the required length
of time before trial, and he should have notice of the day and hour of the trial, and
if the brot&er is convicted the renalty should be (1.) suspension for twelve months.
And, should the brother stil refuse to pay his dues after the expiration of twelve
months from the date of such suspension, then he may be re-charged in writing, as
before, and re-tried for such continued and willful failure, and If convicted the penalty shall be exclusion, with recommendation to th~s Grand Lodge for expulsion.

We think you are right, Bro. RoBBINB, and in that observation yon settle the
question of perpetual jurisdiction. .As to the rights of a Masonic Lodge, nnder the
American system the Lodge is the foundation of the edifice. The tendency of the
last half century has been steadily increasing to restrict the rights and privileges
of the Lodge, making that· body entirely dependent upon and subject to the Grand
Lodge for the direction of all its business interests. It has no inherent rights, the
Grand Lodge having assumed the power to regulate its wants and provide for the
supervision of Its expenditnres. Nevertheless, there are maity brethren, loyal Masons,
" who hold in veneration the original Patrons of the Order or Masonry, and their
regular socceBBors, supreme and subordinate, according to their stations, and who
submit to the awards and resolution& of their brethren, when convened, in every
case consistent with the constitutions of the Order," who believe that, havlug fully
performed their duties to the Grand Lodge in loyal service and the payment of all
does and demands, they should be permitted to regulate their social duties to their
brethren and to the Lodge by establishing an intimate social communion amongst
the members, by making the meetings of the Lodge both pleasant and attractive,

The following definition of what constitute "legal Masonic information "is taken
from the correspondence of West Virginia, and Is or practical nse:The Committee on Work asks for a definition of what constitutes " legal Masonic
Information." As to this, we would answer that no rigid rnle can be laid down.
The info'tmatlon should be each as to con?ince a prudent man beyond any reason·
able doubt. This may be had from "strict trial" and "doe examination "-that is,
that the trial or the examination should not be slight, trival or loosely conducted.
And the legal Masonic information should possess similar certainty and be based
upon carefull) ascertained truth.
To insist that a Mason cannot vonch for another unless be has sat In Lodge with
him is to confine the power of vouching within limits unreasonably close. There are
ot.her means of information as to Masonic character just as trustworthy as the fact
of having met a brother within the tiled recesses of the Lodge. In fact._ the power
of ·avonchment may be safely left to the good common sense and sound Jndgmeot of
a cautious man, and it_ cannot be properly limited b.v.cast-iroli roles which.m~st In
all cases be complied WJth; and hence the best defln1t1on of "legal Masomc rnfor·
matioo " which we can readily frame lo words, Is that already mentioned, viz: It
most be each as to satisfy a prndent man beyond any reasonable donbt. It may be
derived from having sat in Lodge with a brother; from the avoochment of one who
has so met the brother in Lodge; or, from other sources equally trustworthy and
equally conclnsive to the mind of a prudent and cautions man.

that irregularities will occur in the old jurisdictions as well as in the new. He
says the Grand Master reported at great length the case of our FREDERICK
MEADE, W. M. of St. John's Lodge:-

Although petitioned to do so, he has refused to issue dispensations which
would set aside the plainly written statutes of the Grand Lodge.
There are two sides to thie question. No law can be made to meet the requirements, circumstance• and peculiar conditions of every caee coming under ite
intent. There are times when the judgment and prudence of the Grand Master
111ay be allowed to determine whether the case ruuet conform to the strict letter of
the law, or whether it is better, for the good of the Order, that the letter of the
law be suspended in that particular case. If the Grand Lodge could be in continuous session there would be no need for such exercise by a Grand Master, but the
Grand Master repreaente the Grand Lodge during its vacation, and should pO&llese
a good deal of its authority and rights.

. He seemed to regard himself a bigger man than the Grand Master, and poeeeseed of the power to defy the authority of the Grand Lodge. His own Lodge
backed him up in this rebellion, and when the Grand Master cited him to appear
at hie office, to ehow co.use why he should not be suspended from office, he came
promptly at the hour named, and, for answer caused to be served by a deputy
sheriff an injunction, signed by a jud¥e of the Court of Common Pleas, restraining
the Grand Master from suspending him as Worshipful Master of St. John's Lodge,
under penalty of one thousand dollare, and summoning the Grand Master to
appear at the court for trial. The Grand Master fileJ a demurrer to the complaint
of MEADE, Thie wae sustained by the court and the case thrown out. The Grand
Master ordered the charter of the Lodge under arrest. MEADE and hie party then
commenced to eat humble pie. They sued for pardon. The Grand Maijter was
leniPnt, but insisted upon strict obedience to all the requirements of the Grand
Lodge and acknowledgments for the wrongs committed. This was done fully and
probably heartily, and the Grand Master restore:l the charter, administered the
reprimand originally required by the Grand Lodge, and peace was restored.

The Master muet be a pattern for imitation bY' the brethren, the Sun for the
illumination of the Lodge, the Custodian of the Work, the embodiment of a gentleman. In the ceremonies of the opening and closing of the Lodge he must be
infallible as he is indispe11sable. Here he is the "observed of all observers."
Other duties may be properly entrustf'd to others- this belongs to him. He must
permit no "short ways " in this beautiful ceremony; it ie too grandly beautiful to
be either prolonged or abridged. To be able to do this duty thoroughly and. well
marks him as the right man in the right place. Indeed, this is the ex?ritnentum
cruc'8 of a "Model Meeter." If he has "gifts and graces," dignity and skill,
agreeableness of manner, tact and erudition, this is the time and place, of all
others, for the intelligent exercise thereot. He must have the monitorial passagea
committed to memory, and so adroitly and ingeniously fit them into the esoteric
paseages, and rehearse tbe whole with such power and pathos as to lend a charm
to this proceeding which the brethren will not, cannot afford to miss. He must
begin at the exact moment specified in the by-laws, and press the proceedings
through in two and a half to three hours. If the propamme is so interesting that
it requires mor~ time, appoint a special meeting. Don't weary the brethren by
too much work at a time. Keep a strict account with wrong-doere; admonish them
promptly; and, if this fails, discipline them. We have no place for the drunkard,
the slanderer, the blas_J>hemer, or the libertine. Such a Master i11 a benison to hie
Lodge and the whole Fraternity. "He shall in no case lose his reward."

the secrecy a.nd sanctity of the ballot.

The Grand Master delivered bis Annual Address, and as a part or an eloquent
introduction sald:-

Iowa has four hundred and sixty chartered Lodges in active work, and a memoorship of 2£,9'2.
The Report on Correspondence is presented by Bro. J.C. W. Con, Chairman,
who declares that:The preparation of this report has been a labor of love. We have found both
pleasure and profit in reviewing the proceedings of more than fifty Grand J urisdictions; but we would have none donbt that it has involved labor-constant, continuous, exacting. We are confident that but t'ew of our brethren are aware of the
real amount of labor involved In the preparation of a Report on Correspondence.
This labor increases each year with the growth of the Fraternity. New Grand
Lodges are springing into existence; many of our older jurisdictions are taking on
new vigor; Masonic research is extending, and new light is being thrown on old qnea·
tlone, while new issues are constantly arising which ca\J for invest.igation and dis·
cuasion. Our real embarrassment is that of riches. A vigilant eye, a retentive
memory, a cautions jndgment, and a prudent conservatism are demanded of one who
wonld do well his work ae a scout on the advanced lines of Masonic progress. Had
we not the aid of the skilled reporters of other jurisdictions, we might well shriull:
from the task. No one man could be equal to It. We have merely borne our share
as we were able. We have read with care more than sixteen thousand pages, to
cnll from them matters of interest to every well informed Mason. The mere reading of these proceedings bas been no holiday sport; to digest, arrange, and present
this vast mass of material has demanded weeks of time and toil. We submit the
work for inspection with a sense of relief, We have found corn, wine and oil by the
way; we find rest at the end.
Whatever excellencies appear in our report are due to the richnesa of the fields
in which we have gleaned; we can claim little other than diligence, and say with
:Montaigne: "I have but gathered a nosegay of other men's fiowers; only the
string that ties them is my own."

Dnring the last year we have passed the semi-centennial mile post of our existence as a Grand Lodge. To the past we can well point wilb feelings of exultation
and pride. Our magnificent growth, the character and standing of our membership,
loyalty to the principles and the usage of the institution, the courage and indepeod·
eoce of thought and action that has ever characterized Iowa Masonry, as well as the
attainment to the very front rank in literary achievement, bas commanded for us in the
Masonic world that recognition due to the eqnal among the best or all the Grand

The Grand Lodge of Kentucky most cordially reolprocates the fraternal greeting
of the Grand Lodge of Ohio, and sends warm southern salutations.
Past Grand Master FITCH, for the Special Committee on "Our Home,'' submitted
an exhaustive report, in which, after giving an account of its establishment and progress, its present creditable financial exhibit, and its noble and satisfactory results,
he says in conclusion:-'Thus thoroughly eqnipped, materially, mentally and morally, to secnre, in an
eminent degree, the comfort, development and happiness of ·an its wards and beneficiaries, with a local management satisfactory to the Fraternity and complimentary
to those in charge, your committee would mingle their hearty congratulations with
the general Craft over the phenomenal success of this noble Masonic achivement.
Inaugnrated RB a well·meant but doubtful experiment twenty-three years ago, with·
out any precedent after which to model its design or forecast its policy, it bas,
nevertheless, furnished a continuous record of unexampled prosperity from the day
of its dedication to the present hour, and bas fully sustained its well-founded claim
to pre-eminence as tbe great original fiJ.e-wader in the advancing column of our Masonio Homes, which are now being hailed everywhere by the Craft as the most
attractive, efficient and distinguishing landmarks of genuine Freemasonry.
To whatever limit, therefore, the success of these Homes can be extended, it is, in
every possible expansion, the proper subject of general rejoicing, and that spirit
which would seek to circumvent their inl!uence, and thus narrow the measure of
their popularity and effect, is a 1Jandal spirit, that counteracts, as far as it goes, our
most efficient agents of Masonic relief, and restores, to the same extent, the reign of
destitution and want over the hapless victims of an adverse fate. But, thanks to the
Universal Father of the fatherless, tbe time for donbt and despondenoy bas passed
forever, as we devoutly believe, so far as our own beloved Home is concerned.
The discordant voice of opposition which, from time to time, has been heard in
tones of ill-advised croaking, has now been completely stilled e.ntl silenced by the
trumpet tones of triumph which are now ringing out and reverberating through the
length and breadth of the land, in exultant joy over its unparalleled prosperity as e.
State charity, antl its diffusive energy e.s e. missionary of mercy to the Me.sonic world
e.t large. It now only remains for the liberality of the Kentucky brotherhood to
keep pace with its advancing progress and increased possibilities. With this assured our Me.sonic Home is destmed, under the blessing of Heaven, to become e.fixed
guiding star in the Me.sonic firmament, shining with e.n ever increasing brilliancy, to
direct and enlighten other jurisdictions in the pathway and purposes of true Me.sonio
charity and relief.

MARYLAND.

The Grand Lodge of Maryland held its one hand red and seventh Annual Communication in the city of Baltimore, November 21, 1893. Thirty-nine sister jurisdictions were represented. There was a large number of Past Grand Officers and the
representatives of ninety chartered Lodges.
The Grand Lodge was opened by the R. •. W.·. Depnty Grand Master with prayer
by the Grand Chaplain.
This elegant volume opens with the portrait, in steel, of the M.·. W.·. THOMAS J.
SBYROCK, Grand Master of Masons in Maryland, and contains a foll and complete report of the dedication ceremonies of the restored Masonic Temple, held at the Special Communication of September 12, 1893, with line engraved views of the Temple
building, of Corinthian hall, the Roman room, the Grand Master's room and the
Library. A roster of the distinguished guests from other jurisdictions who participated in the ceremonies, with a report of the eloquent speeches made daring the
ceremonials and the concluding banquet, the whole forming a valuable souvenir of
this restoration of the abiding place of the Grand Lodge of Maryland.
The R.·. W. ·. Deputy Grand Master directed the Grand Sword Bei.rer and Grand
Director of Ceremonies to inform the M.'. W.·. Grand Master the Grand Lodge was
opened in doe form and awaited his pleasure.
After the appointment of the usual committees the Grand Master delivered his
Annual Address. He gave thanks to the Grand Arcb.itect of the Universe for the
privilege accorded them of again assembling in Annual Session to renew their obligations to each other, and to testify by thelr presence continued interest in the welfare of the Fraternity thronghoat their Grand Jurisdiction. He recalled the principal events in connection with the restoration and dedication of their restored
Temple, and gave them hearty congrutalations upon the condition of their finances
at the completion of their great undertaking, and then, with feelings of deep sorrow,
called their attention to the many vacancies caused by death among the eminent
brethren of Bister Jurisdictions.
The Grand Master reported his official acts. The decisions made were mostly
controlled by the local reg11lations of the Grand Lodge of Maryland, and all in accordance with general usage.
The Grand Lecturer reported elaborately the condition of the Lodges, from which
they would seem to be enjoying a fair degree of prosperity.
The Grand Lodge of Maryland was represented at the Masonic Congress by a
very able committee of which Pasll- Grand Master JoaN M. CARTBB was Chairman,
and Bros. EDWARD T. SCHULTZ and GEOBGE L. MCCAHAN were members. The committee reported the proceedings of the Congress with the recommendation that the
conclusions of that distingnished body be published in the proceedings of the year.

was presented by the R. '. W. ·.DANA J. FLANDERS, and adopted by a rising vote.
The R. •• W. •. CHARLES C. DAME presentiid the following report concerning the
Symbolic Grand Diet of Mexioo, which was acceptl)d and the recommendation
unanimously adopted :The committee to whom was referred the request for recoiniition from the
Symbolic Grand Diet of the United States of Mexico, a body claiming to exercise
exclusive jurisdiction over the degrees of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and
Master Mason in the Republic of Mexico, b0ll' leave to report that they have given
careful attention to the subject, but find themselves unable to recommend the
granting of the request.
We had hoped that the organization of the Grand Diet had put an end to the
rivalry and want of harmony that have so long been characteristic of the several
so-called Masonic Grand Bodies in Mexico; but our latest advices lead ue to
believe that Masonry in our sister Republic is not yet in that condition of harmony
that would warrant this Grand Lodge in recognizing, for the present, any of the
so-called Grand Bodies. We therefore recommend that the request for recognition
of the Symbolic Grand Diet of the United States of Mexico be not granted.
The Grand Secretary presented a communication from the Grand Master of
Illinois, stating the proposed arrangements for the preliminary orll'anization of a
"Congress of Masons," composed of delegates from certain Grand Lodges, to be
held in the city of Chicago on the fourteenth of August next. An explanation
was made of the purpose of the proposed Congress, and the origin of the ca.II for
it, with a statement as to the jurisdiction to be represented.

A second Quarterly Communication .of this Grand Lodge was held in Boston
September 13, 1893,-the R. •. W. •• HARVEY N. SHEPARD presiding as Grand Master, the R. ·• W. ·• S:ERJi:No D. NIOKERSON, Grand Secretary. There were in attendance a large representation of the Lodges and permanent membera, with Past
.Grand Masters CHARLES c. DAME, CHARLES A. WELCH, SAMUEL c. LAWRENCE,
HENRY ENDICOTT and SAMUEL WELLS at the head of the column.
The Grand Master introduced the M. •• W. •. JOHN WINBURN LAURIE, Lieutenant General of the British Army and Past Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
Nova Scotia.
General LAURIE was greeted with the Grand Honors, and, in acknowledging
the compliment, made eloquent allusion to the great loss of Maesachuset.ts in the
death of her executive head. From his feeling and appropriate address we quote
the following lines :Tbe solemn strains of the impressive "Dead March in Saul," to which we
entered this hall, brought again to my mind the sad loss your Grand Lodge has
sustained, the sad calamity ;which has befallen you. I say, advisedly, calamity,
and yet as I listened to the fervent appeal of your Grand Chaplain to the Grand
Architect of the Universe, and the touching manner in which he expreRsed grati.
tude for the many noble qualities of our deceased brother, for the bright example
he had given to his brethren and to the world at large-I felt, as we all must have
felt, that whilst we cannot venture to draw aside the veil that protects the sacredness of the famil;r sorrow, we, as fellow members of the Craft, may at least feel
that in endeavorrng to live up to the example he set for us, and to which the suddenness of his removal has so prominently called our attention, we shall best do
our duty to him, whom his brethren so warmly esteemed, bv raising higher our
own ways of thought and habits of life ; and that thus oul' loss, great as it is, may
in that sense be a gain to the Fraternity.
The R. ·. W. ·. HARVEY N. SHEPARD addressed the Grand Lodge, announcing
the death of the Grand Master in a few well chosen and affectionate words. The
quartette sang a selection by Whittier. The Grand Chaplain read from the
Scripture passages appropriate to the occasion. The quartette sang "Rock of
Ages."
The R. •• W. •• SAMUEL WELLS, in behalf of the committee, presented a memorial tribute to the dead Grand Master, which was accepted and adopted by a rising vote, and ordered spread upon the records. The memorial service was closed
with the singing by the quartette of the sacred selection, "I will not be long."
The most interesting incident of this Communication was the eloquent speech
of the venerable Past Deputy Grand Master, the R. ;• W. ·• Lucrns R. PAIGE,
D. D., now in his ninety-second year-irteresting to the writer because we were
made Masons in the same old Lod~e in the Mohawk Valley, in the State of New
York-Bro. PAIGE in 1824, 'and this writer in 1849, twenty-five years later.
Bro. PAIGE said:R. •• W. •. Deputy Grand Master: I intended, at this session of the Grand
Lodge, to resign m;r office as Trustee of the Masonic Education and Charity
Trust, old age and mfirmity having rendered me unable to perform its duties.
But as that office will terminate, by its own limitation, at the next annual meeting, I have been persuaded to withhold my resignation. Although there is not
the slightest probability that the Grand Lodge would even offer to place such an
old man in that important office, I may be pardoned for me.king the useless declaration that I am not a candidate for re-election. I must thus discontinue all
active service to the Masonic institution, with which I have for so long been
connected.

Thie is not designed to be a farewell address, for I intend to visit the Grand
Lod~e again, if life and sufficient strenirth be syared. Though unable to hear the
voices, it is pleasant to look into the faces o so many brethren, and mentally
compare the present season of peace and prosperity with that dismal period, sixty
years a!fo, when the furious tempest of anti-Masonry swept over the'land, leaving
desolat10n in its path.
Whether I meet you again in Grand Lodge or not, I hope I may never forfeit
your friendship and good will; but rather that I may be met as a true and loyal
brother, and remembered as one who endeavored to walk uprightly before God
and man, as strictly charged when he stood in the north-east corner of the Lodge
as the youngest Entered Apprentice.
God bless Bro. PAIGE; may his years of usefulness be continued and the G?and
Lodge of Massachusetts honored with the presence of the veteran of 1824 beyond
the present century.

An incident that comes to my mind will not apply to the Most Worshipful
Grand Master, but it will to myself. You have all of you seen, in your travels
through the country, a dilapidated old farmhouse, with broken windows, and an

Grand Lodge in just the same way that that old hat is a part of the window-put
there for another purpose than that of receiving and giving light.
At the last Communication of the Grand Lodge, when the Grand Master was
elected, the Commissioners of Trials being presumably the law department of the
Grand Lodge, passed upon the question whether they, as Commissioners of Trials,
had a right to ballot, and decided that they had not. Worshipful Bro. BLAIR and
myself held no other office in the Grand Lodll'ei but were duly appointed, and performing the duties of Commissioners of Tria e, as we had been doing for years,

reports. But when we realized our position, that we could sit in the G:rancl Lodge,
but h~ve no vote or ballot, I told Bro. BLAIR that it reminded me of the unfortunate individual in New York, who, having partaken of too much of that fiuid
which is more balmy than embalming, went wandering about to see if he could
find some place of amusement and entertainment. Presently he saw a bright light
in a building, and many people going in; so he concluded that it was a place of
entertainment. He waited until all was quiet, and walkeJ in through the swinging doors, At the moment when he entered the church, for such it was, the
preacher had just concluded his exhortation, and asked those who believed in the

go to heaven, stand up." Every member of the congregation remained seated

what question (hie) is before the house, but vou and I (hie) seem to be in a hopeless minority."

R. ', W.·. Bro. WOODBURY spoke as follows:Most Worshipful Grand Master: I came here to-night to congratulate you on
your accession to this high office, and to express the great comfort and pleasure
that I have in seeing you there, and the faith which I have that Masonry will
derive great benefit from your term of office.
I did not come here, sir, to act as arbitrator, or judge, in this tussle between
the reverend clergy and the irreverent lawyers, which has sprung up all of a sudden. You may say that the isaue is, "let her go, Gallagher!" or you may say that
the issue is, "let her go, parsons!" but I must say when I was a boy I loved to
see a good, fair wrestle; and now that I am old the feeling has not departed from
me.
This little stir-up between my reverend friends and my secular friend, Bro.
AVERY, has been a very pretty little "scrap" so far as it has gone; but I am aware
that he was accused of quoting scripture iacorrectly.
Now, it is not a great professional offense for a lawyer to quote law incorrectly
to a judge, but if he quotes scripture incorrectly, woe betide him when the church
sits here to correct him.

But I was referring, or meant to refer, to some thirty or forty years ago, when

one case, and that was by Dives, when he was in Hades, where he ought to be."

has adopted no" medals" or "jewels," except jewels of office worn by Grand and
subordinate Lodge officers, I presume the" medals" and "jewels" worn by Bro.
ComrnANE appertained to other organizations, over which the Grand Lodge has no
control, and that he had a right to wear them, onder their regulations. This, however, is a matter of taste, and cuts no figure in the question.
We recognize the right of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, and of every other
Grand Jurisdiction, to adopt such. laws and regolations for the government of their
members as they think proper, and we claim the same right for .Missouri. Visitors
from Pennsylvania, who come doly accredited as regular Master Masons by their
Grand Lodge, will be welcomed as brethren by Missouri Lodges, without inquiring
as to whether they had complied with all the Missouri requirements. It is enoogh
for us to know that the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania vouches for them as regularly
made onder its laws. Yon do not claim the right to say what shall be the qualifications of petitioners in Missouri, and yet you assert the right to discipline a member
of I\ Lodge in Missouri because he failed to comply with the requirements of the
Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania.
