MONTANA.

The Grand Lode of Montana held its twenty-ninth Annual C.ommunication in
the city of Helena October 11th, 1893,-the. .M. •• w.·.~ MosES MOBBIS, Grand
Master, the B. •. W. •. CORNELIUS HEDGES Grand Se9retary., There were present
•ev~ Past Grand Masters, sixteen representatives of sister jurisdictions, and thE!
representatives of thirty-three chartered Lodges. The Grand Lodge was opened
with prayer by the Grand Chaplain.
·
The Grand Master deli.vered his Annual Address, and, after extending a fra~
ternal welcome to the brethren, said : We are gathered to the twenty-ninth Annual Communication.und~r ciroui;n•
stances of unusual discouragement and depression. For the first time m our history as a Grand Lod!(e there are seats vacant and Lodges unrepresented becau~e
duP• are unpaid. Lodges cannot collect dues from members, others have their
funds in suspended banks, and hence are unable to pay Grand Lodge dues.

1894.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

669

The situation is humiliating as well as disheartening. But, brethren, look
again, more carefully, calmly and widely, and it will appear that we have no cause
to adopt the creed of the pessimist or re-echo the false and gloomy prediction of
tbe prophets of evil. We are members of an institution whose historical existence
can be traced back for centuries, and traditions carry us still further back beyond
the era of recorded history.
And further along he offers his brethren this consolation : Very unusually fortunate are we, in that death has not entered the ranks of
our Grand Lodge, though from our custom of changing annually, we have a larger
list of Past Grand Officers than many of the older jurisdictions. It is not becausedeath has not been abroad in our land, for nearly every jurisdiction has been called
to look into the narrow house where the coffined remains of beloved and honored
brothers have been laid away with the symbol of their faith in a resurrection; but
it seems mvidious to name one without naming all who deserve to be mentioned.
The story of their good deeds and well ea.med fall'.lll is to be found in the several
volumes of the printed proceedings of our sister jurisdictions, told in words of
tender and affectionate regret and honest praise. We mourn with all who thus
mourn, as we rejoice in their joys and prosperity.
In regard to the representative system he makes the following euggestions:We have received official notice from the Grand Masters of Pennsylvania and
Iowa that their jurisdictions have abandoned the representative system as a hindrance rather than a help to closer fraterna.I relations. And, notwithstanding the
partial endorsement that the custom received from the late Masonic Congress, we
can hardly understand what it means by any "changed conditions" that offer any
promise of greater utility. If we are to have any special representatives in other
jurisdictions capable of doing us any service in an emergency, we want the best
ones to be had. Why not then, by general resolution, adopted b:y Grand Lodge,
confer this honor upon the Grand Master of each jurisdiction, or, 1f you want more
permanent representation, select the Grand Secretaries, who are less frequently
ohanged?
The Grand Master refers to the cost of a session of the Grand Lodge being
made excessive by reason of the allowance of mileage and per diem to each delegate in attendance. With us in California the allowance is for one delegate or
representative from each Lodge, the object being to insure a representation from
every subordinate Lodge if possible, for although the Master, Past Master and
Wardens are members of the Grand Lodge and have voice and vote in its proceeding, yet our allowance for expenses of attendance is provided for one from each
Lodge. The Grand Secretary recommends the printing of an increased number
of Grand Lodge Proceedings to meet the increased demand from Libraries, both
Masonic and Secular.
All right, Bro. HEDGES, euppl;t your libraries and then let us prepare a. plan that
shall result in the placing of a copy of the proceedings in the hand of every affiliated Mason in the jurisdiction. In other words, give every Mason's family the
nucleus of a Masonic Library, and the Fraternity will reap from the seed thus
sown an abundant harvest in the future.

The whole world was represented in California in Masonry, as in peoples. A
Masonic Lodge organized in California would probably have a Master from
Maine or Miseissippi, a Senior Warden from New York or Texas, a Junior
Warden from Georgia or Ohio, and a Senior Deacon from Connecticu t. In conse.quence the Fraternity and the initiate were favored with a decidedly conglomera te
rendition of thQ ritual. Lodges were opened up and closed down "upon the centre or on the square," or "by the authority in me vested," the modes of recognition were as varied as the climates of the countries from which the wayfarer
hailed, while the obligations were beinir gradually lengthened by saving points to
"thirteen and a proviso." Tiie Grand Lodge of California bad within its organization intelligent and well informed Masone, and the Grand Lodge, advised by

We are surprised to notice that the brethren of the Grand Lodge of New Hampshire "view with great apprehension the con_ditions reported from certain sections
or that Grand Jurisdiction relative to the so-called Eastern Star.'' They say, through
their Committee on Doings of Grand Officers, "It is more than probable that certain
Lodges have permitted, and are now permitting their lodge-rooms to be occupied
by Chapters of the Eastern Star," and they further say, "If said conditions do
exist, and there can be little or no donbt of the fact, it would appear to be in willful
violation of the law of the jurisdiction, and should be met with prompt and suitable
discipline.''
We don't understand why the organization of the wives, sisters and daughters of
Masons for purposes of charity and pure beneficence should be viewed with great
apprehension by any other association of American citizens, more especially Masons,
bot as oar New Hampshire brethren are presumed to know whereof they speak, we
make no comments. We have no acquaintance with the organization known as the
Eastern Star, and jndge it entirely by its reported charities for Masonic purposes,
. which we think eniitles it to some consideration.

Grand Master's office (of thA more important of which press copies have been
Blade) during the past year have numbered nearly two thousand. In fact, without

the work connected with the correspondence of the Grand Master, as performed
by his Private Secretary, I am perfectly satisfied-where before I simply believedtbat the salaryjaid to the Private Secretary is entirely inadequate, and I therefore recommen that it be increased to a sum more nearly commensurate with the

Under District of Columbia Bro. VEHSLAGE quotes from tht> eminent student
and author, Bro. WILLIAM R. SINGLETON, the following condensed statement
defining the prerogatives and powers of a Worshipful Maater, which we extract
for the benefit of the brethren in California :~
The Master of a Lodge is invested with so many important prerogatives and
powers, conferred by the ancient Constitutions and Regulations, by Grand Lodge
legislation, and by general Masonic usage, that some may fall into the error of
supposing that the Lodge bas no poW"lrs or rights which the Master may not of
himself exercise, if he wills to do so, irrespective of the will or desire of the Lodge.
That, in fact, to all intents and purposes, he is the Lodge.
It is true that his responsibilities are great and his powers and J?rer()jtati ves are,
and should be, commensurate with these responsibilities ; and he 1e not amenable
to his Lodge for the exercise or the abuse of them. He is, however, circumscribed
and bound by the obligation~ of his office, his promises and agreement at the time
of his installation, one of which was: "To submit to the awards and resolutions
of yoor brethren when convene<!i_in every case consistent with the Constitutions
of the Order." Now, while the Worshipful Master has entire control of the work
of his Lodge, may open and close it at his pleasure, and must see that the regulations and edicts of the Grand Lodge are carried out, and that none of the land·
marks or regulations of Masonry are violated; while his decision upon any ques·
tion of order.is binding upon hia Lodge until such decision, upon appeal from it by
the Lodge, is reversed by the Grand Master or Grand Lodge; and while he has
other well-known powers special\y delegated or are his by cust!>m and ~sage, yet,
outside of these, he must "so bm1t to the awards and resolutions of hlB brethren

delegated powers, he must abide by the expressed will of the majority of his

powers of a Lodge." Has it any, under the Ancient Landmarks of the Order

The Grand Master of South Australia in hie installation address, gave expression to many loyal and patriotic sentiments, and, before closing hie address, said :
The benefits of Masonic Union find their fullest developmen t in the
principles of our Order-" brotherly love, relief, and truth.' It has oftengrand
been
aaid that Freemason ry is not a creed. No; but it is a faith. Our belief
in the
Great Architect of the U Diverse is the keystone of the whole Masonic fabric.
Thank God that nowhere in these lands has there been any sign of perversion from
this ruling principle of our Order. And second only to this is our testimony to
the Brotherhood of Man. Ours is not a benefit society or an insurance association.
Praiseworth y and beneficial aa those institutions may be, our organizatio bas
higher, nobler aims. 'Ne are Freemasons not for what we can get, but fornwhat
we can do. We seek to promote the social virtues, and we manifest our sympathy
to others. Yon will not, M . •. W. ·. Grand Master, find Masonic Ychools and
orphanages in Australia. Our conditions have not necessitated their establishment. But on examining the records of this Grand Lodge J'Oll will find that in
the few short years of its exi•tence it has created an Orphan Fund with £17,000 in
credit, and that it has distributed thousaads of pounds for the relief, not of poor
and distressed Masons alone, but of poor and distressed humanity. The recent
disastrous floods in Queensland and in this Colony, misfortune and distress of
every kind, have been and are opportuniti es eagerly seized for putting our
princi·
pies into practice. Every pri vate Lodge has its Benevolent Fund, aoa every
true
Freemason, who has the means, endeavors himself to help the poor, the bereaved,
.ud the suffering.

of this Grand Lodge are furnished to each Subordinate Lodge for your information
and guidance, and if yon studied them as yon should do, nine out of every ten qnes·
tions propounded to the Grand Master would be answered by yourselves. I cannot
bring myself to attribute tbi~ desire for propounding the simplest questions to ignorance, but rather to convenience. It seems to be simpler and.easier to dash oft' a letter to the Grand Master than to look up the law on the subject, and yet, ifH1e
questioner stopped to think, he must feel that the Grand Master cannot help but
consider that man wholly incompetent for the J.>Ositlon of Master of a Lodge to
which. his brethren have elevated him, when he w11lfollf, displays eoch unpardonable
ignorance of the common landmarks of onr institution. '
The above is certainly very severe language to apply to a Masonic organizationto charge a Master of a Lodge with unpardonable ignorance Is to declare him unfit
for the duties of his office, and if willfolly, &c., he deserves to be disciplined. In
this case, the Grand Master having but eleven Lodges under his supervision, it

1894.]

Grand Lodge of California.

697

The law of this Grand Lodge is, that an objection once made continues until it
has been removed by the jurisdiction in which it was made. Of course we cannot
enforce our views upon other Grand Lodges, and will not attempt to do so; but we
have a right, when other Gre.nd Lodges accept our r ejected material, to say t hat the
persons so rejected shall not visit any Lodge in this jurisdiction or have any Masonic
recognition, and consequently I have, in some inHtances, issued edicts to that effect.
Of making Maeons at sight, the Grand Master says:The prerogative of the Grand Master is of ancient origin, and while used in but
few instances at the present time, nevertheless, as the prerogative exists, I have
deemed it proper to exercise it in order that it might not be said the.t it has become
obsolete by non-use. The Ahlman Rezon enumerates among his powers, " To ce.use
Masons to be made in his presence," and "To grant dispense.tions for me.king Masons." Many years ago it was quite usual for the Gre.nd Master in person, or by
dispense.lion, to make a Mason at sight. It was done at the.t time upon merchants
and shipowners visiting the city from foreign ports, who, during the time occnpied
in disposing of their wares and laying in return cargoes, became desirous of being
initiated into the mysteries of Free Maeonry, In order that they might have the
rights and privileges of brethren while they were among us, as well as elsewhere.
'This act is now done only upon persons within our jurisdiction, or, in t he case of
TeBidents of other States, we request a waiver of junsdiction by the Grand Master
thereof before conferring the degrees.
We have quoted the Grand Master upon this subject for the information of our ·
California brethren. Upon this question the Grand Lodge of California he.a said:This Grand Lodge does not acknowledge the doctrine that a Grand Master may
make Masons at sight, or at will, except in a regular Lodge, by the unanimous coneent of the members thereof present; aud that in its opinion Grand Masters possess
no powers except those contained in the constitutions of Masonry, and those clearly
and expressly delegated to them by their brethren.
The Grand Master is evidently no believer in cremation. He says: " A vault is a
grave-a furnace is not.''
The Grand Master says:1 have been asked whether a member does not violate his Masonic obligation and
become liable to charges for personal solicitation of votes for himself, 11.nd replies :
"My predecessors he.ve issued edicts on this subject, declaring oauce.using, nominating and electioneering to be unmasonic. I am not aware that any attempt has been
made to enforce the edict by t rie.l and punishment, but perhaps some steps in this
direction will have to be taken in cases of violation of it. The right of the brethren
to stand as candidates, and of their friends to recommend them, cannot he gainsaid,
but the m ethods of public politics would be destructive of the welfare of the Fraternity. The spectacle of brethren standing in the ante-room of a I¢ge, or even inside,
electioneering and soliciting votes for themselves, cannot be too severely reprimanded. It exhibits a want of delicacy and refinement which should not be shown
in a fraternity like a Maeonic body. Brethren have been seen not only handing out
tickets with their own namee upon them, but also casting a vote for themselTee ; a
1tatement of this conduct ought to be sufficient to show the indelicacy of it, 11.nd
cause every true Mason to refrain from It. Friends of candidates may write letters
to persons known to them , r ecommending brethren for preferment; but the wholellllle issue of printed circulars to persons unknown, as well as known, to the sender,
is highly improper, and wiJl, if not checked, tend to degrade the Fraternity as to
printed tickets for candidates. I see nothing improper in them. It saves much
time at the meetings, in the preparation of tickets; to have them all prepared and
accessible by the brethren, but they should be distributed by friends of the candidates, and not by the candidates themselves. They should be distributed in the
Lodge-room daring the time when the Lodge is called off preparatory to going into
an e1ection. The Lodges ma:v, and frequently do, prepare ballots for those offices
which are not contested, having blanks for those which are. It is earnestly hoped
that no brother will violate the proprieties on this subject, and expose himself to the
danger of becoming an example to others which will not be pleasant for him.

The Grand Master gives this account of the progress of the Grand L odge :We have now entered on the twenty-fifth year of the existence of this Grand
Lodge, which was organized on October 20, 1869, and this is actually the t went yfifth Communication of the Grand Lodge of Quebec, though our proceedings number from the Annual Communication held a year afterwards.
Grand Lodge at its organization comprised but 21 Lodges, which have increased
to 57; and during this period 5375 initiates have been brought to light in our
Lodges.
When we consider that we solicit no candidates for admiSBion into our Order,
but, on the contrary, insist that every applicant shall have a firll',I belief in Almighty
God, the Creator and Ruler of the Umverse; shall be a loyal subject, and a good,
IJIOral, law-abiding citizen, having a good reputation among hie fellows ; and that
no mercenary motive exists to offer an inducemept t o join us-it would be no wonder were our numbers to be but a small proportion of the community; but when
we consider further the fact that, owing to ignorance of our principles and a false
impression of our tenets, a very large majority of the pc>pulation of this Province
iii, on sectarian religious grounds, opposed to us, I think we may well deem it a
reason for congratulation that so many have, of their own accord, sought, and,
after strict examination, been fo)llld worthy of, admission.
.

tion. It has e.SBets of cash· a11d bonds of $11,654..88.

Within convenient dietan·ce of L odi;:e-rooms, and who have apparently no reason t o

ye&rB ago, in their pockets, and live in the beneficial shadow of the Order, without
ueuming anr of its charges and responsibilities. This bas a very depressing effect
11pon the legitimate growth of Masonry.
.

of the Nineteenth Century, it remains only to the Pope of Rome and bis subordi.
nates, through jealousy, bigotry, and fanaticism, to openly antagonize Free·
masonzy. Pope Leo XIII, following the example of some of his predecessors, in

friends among the more liberal of the Roman Catholic denomination, whom we

ever lost to the world, and the institution destroyed, it will be from internal, and
not from external, ~uses; it will .not be from defects in the organization itself,
but through the unfaithfulness of its members to the Order and to themselves in
not living up t~ its teachings and principles. The foundation principles of 'the
Order have reman;ied. the sam,e throughout all the ages of the past, and it is a canon
of. Masonry that it beth not m the power of any man or body of men or Masons
to make changes or innovations in the Ancient Landmarks of the institution'.
We may reasonably believe, and with full confidence predict, that Masonry will
remain, for all. coming time, in all its essentials the same 11.nd unchanged. Based
np.lD truth .as. its eternal corner-stone, it has stood, and will defy all the ravages of

are ever lost to th~ "Y'orld, it will only be throuR"h the infidelity of the Craft

and thus shall Masonry be perpetuated to the latest generations of earth, until.
there shall be a practical realizatiCJn of the sublime truth that
'

Under the head of discipline the Grand Master reported the arrest of a charter
for violation of a "Landmark" and the Constitution by conferring the E. A.
degree on a candidate having only one eye. He also reports that he has received
information that one or more Lodges in the State have been guilty of the vicious
practice of admitting applicants to take the degrees in Masonry for less than the
prescribed fees, and some Lodges are perhape at fault in the practice of taking.due
bills for fees, instead of requiring the same to be paid in cash. If such practices
have obtained in any of our Lodges, they are warned that all such practices are
vicious and a.re positive violations of Masonic law, and, if they do not cease, the
sanction of discipline will sooner or later overtake them.
The Grand Master seems to be fully alive to the responsibilities of bis office.

After opening the Grand Lodge the Grand Master delivered bis Annual Address. He thanked the Great Ruler that they had been permitted once again to
assemble in Annual Communic'lt1on to resume their fraternal duties.
The Grand Master issued forty-five special dispensations and refused ten ap.
plioations; he issued but one dispensation for the formation of a new Lod~. He
reported thirty-one "official rulings," mostly of local import.
While enp;aged in making his official visitations the Grand Master was overtaken by sickness, which prostrated him for a period of more than four montbi!.
He writes as follows of his miefortunes:Thie closed, for four months, my official visitations, as a few days thereafter
disease, in the shape of malarial fever, laid hold of and prostrated me, and for over
four months I was racked by pain and suffering, until finally it developed a condition necessitating a most serious surgical operation, the result of which could not
be determined for many days, and it was not until the first of this month that I
was sufficiently restored to take up the work again. Of course it was then too
late as other business demanded my attention at that time. When stricken with
diee'ase I h8d many appointments ahead which I was compelled to cancel by telegraph. Had my health permitted, I would have visited and worked for many
Lodges, and my failure to do so is alone attributable to my sickness.
He reported as follows upon the joint occupancy of Lodge rooms:-

N otwithstanding there is a strong recommendation on our statute books ad vising BUbordinate Lodges to meet by themselves, yet I found, in my official visitatio1111, many instances where the Lodge room was used in common with several
other secret societies, and in every instance I found these societies sapping the
life-blood of the Lodges. I have advised against this practice wherever I have
been, and have about concluded that a Lodge that can not maintain itself without
the assistance of outside societies had better quit and surrender its charter, as it
fa only a matter of time when it will die. I would recommend that an edict pro·
,
hibiting this practice be passed by this Grand Lodge.

McCULLOCH, and of the many eminent brethren of sister juriedictione of whose
death he had official knowledge. To each of the jurisdictions be extended the
heartfelt sympathy of Tenn1!81Jee, and with them mourned their honored dead.

orphans of Tennessee, that the Home is nearly free from debt, and he expresses

Verily, this is a rather stormy illustration of the reductio ad abaurduml A MallOD visits a town, as a stranger, and learns from some one that a Lodge meets on
that night at a certain hall. He repairs thither, hopeful of fraternal aeeociation.
Gentlemen come out . into the ante-room and offer to examine him. He does not
know these a-entlemen, and remembering hie vow about thing& clandestine, sugpsta the common courtesy of a mutual satisfying; he must·not visit a clandestine
body; they must admit none but Freemasons. Could a gentleman ask less? Could
a Lodge demand le88? A courteous committee would not hesitate a moment, indeed, such an one never did. But all committees are not courteous, in our individual, personal knowledge.
To be sure, the Lodge may lawfully refuse to show its charter, and it may
pfuse to admit any visitor. The visitor does not "demand," he politely "asks."
Jf refused he withdraws. Result: a good brother is wounded in the house of his
friends, and the "friends " feel & trifle beepoiled over their lack of fraternity.

The Committee on Correspondence submitted a very interesting report relating
to the condition of Masonry in Mexico in response to mention of the matter in the
Grand Master's Address, which was referred to them. The committee eay:The reorg1mization and unification of Masonry in Mexico a few years a.go, result.
Ing in the formation of the Gran Dieta of the United States of Mexico, and the
prompt action of the Grand Lodge of Texas recognizing the Gran Diets and extend·
mg to it the fraternal hand by the ratification, in 1891, of" The Treaty of Monterey,"
was calculated to ca.II forth Pome discussion in Masonic circles, and we find that
many of the Committees on Correspondence have spoken approvingly of our action,
and we doubt not that in due time the Gran Dieta will be generally recognized as the
governing Masonic body in Mexico. There are, however, some who have taken exception to and criticized our action, but their strongest objections lie in their opposition
~ the r.ecognition of Scottish Rite Masonry by Grand Lodges of the York Rite. This
iii not an open question in Texas, as we have had for many years a standing resolution
recognizing the Scottish Rite, and there is no valid reaso12, in the opinion of your
oommittee, for reversing our action.
· The severest criticisms of Mexican Masonry emanate from one who claitned to be
and doubtless was the Worshipful Master of ToUeo Lodge, No. 520, at the City of
:Mexico, including the documents mentioned by the Grand Master. Tolleo Lodge
was chartered in 1~82 by the Grand Lodge of Missouri, with the consent of the then
existing Grand Bodies of Mexican Masonry, and was composed In the main of Amer·
leans residing in Mexico. From facts in possession of your committee we are fully
warranted in saying that these criticisms were not inspired so much by a zeal for
Masonry as by .a desire to ret!Un the charter of their Lodge and the prestige of their
poeition as the only Masonic Lodge in Mexico with an American charter. All of these
oriticisms have been ably met and fully answered by the Gran Diet&, and the regularity of the work of the Mexican Lodges is a.Iso fully attested by well informed
brethren of this.jurisdiction who have recently visited the City of Mexico.
We would not be understood as intending in this report to dignify with any attempted re1;>IY the various pamphlets, letters, circulars, etc., emanating from the
above mentioned individual, and which have been 11C&ttered broadcast over the land,
for we regard these publications as the natnrllol result of chagrin on the part of their
author. and so being. we do not believe they can properly come before this Grand
Lodge for notice, and they are only referred to here (and by our Grand Master, we
llllSWDe), because they have been very generally circulated among the AUleriCBll Grand
Lodges, and have, we think, been accorded more notice than they deserved.
Having recognized the Gran Diets, and now holding fraternal correspondence
with that Grand Body, the Grand Lodge of Texas does not propose to take notice of
&Uiqtures upon iteelf and upon the Gi:an Diet& by individual Masons or individual
Lodges, especia.lly when such strictures are couched in terms, to say the very least,

Under Arkansas, he presents the first brief we have noticed in favor of NatnraJi.
zation as a prereqtilaite for initiation. He says:The Grand Master decided that a foreigner can be a Mason withont being natnralized as an American citizen. There is some doubt about this, in our minds. It
would be all right, provided he comes to America to remain permanently. But
suppose be is only here temporarily, and while here applies for the mysteries of
Masonrv and is received; aud suppose also that he bas been rejected at bis home
in the Old World, would we not get oarselvea in trouble with the Grand Lodge of
that country? We have in mind a case in point : A man from Scotland-a coal
miner-came to West Virginia. After remaining here a short time, he applied for
membership in one of onr Lodges. He was rejected. Shortly afterwards he _returned
to Scotland and there was made a Master ·Mason. He came back agam to the
United States and bronght with him a Master Mason dlmlt, and preaen~d !t to the
Lodge here that bad rejected him. The Lodge properly refused to admit b1m. We
bold that tbe Grand Lodge of Scotland erred in considerln_g. bis application, because
the man bad come to the United States and became a citizen thereof. Therefore
the Grand Lodge of West Virginia bad jurisdiction over him, He was consequently
Irregularly made a Mason.

'IJJhy he 10 11ot11cl. Thia is the only safe-guard to the "outer door.'' If the rejected
party can demand an investigation, the secrecy of the ballot is forever done away
with.

Bro. ClU.BLBS RAT GRITMAN has passed to his eternal rest. From his brethren in
Napa, with whom he bas long resided, we learn that his last words were expressive
of bis atfectioo for the Grand Lodge of California. Io 1he memorial tribute submitted by his breibren to Napa Commandery, of which he was a member, the committee, consisting of old-time friends and neighbors, say: "His mind was clear np
to within a few moments of bis death, A short time before he died he seemed to be
passing along the streets of bis loved city, and to be ml'eting his fraters and friends,
to each of whom he addressed an affectionate 'good-by; ' and, after he had bid
them all adieu in this manner, his mind seemed to linger n11on that body which had
bestowed honors upon him, and in which he had passed many pleasant and happy
hours ; and, after reflecting lo silence a few moments, he summoned his remaining
strength, raised his emaciated hands to his lips, and, fondly kissing them, said :
'Good-by, Grand Lodge,' and his spirit passed over the river and rested."
Bro. GRITMAN was made a Mason in Manhattan Lodge, No. 62, New York Oity,
In 1865, a Royal Arch MRson in Bridgeport, Connecticut, in 1866, and a Knight Templar in California in 1882. Bro: GBITHAN served as Chairman of the Committee on

term of office expiring only one month prior to his death.
Bro. GRITMAN was born in the City of Providence, Rhode Island, in the year 1838;
was a graduate of Yale College and a veteran of the civil war. He was at the time
of his death Cashier of the Bank of Napa, He was universally honored and beloved. Bro. GBtTxAN leaves a wife with whom he bas journeyed through life for
more than a quarter of a century. May God sustain the widow in her lonely home,
and be to her a guide and comforter.
"Alone she wanders where with him she trod,

We are of the opinion that to allow a jndgment of expulsion arrived at in this
way to stand, wonld be to establish a most dangerous precedent. A trial commie·
sion is a jnry, invested with the power of determining the question of gnilt or
innocence, and adjndging, within the limits fixed by the Constitution, the penalty to
be imposed in case of gnilt. The scrnpnlonsness with which, in courts or jnstice, the
law gnards jnrorsfrom the approach of improper infinences, after the submission of the
case to them, by confining them in a room by themselves anti! they have finished their
work, and allowing no one to approach or commnnicate with them, is a matter of
common knowledge. Such a seclusion is almost essential to a proper determination of
a case by a jnry, and we have no donbt as to the intention of the framers of Seo. 8,
Art. IV, Part VI, of oar Constltntion, when they provided that" After all the testimony
shall have been received, the commissioners shall proceed to deliberate npon their
verdict and sentence, with none present save themselves, the :Master and the Sec·
retary. • • • The judgment of a majority of the commissioners shall be taken
as the deoision of the wliole." ·.rhis, in onr opinion, requires that the commission·
ers shall proceed to deliberate npon their verdict and sentence immediately after
the case Is snbmltted to them, and shall continue their deliberations, with none
present save the Master and Secretary, until a decision is arrived at, or it becomes
apparent that an agreement cannot be reached. It will be observed that Sec. 7 of
the same Article provides that the period within which the dnties of the commie·
sioners shall be conclnded shall not exceed ten days, unless, for good reasons shown,
the Master shall grant them farther time. Sorely It was never contemplated that
twenty-seven days might be allowed to intervene between ballots, dnrlng which time
the commiPsionere shonlct be allowed to wander at will, exposed to the many im.
proper infiuences that ordinarily beset men charged with the important duties of
jnrore.

It is as water to the thirsty palate, as copious showers to the parched ea.rth. In
union there is strength. In fraternal intercourse may be found the elixir which

We need the incentive of encouragement and hearty co-operation as a prompter
to continued action.
The projectors of templee and cathedrals in which vast assemblages could
congregate and unite in unit of action, realized this fundamental truth.
Silent prayer may attune the soul to harmony with the divine will, but it is the
full voiced invocation in the "golden cadence of poeey" which lifts it to the
celestial plane.
The Annual Convocations of this Grand Lodge, it is submitted, should be so
conducted, the association of its members so arranged and so intimate and full in
expreasion and sentiment, that each may return to his abode, with ~ consciousn~u

A half century eince, and the orthodox Mason was suppoeed to believe that
while the world moved and mutation wae impre11ed upon all other sublunary
things, Masonry a.lone stood as a crystallized entity, embodying the same eSBen•

signs and 1ymbols aa in the days of King Solomon.
To-day the consensus of opinion, as I think, regards it as a product of evolu.
tion aa a' product of that change under natural and fixed laws, which involvee
continuous progress from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous, in structure, and
from the single and simple to the diverse and m!Ulifold in quality and function.
It applies to Masonry as to the growth, development, expansion of institutions, manners, languilge, civilization and all other products of human activity.
• The laws which irovern the procees are often obscure and difficult of analysis,
but however difficult the rationale of the theory, we can usually trace the progress
of change from result to premises through even its dim manifestations.
Viewed in this light and what seems to us the origin of Freemasonry beoomea
conaistent with history and easy of comprehension.

The Greeks were far in advance of all their neighbors in a knowledge of the

arts and sciences. Architecture with them had reached a degree of perfection not
elsewhere attained, and it may well be doubted if much has been gained even to
the present time (except in modifying their forms to meet modern wants}, over
the knowledge possessed by these ancient architects.
The religious mysteries of all former ages were familiar to them. When, therefore, a colony of the inhabitants of ancient Attica, driven by the exhaustion of their
soil and by overpopulation to ab~ndon their own country, they carried with them
to Asia Minor not only a riper knowledge of science and art than was possessed
by their new neighbors, but also the mysteries of Athene and Dyonisius in their
originIll purity.
Located in Tyre, surrounded bv a people between whom and themselves there
Wall little in common, pouessed of information to which their new neighbors were
entire strangers, finding their acquirements could be turned to good account in
their new abode, and animated by a strong desire to perpetuate among themselves
and their descendants the knowledge and the ennobling principles inculcated
among them in their former environment, it is not strange that they organized
themselves into a society for mutual benefit and improvement, or that such ·society
ahould have taken on the mystic character of the religious associations of their
native land.
The members of this society became the architects and artificers, the projectors
and builders of the temples and pa.laces of Tyre.
·
They hewed the rough stohee of the quarry into forms of strength and beauty.
They carved the trees of the bountiful forests of the mountains into objects of
symmetry and usefulness.
Their devotion to principle, their fidelity to their brethren and to their art,
1tamped them as worthy of the approbation of the Tyrian King. They beautified
and adorned Tyre; and Hiram, its King, upon ascending the throne, extended to
them his protection and became a recipient of their garnered knowledge, a patron
of their mystic rites.
Their isolated position at first, and t.he fame they acquired a little later, together with the ever present necessity for mutual aid and protection, all tended to
cement them together as a close corporation and to impress upon them a distinctive
character.
Their fame havinl{ extended far and near, it was but natural when a little later
King Solomon desired to erect a temple to be dedicated to Jehovah, the resplendent lustre of which should eclipse the world, that he should apply to his royal
neighbor, Hiram, King of Tyre, for a detail of the famous designers, architects
and artisans to consummate the great work.
A t the head of this body of men, as our traditions inform us, was the son of a
widow, Hiram Abiff, under whose auspices something akin to our organization was
formulated for the government and control of the various bands of the workmen
confided to his care and guidance.
The ritual of the Order of Free and Accepted Masons abounds in evidence of
not only the belief of those by whom it was prepared in the Scriptures, and of the
grandeur of the Temple, but in all the canons of the church of the earlier days,
and the mystical and symbolical views ~ntertained among the Hebrews in relation
to the temple are pretiy faithfully copied by the Craft.
To trace the course of operative Masonry through the middle ages and down
to the laet century is much easier than to discern it.I connection as a conaistent and
continued Order.

The first Gothic Cathedrals of the middle ages-many of which as a matter of
fact greatly excelled in size and grandeur the temple of King Solomon-were . as we
are assured by the historian of the day; erected by companies of builders who
po9861180d a peculiar social organization, which enabled them to preserve moat of
their professional secrets, and furnished facilities for mutual defense and assistance
in the midst of rude and turbulent communities.
Among them there was always a governing head from whoae decision there was
no appeal, and "every tenth man was called a warden, and overlooked each nine."
In this manner and by these Freemasons were built the magnificent convent
of Batalha in Portugal, about the beginning of the 15th century, the Cathedral of
Strasbourg, from 1015to1439, of Cologne, whioh occupied centuries in its construe·
tion, and many other famous structures in England, Italy and various parts of
Europe.
In England and Scotland they were incorporated guildll and were early known
as Freemasons, a name assumed by reason of the many exclusive privileges which
they enjoyed as a corporation of builders.
All these remarks are trite. and are only indulged as a predicate for the enforcement of the central idea, which is, that from this practical organization, having for its main object the advancement of the material welfare of its memben,
has evolved the grander organization of speculative Masonry, with the higher and
nobler purpose of advancing the moral and intellectual forces of its members.
The practice of admitting to their ranks men distinguished for their profound
learning and their attainments in the arts and scienoes, prevailed from an early
period, and little by little, as this practice continued, 1'nd knowledge increa.aed the
rank ancJ file of the Order was filled by men of genius and culture, who, animated
by high aims and noble purposes, gave to the body an accelerated impetus in the
direction of a broader culture, a grander destiny,
Thenceforth its ranks were sought by men, not so much intent upon advancement in a chosen vocation, as by a desire for a higher and broader culture in the
social amenities, moral perceptions, intellectual acquirements. It became an educator of the age, an intelligent mental force of the times, around which clustered
the deepest thinkers, the broadest humanitarians, the grandest moralists of every
land graoed with its presence.
Man is a gregarious animaL It is only in the society of hie fellows that his
higher attributes find full play. In solitude, he dwindles into insignificance.
Sagea may sigh for that solitude as affording opportunity to formulate wise theories
founded upon the garnered knowledge coming from contact with their fellow men ;
a suitable place in which to marshal, count, eoan and value the gems of thought
gleaned along the busy paths of life. It furnishes no mines of mental wealth in
which to delve for hidden treasure.
The gratification of the social instinct inherent in man has opened the avenues
for hie advancement from the Btatm of the cave dweller to hie present condition.
Speculative Masonry has seized upon this social instinct of mankind and ma<le
it the basis of all its action. It ha8 realized that just as certainly 1111 certain game
may be found frequenting the salt licks of its environment, so may the average
man be found converging to his fellow men in .quest of that social pabulum withou,t which he cannot exist.
Were I asked to designate the highest attribute of wisdom exhibited in the
formulatiop of Masonry, I should respo.nd, ·i t was in seizing upon the soci~l in·
stinct and making it the basis for moral and intellectual culture.

circumspection and a care to the dignity of the Order, than where its membership

In the latter case, individual effort counts for little; in the former for much.
It may not be either logioal or complimentary to say thia, but it is believed exper·
ience and observation warrant the i:emark.
. Wherever labor is nnprolific of practical results, it is likely to cease. Tuiduce
the grade of a Masonic Lodge to the plane of the lowest intelligence of the COin·
munity in which it exists, and its power for good will be reduced to a minimum.
We are judged largely by the standard of our unworthy members.
If their conduot is such as to bring reproach upon the Order, all its members
must inevitably be the sufferers.
That we have sometimes been too lax in receiving improper material, and more
frequently too indulgent in retaining it when once received, is everwhere apparent.
The excuse of weak Lodges, and the specious reasoning that greater numbers
will add to their efficiency, regardless of the character of the material, has done
much to reduce the high standard of character which should everywhere pervade
Masonry.
· You, my brethren, can perform no more useful service to Masonry, than in
keeping from its ranka unworthy material; except, perhaps, it may be in expelling
from those ranks such as, having become members, have demonstrated their unfitness to remain such.
It is often necessary not only to avoid evil, but the appearance of evil. The
presence of unworthy members is a constant menace to our standing, and greatly
detracts from our power for good.
It must follow that we should exercise freely the right to deny acoeBB to our
ranks, to such as are either by nature or education unfitted to illustrate the exalted
principles by which Masonrv is animated ; and that the pruning process should be
freely exercised to tbe end that its members may stand as indices, as exemplars of
those principles.
If the realm of Masonry cannot be extended without detrjment to its high
character, better that it be confined to narrow limits.
THB RELIGIOUS TEACHINGS OP MASONRY,

The Fraternity exacts from all its members evidence of a firm belief in, and
reliance upon, a Supreme Being, the Creator and preserver of all that exists- a
Heavenly Father, whose children we are and whose loving care is extended over
all.
It advances no collateral dOll'Illas, a belief in which is eeeential to admission
within our walls. The wisdom of thus confining the requisite belief of the Order
to the _great underlying truth upon which our holy religion is based, is worthy of
commendation.
Men are so constituted that their affections, sentimentR and religious belief,
never quite keep pace with their intellects. In the coul'l!e of human development,
in the advance of science, the fallacy of many of our religious theories is from
time to time demonstrated.
·.
Tuiason discards the error when discovered ; faith clings to it as an essential
element in a grand scheme-as a necessary factor in the great problem of religion ;
and thus upon matters merelv ancillary or collateral to religious belief, men, impelled by sentiment and sustained by,faith, sever in their views, and the bond of
union between them which seemed a chain of forged steel, of triple braes, becomes
a rope of sand.

That vast changes must, under natural laws deeply affecting the condition of

demonstrate with some plausibility:·l. In another century the ratio of increase maintained during the last hundred years will give us a population of six hundred millions, or say equal to that
of China.
.
2. A population of such density must entail untold deprivation and B?ffenng
upon a majority.
3. A suffering people are always a discontented people and are prone to
attribute all their woes to their form of government or its administrators.
A suffering majority in a free gcvemment, with the power in their own hands,
invariably seek to change such government, and, in most if not every instance, end
in anarchy and final despotism.
This theory, so far as founded upon past experience, involves the predicate of
ignorance among the masses, and may serve for senile men who find signs of decay
exhibited on every hand.
To you and me, in the heyday of youth, no such dark visions rear their horrid
front. We realize full well1. That under well established laws, epidemiai, plagues and war come &11
cheerful meseengers, to stay excess of population.
2. That the general diffusion of knowledge is steadily elevating the masses to
a plane where anarchy and despotism cannot exist.
We believe, too, that great as has been the strides of progress and ".8pecially of
invention in the past, that it is as yet in its infancy, and that the co1111ng century
will outstrip the past in new discoveries tending to human comfort.
Already it is aeserted that from oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen and carbon and a
fe\v compounds, eggs, beef, bread and other articles of food may be produced in
factories with as much ~ and certainty as cloth is now woven.

Professor Berthelot of Paris, claims that be can now produce in his laboratory
a three year cild beefsteak iu twenty minutes ; while by a combination of gases,
sugar, it is claimed, can be manufactured at a cost of one cent per pound.
Coal tar, it is Void, is to be debased into the form of tobacco, while the fuel of
the future will be drawn from the underlying heat of the earth.
Electricity will become the motive power of the world, and the friction of moving trains of cars will go far toward generating the power needed for their propulsion.
Men will navigate the air, making the trip across our continent perhaps in
twenty-four hours; sail in ships beneath the surface of the ocean, thus avoidfog .
the force and effect of storms upon its surface; and in a thousand ways alleviate
the disoomforts of life and add to the means whereby that life may be sustained
by other and superior means than those now in vogue.
Already men are talking of a fourth dimension, a description of which will be
left to those who oan comprehend it, as we cannot.
Of one thing we are aasured : the genius of coming ages will be found adequate
to grapple with its great problems, and to solve them in the interests of humanity.
To us those problems are as a fourth dimension, past finding out; to them they
will become plain, and of that life they will form a part.
Will Masone rise to the level of these new conditions, lend their aid m molding public opinion and guiding the destinies of the people amid the astounding
changes that are sure to occur?
. Their opportunities will be many, ·and if they reach those sublime heights
from which they can survey the whole field of progreas, and enter with a ze~ born
of knowledge upon the great work of leading countless millions to higher views of
usefulness, to nobler practices, then, indeed, will they become important factors in
the regeneration of the world.
To drift with the current is easy. To meet and subdue error, to lead in the
battle of progreBB, to sway men into paths of greater usefulness to themselves and
the world, calls for the exercise of the highest attributes, the sublimest courage,
imparted by deity to mortal man, and nurtured by the ennobling leBBons of
Masonry.
If we perform well the duties devolving upon us, and leave to them bright examples for imitation, we may reasonably hope that, profiting thereby, Free and
Accepted Masons, in the goldeu future as in the prosy past, will so live and conduct themselves and so illustrate the Masonic virtues that the very name will
stand as a synonym for all that is pure and noble.
Then will it be said of those who have constructed and adorned the grand ·
structure which we call Masonry: They builded better than they knew.

Your Oommittee, from the tables before them, embodied in this report, and from
Information received from the Grand Secretary, find that the Lodges in the jnr!Bdic·
tion, speaking generally, have conferred fewer degrees during the past year than
bas been usual of late.
This falling off in the number of initiates, your committee think, is fully accounted
for by the unprecedented stringency In the money marke$, causing what are com·
monly known as "bard times;" during the year many good meu and true, who
would otherwise have desired to enter our Fraternity, hesitating to appropriate the
large sum of fifty dollars, required for the purpose, from their already straightened
means. This cause, however, and Its inevitable effect ln reducing the number of our
·neophytes, Is, ln the opinion of your committee, already In the course or passing
away and the return to general prosperity, whiob bas begun, will show itllelf as well
iD the Increased nn'!lber of applications for membel'Bhip in our Society, as In a gen·
eral slackening or the purse-strings in other directions.
It ls a matter of great lmportanoe to the proper conducting of the duties of the
Grand Secretary's office, that the returns of the Subordinate Lodges sba.11 be
promptly forwarded within the time prescribed by the Constitution; the.t they shall
be correct; and last, bot not least, that the dues of the Grand Lodge shall, In all
cases, accompany them. Your committee have, each year, for several years past,
·endeavored to Impress upon the Masters of Lodges a sense of their responsibility In
this matter, and that it is their duty, as much or even more than that of their Sec·
retaries, to see that the returns which they oertlfy to by their signatures as correct,
are not only absolutely so, but that they are transmitted to the Grand Secretary in
proper time, and are accompanied by the does.
·
These endeavors on the part of your Committee have been only partially success·
ful, as is evidenced by the faot that this report shews that seventy.two Lodges have
been, this past year, delinquent or irregular in one or more of these particulars.
Yonr committee think that a probable cause of their partial failure in this regard
may be found in the fact that Masters of Lodges are frequently changed, and the
new Master, supposing that be reads the report of this committee for the preceding
1ession of this Grand Lodge, fails to see the application of the remarks or admoni•
tions therein contained, to himself. Like all the rest of us when listening to a sharp
admonitory sermon, be thinks it is "the other fellow" who is referred to, and when
his own time comes, be forgets all about It. Under these ciroumatances, and a.fter

15

giving the subject careful consideration, yonr 'committee recommend that the Grand
Secretary be instrncted, so soon as he shall forward the blanks tor the returns to the
snbordinate Lodires, to notify the IDBpectors of the several districts that he has so
done, and that it shall then become the duty of the said Inspectors to see to It, as
far as lies in their power, that the Lodges comply with the reqnlremeots of the Oonetltntion in this regard. Your commiitee are of opinion that this course will result
.
in a great Improvement in the making and forwarding of the returns.

presented the following reports:Po tM JC.·. W. •• Grand Lodge of Oaltfomto.:Y our oommittee, to whom was referred the transcript of the trial record
wherein ROBERT J. PADBN was expelled from all the rights and privilegee of
"Masonry by Sa11ger Lodge, No. 316, on the 16th day of August, 1894, have had
the same under consideration and report as follows:The charges are of such a serious na~ure that, if fully sustained by the testi.
mony, would warrant the infliction of. the severest penalty known to onr Maeonio
law, and we regret that the transcript sent us is not worthy of commendation-is
so fatally defective-in that the entire testimony ie not before ne in the manner
prescribed by our forms; and we desire to airain impress upon enbordinate Lodges
the neoeeeity of corumlting and following the forms and regulations of the Grand
Lodge in making up these records, as a failure so to do almost inevitably results
in a reversal of the judgment.
'fbe record does not show the necessary jurisdictional facts; but the accused
was present at the trial, stated that he was satisfied, and answered to the charges,
wbioh cured the defoot; · bnt, in all cases, it is the duty of the trial cominiBBionere,
the Master and the Secretary, to follow in all particulars the ~lations of our
Constitution, and incorporate in the transcript all matters required to be therein
under our law and forms.
There was no testimony in this case except that of the accused, and only a
portion of hie testimony ie lfiven; the testimony was not written out in full by the
Secretary, read to the witness, and signed by him, as reqnired by Sec. 5, Art. IV,
Part VI, of the Constitution, and by the fourteenth subdivision of our form of
record of trials, and the transcript shows that a synopsis only of the testimony
questions and answers
was given, except ae to a small portion thereof where
are written. Thie was error.
There are six specifications, and the accused was found guilty on all but the
fourth. There is no written evidence at all to e~tain any of the epecificationR,
except, poSBibly, the first and second; but without the entire testimony the case is
not fully and fairly presented to us.
Your committee recommend the adoption of the following reeolution:.Ruowed, That the proceedings in the case of ROBERT J. PADBN, who was
expelled by Sanger Lodge, No. 316, on the 16th day of August, 1894, from all the
rights and privilt"gee of Masonry, be and the same are hereby disapproved and set
aeiC:le, and said case be remanded to Sa'llflW Lodge, No, 316, with directions that
the Lodge immediately retry Bro. RoBBRT J. PADBN in accordance with our
prescribed form.

out of thirty-nine Inspectors have failed to report, and those two, Nos. 4 and 6,

are not at hand;

him in the discharge o( his very important duties.
.'
The reports ·of the several Inspectors show the demands which have been made
upon his time, and that the results have been invaluable to the Craft.
Some of the Inspectors report that owing to the very hard times in their districts, the growth of the Order has been retarded to a great extent ; but notwithstanding the great financial depression throughout the State, however, we find that
the membership of the Order has increased, which, no doubt is due to a great extent to the faithful work of our Grand Lecturer and the local officers.
W e hereby commend the effort.a that have been made in the past to increase

and en:able him to visit each district at least once a year; but as these efforts have

Bao. WILLIAM ERSKINE SLOAN, Inspector of the Thirty-sixth
Masonic District, presented the following:To t'M M. '. W. ·• Grand Lodge of Oaliforni.a:On or about the 30th day of December, 1893, I received a letter from the
Master elect of Evergreen Lodge, No. 259, of Riverside, Cal., to-wit, Bro. C. W,
FILKINS, informing me ~f his election as Master, and asking me to send him a
certificate of qua.lification, without examination; at the same time statinl!' that if
I had doubts as to his proficiency he would refer me to the Grand Lecturer,
E. c. HABE. I did have doubts as to his proficiency, having never· examined him nor had
the opportunity of seeing his work in either the second or third degrees. Neither
could I see any reason why I should refer the matter to the Grand Lecturer, at a
distance of nearly six hundred miles, when only twenty.five miles intervened
between the applicant and myself, and the distance covered by a good railroad. I
therefore replied that I could not grant the certificate without examination, but
that I would call on him in Riverside within a week, and examine him, if he so
desired; or, if he could not wait that long, I would advise him to call on me at
Elsinore. To this he made no reply, and I followed it with two other letters, in
both of which I repeated the offer.
In the m~antime I went to San Bernardino, by invitation, and spent several
days with the brethren of Phania: Lodge, and my third letter was written from
that point. I invited the brother to call on me there-the distance being short-at the same time repeating my offer to go to Riverside if invited. To this he
replied, giving me clearly to underataod that he would not submit to an examination from me, and demanding that I send him a certificate. To this I wrote my
fourth letter, declining to issue certificate without examination, and repeatinl!'
former offer, which ended our correspondence.
On my return to Elsinore, I was astonished to find a letter from Grand Lecturer
BABE, asking me, as a special favor to himself, to send a certificate of proficiency
to the Riverside brother.
To this I replied at some length, endeavoring to show him that such a course
would not be in accordance with law, which clearly provides, in Section 25 of the
Regulation, that only where the Inspector, from any caW!e, is unable to examine
an applicant, the Grand Lecturer may examine and give certificate-not vouch to
Inspector-and that in this case there was no occasion for any straining of the
law. I closed by saying that if he (the Grand Lecturer) insisted on the brother
having a certificate without examination, he would have to issue it himself, as I
would not. At the same time I suggested that any interference on his part would
cripple the influence and efficiency of the Inspector's work, and thus detract from
his usefulness in the Lodge. Three days after the mailing of this letter to the
Grand Lecturer, I received tlie following, by wire:-

758

Proceedings of the

[Oct, 11,

Los ANGELES, Jan. 19th, 1894.
W:ar. E. SLOAN:Returned from San Francisco. Saw correspondence; Both Grand Leotnrer
and myself say you ought to ieaue oertificate to FILKINS. Send it to him first mail,
as they have double public installation.
H. S. 0BD, (}1YJ,nd Master.
This was followed by a letter confirming the order.
Here was a positive mandate from the Grand Master, commanding me to
certify that after careful and personal examination I had found a brother to be
fully qualified, etc., when, in point of fact, I had never examined him, and knew
nuthing about hie qualifications, except that I knew him to be deficient in the
first degree.
It is needless for me to say I was in a great strait on reoeiving the Grand
Master's order, and knew not what to do. I believed then, as I do now, that the
order was clearly an abuse of power-or, rather, a usurpation of power-and without the sanction of Constitution or laws; yet it was my desire to pay the highest
respect to the exalted position which he representeil, and I regarded it as a seriou~
thing for a Past Master to refuse obedience to the commands of him whose power
has been designated as'.' well nigh absolute," and iri whose hand "the· gavel should
never sound in vain."
Having but little time to think the matter over, I hutily Cllnsulted several
Masters and Past Masters of the District, and the conclusion was reached that
although the Grand Master's mandate was arbitrary in the extreme, yet it would
be best for me to at least make some show of complianoe therewith- that is to say,
I would obey the order so far as I could do so without actual dishonor to myself,
and then submit the whole matter to the Grand Lodge at its next Annual Communication, and rely upon that body for a redress of what I believed to be a
grievous wrong.
I therefore prepared a certificate by striking out from the regular form the
words, "after careful and personal examination," and inserting at the top the~e
words: "Issued without examination, by order of the Most Worshipful Grand
Master;" and I signed the paper in the following manner:By order of the M. •• W. •• H. S. ORME, Gf'Ond Master.
W. E. SLOAN, Imputor.
Thus prepared, I forwarded the paper to the Master-elect of Etierg'l'etm Lodge,
and he was thereupon installed.
I should have stated that the Grand Master's order was followed by two explan·
atory letters, from which I quote the following:! saw your letter which was forwarded to Grand Lecturer HARE at San Franoisco1 and the Master-elect ought to have made an aI>pointment to have met :you
at Riverside, as you sug1rested. But both the Grand Lecturer and myself think
it best, under tlie circumstances, not to insist too strongly on the point, but to
give the certificate as he wrote you and I wired you.
And again in his second letter:! note what you say as to your objections to iBBuing the oertificate without a
knowledjre of the competency of Bro. Fu.x!Ns, and know that you were governed
by a strict desire to conform to the law, etc.
These statements show clearly that the Grand Master was fully acquainted
with the fact that I had offered to meet Bro. FILKINS, either at his home in Riverside or aiiywhjjre else, for examination, and that the interference was made solely
to screen the brother from examination and not to save him either expense or loBB
of time.

759

1894.]

After these months of reflection, I have become thoroughly con~inced that the
paper i issued to Master-elect FILKINS should never have been issued, as it did not
comply with the law in any particular. My proper course would undoubtedly
have been to refuse obedience to the Grand Master's arbitrary order, _a nd, at the
same time, tender my resignation as Inspector. Such a course would have placed
me in a better light before the Fraternity. But, for reasons before stated, the
thing was done, and could no~ afterward be revoked.
·
I therefore submit the foregoing statement of facts, in the hope and belief that
this Grand Body will, in its wisdom, establish a ruling by which Inspectors, while
engaged in the honest and faithful discharge of their duties, will be protected
from such humiliation as I have had to endure; and I close with thii! query: Has
the Grand Master power to require an Inspector to certify to something he does
not know to be a fact? Or, in other words: Does the Grand Master control the
consciences of Inspectors?

Bro. WILLIAM: CALDWELL BELOBER, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports:To the M. •• W. •, G'l'and Lodge ~f Califamia :-

Your committee liave given attention to the matters referred to them, and
respectfully report:-

I. Relative to special dispensations issued by the Grand Master.
Of these dispensations there were twenty ieeued during the year: FO'l.l.1' for the
formation of new Lodgee ; two to receive petitions of pereons belonging to the
U. S. Navy; nine to elect officers; flve to reballot upon petitions for degrees.
As to all these mattere the Grand Master is required to exercise hie discretion,
and hie determination ie conclu,eive. We have examined the papere and find them
all in proper form, and recommend that hh action be approved.
II. Relative to decisions upon questions of Masonic law, reported by the
Grand Master.
These decisions we number and state in substance, with euch criticism ae eeems
to us pertinent :

1. When a resident of California makes a visit to another State or country,
for busineBB or pleaeur~, and while away from his home, without permiBBion of
the Lodge nearest hie residence, applies for and receivee the degreee of Masonry
in a regularly constituted Lodge, he i11 a ¥aeoi;i, and cannot be cl!M'sed &B clandestine ; yet no Lodge here can rec:ognize him ae a M&eon until he has made
apJ;>lication to and been received air a member by the Lodge nearest his place of
residence, and that Lodge IP&Y demand of him, as a condition for receiving his
petition, the payment of the full fee for the three degrees; and when, under such
circumstances, the party baa received only the firet degree, or the firet and second
degrees, no Lod!l'e m this State ehould, even at the request of the foreign Lodj!'e,
confer the remaming degree or degrees without the coneent of the Lodge havwg
jurisdiction over hie place of residence.
The decieion was called for by Clay Lodge, No. 101, npon the following facts:
WILLIAM N10HOL8, Ja., wae born at Newgnay, county of CJornwall, England,

but. when a boy, emigrated to this State and settled a't Dutch Flat, where he is
no~ and for about thirty years has been a resident and engaged in bueinese. After
a reeidence of more than twenty years at Dutch Flat he returned to hie native
plaoe for a visit; and while there, at the auggestion, or at least with the approbation, of some members of hie own family who were membere of F<Yl't Lodge, No.
1528, E. C., he made application to that Lodge for the degrees, and, during hie
stay, received the firet and second degreee. After hie return here, F<Yrt Lodge
made formal request to our Nevada Lodge, No. 13, to confer upon him, as an act
of cou~y, the third degree, and eo complete the work. Nwada Lodge conferred
the degree on the 27th of July, 1892. Subsequently, and after having received
him &e a visitor, Cla11 Lodl{e inquired of the Grand Master: let-Whether
NrnnoLB wa11 to be claeeed &B clandestine; and, if so, how could he be healed? The
Grand Master very properly replied that F<Yl't Lodge waa a subordinate of the
Grand Lodge of England, therefore its work could not be clandestine and needed
no healing; but he thought that its work w&e irregular because the applicant wa11,
and was known to be at the time, a resident of California.
The old law,. as we find it in the Ancient Charges, did not make previons resi·
dance at the particular place, or even in the country, a condition, without which
no applicant could be received and employed as an apprentice.

We have made a new regulation, that no Lodge shall receive an application fOr
initiation until the applicant has resided in this State twelve months, and eix

The Grand Lodge of England has never adopted such a regulation nor any reg~tion restricting its subordinates to particular territorial limits, or prescribing
any rule 'as to residence. The same is true, so far as we are ad vised, of all the
Grand Lodges of Europe, and the Grand Lodge of England has always insieted
that Lodges under its obedience, in determining upon the propriety of receiving
particular applications, were bound to consider only the physical and moral fitne88
of the applicants. The framers of our Constitution recognized the fact that the
requirement as to residence was not a part of the fundamental law of M&eonry,
and for that reason not only made special provisions for the government of our own
Lodges in that regard that no Lodge ehould receive an application from any per.
son until its membere had had an opportunity to judge of hie fitness from hie residence among them for at least six months, but they made the further provision
that if any one residing here should go abroad, whether to another of our United
States or to some foreign country, and while there receive the degrees of Masonry,
that no Lodge should be allowed to recognize him as a Mason until the particular
Lodge within whose territory he resided should have received him as a member.
Onr new regulation as to territorial jurisdiction of Lodges and residence of applicants has been and will be etrictly enforced in California, but we could not give it
effect elsewhere. Hence, ae the moat convenient, if not the only way to protect

make application for and receive the degrees of Maeonry elsewhere, yon will not
be recognized- here until you have been received by the Lodge, within whose territory you have made your residence, as one of its memhere." The Grand Master

In the "old regulations" adopted by the Grand Lodge of England in 1721, the
provision was:In case of eickneaa, death, or necessary absence of the Ma8ter, the Senior
Warden shall act as Master, pro tempore. if no brother ie present who has been

Two years later, in 1723, this regulation was so modified as to provide that

right fill the Master's place till the next election, and such we understand to be
the rule of that Grand Lodge now.
The provieion of our Constitution, Sec. 2, Art. III, Part IV, is:In the absence of the Maater, the Senior Warden (and in hie absence, also, the
Junior Warden) shall succeed to and be charged with all the powers and duties of
the Master.

Sec. 2, Art. I, of the said Part IV, also provides thatIn case a vacancy shall at any time occur in either of the offices of Master or
Warden in any Lodj!'e, upon proper representation of the necessity therefor, the

Secretary. ·
Con~truing the provieions of these sections together, it seems to us that in case
of the death of the Master the Senior Warden by right succeeds to the office, and
that, if he is qualifip,d or willing to qualify himself for the position and to accept

Catholic parents, and had, during his minority, been a regular attendant in that
church, and had, at the time of its organization and for some short time after,
been a member of the Young Men's Institute; but that be ba.d not, for more than
fourteen years, been an attendant at that church or considered himself as a member of it or connected with it, otherwise than that be was, so to speak, born in it;
and that be bad 11ot for several years had any connection or aBSociation with the
Young Men's Institute, and had never attended more than two 9r three meetings
of the society; and, further, that the ca.use of objection assigned was not a valid
or Masonic cause. The report by the coui~ittee was presented and received at
the next stated meeting after Lheir appointment. The Senior Warden, presidiog
in the absence of the Master, ordered a ballot, to determine whether the candidate
should be advanced. A ballot was had, and was adverse to the report, an<i thereupon it was ruled and announced that the objection was sustained, and ordered
that the fee for the remaining degrees be returned. The whole proceeding was
immediately reported to the Grand Master, who, after careful consideratioQ. and
inquiry, advised the Master that the cause aBSigned wa& not a valid or Masonic

Proceedings 'of the

[Oct. 11,

one, and that no Lodge could, in any form, entertain an objection for sncb cause,
and directed him to proceed to confer the remaining degrees, unless objection for
other cause should be interposed and sustained.
We fully agree with the decision of the Grand Master, and recommend its
approval.
·
It is a fundamental law and a part of "the body of Masonry" that no man can
lawfully be made a Mason who does not unequivocally declare at the tbrl'sbold
his belief in God and a future existence, and that no inquiry can be made of him
as to the creed, or sect, or society, or people to which he belongs or with which he
affiliates.
That law is older than Grand Lodges, and is a landmark which no man or body
of men has power to change. In recognition of that law we have declared the
rule to be inflexible that thfa Grand Lodge will not interfere with religious or
political matters or controversies of any kind. Masons may represent all shades
of religious and political opinions, but when assembled in Grand or subordinate
Lodge they cannot even discUBB them.
In the case under consideration, the party bad, before admiBBion, been subjected
to the only religious test to which he could lawfully be subjected, and had been
made a Mason. The only cause of objection assigned was that be was a member
of a particular Christian church, and of a society reputed to be composed principally if not wholly of adherents of that church. The report of the committee
showed that the specifications of the charge were not true; that he bad been a
member of both church and society, but bad years before practically severed his
connection with both. But if his membership in both had continued, that would
not have constituted a Masonic cause of objection; and the Grand Maeter, as was
his duty, declared, as soon as the matter came to his knowledge, that such an
objection could not be entertained by any Lodge.
·
The Senior Warden appeared before us and urged that neither the Grand Ma@ter nor Grand Lodge could properly consider this matter, because the objections to
bis decisions while acting as Master bad not been laid before the Grand Master in
the formal way prescribed by Art. II of Part VI. Our atlswer was that whenever
the Grand Master is informed, no matter bow, that any Lodge in its action,
or any Master by his ruling, bas violated or disregarded a Landmark of the
Order, his duty is to investigate the matter immediately and to make such orders
in respect to it as the case may require, and to report it to Grand Lodge that it
may take such action as wilr ellectually prevent the recurrence of such offending.
The proceedings under Sec. 6, Art. III, Part III, are in effect a trial. The
objection is the charge, but without specification. The committee are the jury or
referees to hear the evidence and report the facts, and, as the Master presiding
construed the section, the members of the Lodge present were made the exclusive
judges, whether the cause assigned was proven, and whether, if proven, it constituted a Masonic cause. But the Grand Master said, and we agree with him, that
it is not in the power or within the jurisdiction of any subordinate or Grand LodgP,
to declare or make the cause assigned in this case a Masonic offense or cause.
The declaration, however solemnly made, would be, in the extreme sense, void.
We do not think that the section referred to should reoei ve such construction,
but as doubts have been expressed we recommend that the section bt1 referred to
our successors, with directions to prepare proper amendments, if any are needed,
and present them at the next meeting of Grand Lodge.
All which is respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM CALDWELL BBLOHER, }

The same subject had been passed upon at the Communication in 1892, when
Bro. PENDLETON, of Pentalpha Lodge, No. 202, introduced a resolution: That for social purposes and for the encoural!'ement and promotion of fraternal feelinij' among the brethren, each subordinate Lod!l'e in the State of California

The committee to which the resolution was referred reported adversely \o its
adoption, and its report was concurred in by Grand Lodge.
For more than thirty years the Grand Lodge bas steadily refused to permit its
subordinates to divert their funds from the legitimate uses for which they were
gathered-for necessary current e:a.penses "and the ever recurring demands of
charity"-and bas, during those years, found many occuions to declare for what
uses those funds should be most carefully preserved. The subject was first
brought to its attention in 1853, by one of the best informed and most earnest
Masons we have ever known-Dr. J. R. CRANDALL, of Auburn-who presented a
resolution reciting that a cUBtom was then prevalent "to convert the funds of the
Lodge to the purchase of jewels, or other ~ppropriate mementos, to be presented
to distinguished brethren as an expreSBion of the esteem and confidence of the
Lodge," and prohibiting such use in the fut~e. (Proc. 1853, p. 241.)
In 1859 it was proposed to authorize the Lodges to make contributions for the
purchase of Mount Vernon, but the Grand Lodge declined to make the author·
iution, saying, in the language of its special committee : "o·u rs is 081lentially a
charitable aBSOciation. Its miBBion is to aid the widow and the orphan; to succor
the sick and destitute. " " " To carry out these objects and secure these ends
it is requisite that we should husband with special care the means by which they
are to be accomplished; and the occasions should be rare indeed when the funds
thus dedicated to charity and beneficence should be permitted to be diverted into
any other channel." (Proc. 1859, p. 110.)
The subject was next brought to the attention of the Grand Lodge by Grand
Maater PRATT, who, in his address in 1872 (Proo. 1872, p. 394), reported:Beveral questions have been presented which involve the authority of mbordianate Lodges in the oontrol and disbureement of their funds. " • • I have
lways supposed that Lodge funds were provided for the purpose of meeting the

. The committee to which that portion of the Address bad been referred; in their

Under our law as it now stands and has stood for many years, a member whose
dues are more than six months in arrears is notified that he must, within a certain
time, pay the. arrears or show cause why he cannot do so, and upon his fitilure to
pay or show cause the Master declares him suspende.d; but he may at any time
restore himself to standing by paying, not only the amount due at the time of his
suspension, but dues for the intervening period, and no action of the Lodge is
required. In that way the Lodge receives from him all that it would have received
if he had paid regularly. The proposed amendment requires that in addition to
such payment be must present to the Lodge a petition stating that he has made
the payment and asking to be restored, and allows him to be restor!'ld only upon a
three-fourths vote of the members present. It seems to us that· the conditions
imposed by our present law are quite as onerous as they ought to be, and we there·
fore recommend that the amendment proposed be not adopted.

And in Article XXIII, of the old r6'l'ulations, it was provided that the Grand
Wardens should prepare and receive the money for tickets to the Grand Feast,
and should procure the pface for holding and provide materials for the feast.
It may be that Lodges in som!l countries are allowed, as the Grand Master
suggests, to expend a certain amount of their funds, at stated times, for refreshments; but we have learned that at least some of them regard the duty of caring
for the sick and needy of their own households as not at all a duty of the Lodge
of which they are members, but of individual brethren among whom they may
happen to be when sickness or misfortune overtakes them, while we count it our
highest duty to care for them wherever they may happen to be. For that reason
we have always insisted that a Lo:lge ought strictly to preserve its funds, and so,
if possible, be ready to respond to the calls of charity, which must sooner or later
come, and which ought to be responded to promptly.
We therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
All which is respectfully submitted.
