IV. Relative to the recognition of the Lodge La ValUe de France in Loa
Angeles.
The Grand Master, in his Address, advises us that for several years there has
been a clandestine Fr~nch Lodge in Los Angeles ; that a eharter for this Lodge
was first given by some doubtful body in Louisiana; but that in November, 1892,
it received a charter from the "Grand Lodge Symbolique :&iossaiKe," and that
the Lodge now asks recognition from this Grand Lodge.
Throulfh the Grand Secretary we have received the following documents re·
ferred to in the address :1. Petition by the officers and members of the so-cs.Iled Lodge, "La Vallie de
France," to this Grand Lodge, asking in substance that they be allowed to transfer
their allegiance to it.
2. A circular letter addressed by the Executive Committee of the Symbolique
Grand Lodge to all Lodges of the first three degrees in obedience to the Supreme
Council of France, looking to the transfer of their allegiance from the Supreme
Council to that Grand Lodge.·
3. The plan proposed ·for this trander and the reorganimtion of the Seotoh
Rite in France in such wise as to permit tbis transfer and to give that Grand
Lodge exclusive jurisdiction over the first three degrees.
We know something of the "doubtful Body in Louisiana "-that called itself
the "Supreme Council of Louisiana," and that it was declared spurious and
clandestine by the Grand Lodge of Louisiana and by the Supreme Council of the
Scotch Rite for the southern jurisdiction of the United States. Of the Body
styling itself "Grande Loge Symbolique Ecossaise," we know nothing beyond
what we learn from the papers in hand, and that is very little. Its motto is like
that of the Grand Orient of France, "Libert•\, E galite, Fraternite," and that
would lead us to suspect that this Grand Lodge, like the Grand Orient. may have
discarded the declaration of a belief in God and the immortality of the soul from
its Constitution, and declared its principles to be "la libertt! absolue de conscience
et la solidarite humaine." We say suspect, because we have been unable to find a
oopy of its Constitution, or to learn the history of that Grand Lodge.
We may fairly assume that, like the Grand Orient, it does not recognize the
doctrine that a Grand Lodge has exclusive jurisdicti ·n in the State in which it is
established, and that it does aesei t the right to invade the territory of such Grand
Lodge and establish therein sqbordinate Lodges which shall work in accord with

1894.]

Grand Lodge of Ocdifornia.

787

it• views. We assume this because, as the Grand Master stat..s, in November,
1892, the Lodge La Vallee de France received a charter from that Grand Lodge.
Our claim of jurisdiction is "the absolute and exclusive control of the degrees of
Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason," and we cannot "hold
fellowship with any Masonic Body of any Rite which seeks itself to encroach, or
which fosters the encroachment of others upon such claimed rights." This we
understand to be the doctrine of all the Grand Lodges of the United States.
In the case before us, the Lodge La Vallee de France was established at Los
Angeles by the Supreme Council of Louisiana, and some of its members were
received while it was working under authority of the Supreme Council. In
1892, it transferred its allegiance to the "Grande Loge. Symbolique l!lcossaise"
and received a new charter; but we are not advised how or why that transfer was
made, or why that Grand Lodge should be willing to put itself in a position of
hostility to our Grand Lodge by assuming the right to establish a Lodge in this
State, or the right to uphold or maintain a Lodge established by any other power,
unless it asserts and iij ready to defend the doctrine of the Grand Orient, that no
Grand Lodge can be allowed to have exclusive jurisdiction over any particular
territory, and that it will not respect any such claim of right. This "Grande
Loge Symbolique l!lcossaise asks nothing of us, not even that we reC01rnize it as a.
lawful body; but its subordinate asks that we recognize it as a lawful Lodge and
its members as Masons, and that we receive them 11.nd their Lodge into our family.
Can we receive the Lodge and its members; and, if so, under what conditions?
The answer to this question is necessarily dependent upon the determination of
several others, as1. Can we enter into any negotiations with the subordinate, except thro'!gh,
or at least with the assent of, the Superior, in this case the Symbolic Grand
Lodge? Our answer to this is that we cannot.
2. Should we seek to enter into any negotiations looking to a. transfer of allegia.nce by the subordinate from that Grand Lodge to ourselves, until we are
advised in some way as to the legitimacy, character and claims of that Grand
Lodge?
We answer that at present that Grand Lodge stands to us as an invader c1f
our jurisdiction, and as a. preliminary to any negotiations lookin!f to friendly rela·
tions we should insist that it must withdraw and cancel its charter to the Lodge
" La Vallee de France." We know that there are two Masonic Bodies in France
(the Supreme Council and the Grand Orient) which exercise jurisdiction over the
first three degrees, and we know something of their history, of their Constitutions
and of their character and standing in the Masonic world, but of this Grand
Lodge we know nothing beyond what the papers before us disclose.
The question then recurs, C~n we receive this Lodge and its members into our
family, and, if so, under what conditions?
We answer that, witll our present knowledge only, we could not recognize or
receive the T..iodge as a Lodge : let, because it was instituted and has been con·
ducted and maintained in defiance of our law as to jurisdiction; 2d, because we
do know1of the irregularities and clandestine character of the Supreme Council of
Louisiana, hy which it wa.s originally instituted; 3d, we do not know the character or claims of the Grand Lodge under whose obedience it now holds, or what, if
anything, was done with reference to those of its members who had been initiated,
while it held under the Supreme Council, to relieve them from the clandestine
character of their making; and, 4th, because we do not know whether that Grand
Lodge and its subordinate had, like the Grand Orient, stricken out from its

ritual the one item of belief that we deem absolutely essential as a prerequisite to
the admission of any person to our Society.

V. Relative to the removal by Paci/W Lodge from Golden Gate Hall to B'nai
B'rith Hall in San Francisco.
Some time in the early sprin!I a resolution was offerecl in Paci,fi,c Lodge to
change its place of meeting from Golden Gate Hall tq the Chapter room in Masonic
Temple, and a committee was appainted to make inquiries whether the Chapter
ball could be secured, and, if so, on what. night of the week. The committee re·
ported that the Chapter hall could be secured for Wednesday night, hut not for
Tuesday, the day fixed by its by.Jaws for its meetings. Thereupon a resolution
was introduced to amend the by-laws by substitutin g Wednesday for Tuesday as
the day of meeting. Notice was regularly given by the Secretary to all the members of the Lodge of the introductio n of this proposed amendment , and that it
would be acted upon in the next stated meeting. At that meeting a vote was taken
and was against the proposed amendment . 'fhereupon a resolution was introduced
to change the place of meeting to B'nai B'rith Hall. This resolution was, at that
meeting, put to vote and carried by a small majority.
·
Some of the minority reported the proceeding to the Grand Master, claiming
that a resolution to·change the place of meeting could. not lawfully be acted upon
unless notice hacl been first given at one stated meetinir that it would be intri>duceJ
at the next stated meeting thereafter, nor then, unless adopted hy at !ea~t twothirds of the members present at such meeting; and that as no notice of this proposed change had been given, and as it had not been adopted by the votes of twothirds of the members present when the vute was taken, under the provisions of
Sec. 1, Art. III, Pa-rt III of the Constitutio n, the action of the Lodge was
irregular.
The Grand Master ruled that the section referred to did not apply to the case
presented, and that the action of the Lodge was regular and the resolution lawfully ad,opted.

18~4.]

Grand Lodge of California. .

We think the ruling of the ·Grand Master correct, and recommend that it be
approved. The language of the section referred to is :
. No Lodge shall r~mov~ its place of meetine; from that named in its dispensatio~ or charter, unless no~ce shall have been given at a stated meeting
that a reso·
!ut1on ~or such removal will be offered at the next succeeding one, nor unlesa
such
resolut10n shall have been adopted by the votes of at least two-thirds of the mem·
bers present at such succeeding stated meeting; nor shall such removal then take
place until the action of the Lodge shall have been approved by the Grand Lodge
or Grand Master.
·
In 1865 a like question was presented in respect to the removal ot a Lodge
from one hall to another, and it was then decided by the Grand Lodge that
"when a Lodge desired to remove its place of meetillg- from one place to
another, in the same town or city, no action but that of the Lodge is necessary"
(Proc. Vol. VII, pp. 21. 98.) The place named in the charter of Pacifi,c Lodge is
the city of San Francisco, and Golden Gate Hall and B'nai B'rith Hall are both
in that city.

VI. Relative to the duty of a Lodge to care for its own members and their
families.
The Grand J,odge of Wisconsin, through a committee of which Past Grand
Master WILLIAM: C. SWAIN was chairman, presents to us this propositio n:It is the duty of each Lodge to take care of its own members in distress
wherever they mav be. I~ ca~e of its. inability so to do, this duty devolves upon
the ~rand Lodge from which 1t holds its charter. It being understood that in no
case ts. t~e L?Jge furnishing relief and asking reimbursem ent to go
necessities without express authority from the reimbursing body. beyond actual
We have an abiding faith in the efficiency of o~ganic charity and welcome
this proposition from our brethren of Wisconsin as a step in the right direction.
We join with that committee in thQ declaratio.n that "it is the duty of each Lodge
to take care of its own members in distress wherever they may be," and we would
add to that declaration that it is the duty of every Lod11e not only to care for and
B81!ist any of its members who, from sickness or misfortnne, need assistance and care,
but to see to it that, when dead, they be decently buried, and further, their widows
and children be protected and cared for; and further still, that it is the duty of
every Lorlge to husband its resources religiously, that it may always have in hand
a fund sufficient to enable it to perform these dutie.i towards the members of its
own immediate family and those who are dependent upon them. We all know
that, from time to time, sickness and misfortune come upan those who have lived
in comfort, perhap3 in afHuence, and that they ar~ thereby sometimes reduced to
abject poverty ·and want. When they are so reduced, or when they need-assista nce,
we should be ready to come to their help. The members of a Lodge constitute a
particular family, and wherever any member of that family may be when misfortu?e overtakes him, whether at home or abroad, the duty of care and protection
arises and should be promptly performed. It is very well to say and is sometimes
said, that the duty of relieving distress is a personal duty which each individual
Mason assumes and must perform for himself and accordin~ to his ability, and
that Lodges were never intended to be dispensers of charity to strangel'fl or sojourners, or to their own members. We accept the statement that each inclividual
should be always ready to help those that need help, according to his ability, but
we do not at all accept or agree with the statement that Lodges were never intended to be dispensers of charity, and so, of course, ought not, as Lodges, t(l
have any care about the sick and needy.

but seems to have been so patent and so recognized as to need ~o e~press1on m
words, and we think it follows as a necessary corollary from what is said.
This Grand Lodge has always recoiUized, and from time to time d~clared a_nd
enforced that duty. In 1864 a member of Grafton L?dge w~ stricken with
paralysis and became entirely dependent upon the charities of his brethren an~
fellow men for the support of himself and family. His Lodge wa~ aw~re of h~s
condition but neglected to do anything for his relief. Yolo Lodge, seemg his necessities made provision therefor, and thereupon applied to Grafton Lodge to refund
the' amount advanced and to provide for his wants in the future. These requests
were refused and the memorial of Yolo Lodge stating the facts was referred to the
Committee ;n Grievances, of which Bros. R. R . HARTLEY and .JAMES L. ENGLISH
were members. In their report the committee say: "Il would be an unfortunate
proposition to establi:ti. that. a Masonic .L odge, devoted, ~s it. shoul~ be, to ch~r­
itaHe objects and the assistance of the di>tr.essed, could wi~h im~umt~ suffer its
members to want for the necessaries of life and thus bnnl!" discredit upon the
whole Fraternity," and the committee proposed and the Grand Lodge adopted. a
resolution requE\Sting the Grand Mn.ster to arrest the charter of Grafton Lodge if,
after notiiication it should still continue to neglect its duty.
In 1880 San 'Benito Lodge was called upon to assist the widow ?f one of its
deceased members and declined, claiming that death se~ered the relation. of membership, and, therefore, that the widow and orphan childr~n had no claim on.the
Lodge, but must look to individual Masons for such a_ssis,:anc~ .as they might
ed Grand Master TRAYLOR said to that Lodge that its position was wholly
~:te~able and at variance with every principle of Masonry;" an~ further, th~t
"when a Lodge of Masons neglects or refuses to care for and reheve ~he necessities and wants of the widows and orphans of its deceased members, ~emg able so
to do its day of usefulness has passed and its existence should cease.
~&in, in 1883, the Grand Lodge approved the deci.sion of Grand Master TAY·
WR that a Lodge is bound to provide relief for the widow of a dec~ased member

1894.]

Grand Lodge of California.

791

even after she had removed from its territorial jurisdiction. In approving that
report the committee said :--'
The duty of the Lodge is to its members, and to their families, without regard
to their place of residence; and the fact that one of its members, or the widow ·of a
deceased member, has removed to some place beyond its territorial jurisdiction,
does not absolve the Lodge from the performance of its well known and necessary
duty.
If a member of a Lodge in California should visit Florida or England and be
there taken sick and die, we should expect that the Lodge in whose jurisdiction
he might happen to be, would, if he needed assistance and his condition were
known, give such assistance as he might reasonably require in sickness, and bury
him decently when dead, and we should expect that his Lodge here would promptly
repay the amount so expended, and that, if it were unable to do so, this Grand
Lodge would come to its aid and make the repayment. It has never yetJailed to
recognize such an obligition, and, we trust, never will.
When Masons come to us from abroad or from other States and are in need, we
recognize our duty to give them such aseistance as their necessities require, and, to
the end that such aesistance may be given to those who ought to receive it, and
that our charity may be efficiently and properly bestowed, Boards of Relief have
been organized in our cities and provided with funds for that purpose. To these
Boards the Grand Lodge hae, from year to year, made liberal donations to enable
them to do their work. \Ve recognize the duty to give relief whenever a proper
case is presented, and, when that duty is performed, we think it only right to
report each case to the Lodge of which the recipient is a member, and to ask, as
we should give, reimbursement, that we may have in hand a fund with which to
continue the good work.
Last year the Board of Relief of San Francisco reported that during the thirtyeight years of its existence it bad expended for relief of Masons of other jurisdictions $116,369.63, and for widows and orphans of other jurisdictions $89,337.56,
making the sum of $205,707.19 for relief of strangers a.nd sojourners from abroad.
In this connection we had the curiosity to inquire of the Secretary of that Board as
to the amount expended for Masons hailing from subordinates of the Grand
Lodges of England and Scotland, and the amounts refunded. His report to us
shows that since 1881 his Board has expended for Masons from the jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge of England $19,435, of which $1231 has been reimbursed; for
Masons from the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Scotland $4076.05, of which
only $69.35 has been reimbursed. And that of the $205,707.19 so expended for
relief of sojourners and strangers from abroad, much less than one-fourth has been
paid back.
Some of our brethren of other jurisdictions tell us, "true, you relieved the dis.
tress of a member of our family, but you were bound by your tem)re to do that,
and to do it without hope or expectation of reward or reimbursement, and to do it
so unostentatiously and quietly that even the left hand should not be advised of
the kindly act clone by the right." That kind of instruction sounds well, but is
not, under the circumstances, at all satisfactory, because we have a very distinct ,
belief that every Masonic family ought to exercise some care over all its members,
and make some provision to protect and care for such as need care and protection.
We do not think that the whole duty of, a Lodge consists in making Masons
and using them so long as they are healthy and strong, and turning them adrift
when by sickness or misfortune they are no lonl!"er able to care for themselves.
Cases have been brought to our attention where a Lodge has furnished to one of

792

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 12,

its own members, who wae sick and poor and absolutely needed assistance to provide the necessaries of life, funds aufficient to transport him to another jurisdiction
and then left him to the care of strangers. A Lodge is au or'ganized society, and
we insist that one of the first and most important purpo•es of its organization is
that it shall protect and relieve its own members when they need protection or
relief, and that, except under extraordinary <'ircum•tances, it is false to its trust
when it fails to do its duty in that regard, and that when another Lodge in the
eame or another Grand Jurisdiction has furnished such relief, it may properly and
of right present its claim for reimbursement.
We therefore propose and recommend the adoption of the following resolution:
Reaolved, That the Grand Lodge of California concurs in and, with slight
changes in phraseology, adopts the proposition presented by the Grand Lodge of
Wisconsin that "it is the duty of each Lodge of M aeons to take care of its own
members and as well of their widows and orphans in distress wherever they may
·be, and that in case of its inability so to do this duty devolvee upon the Grand
Lodge from which it bolds its charter; vruuided th11t the Lodge furnishing relief
shall, in no ca~e, go beyond actual necessities without exprees authority from the
Lodge to be charged.
VII. Last year Bro. ANDERSON offered this resolution :That it is the opinion of this Grand Lodge that, in the case of non-affiliated
Masons who have been suoh for a period of six months, the payment of a sum
equivalent to six months' dues simply continues the brother paying the same the
privilege, if rejecte'd, of making subsequent applications in case of rejection, for
the period of six months, and, if said brother bas not been elected to membership
prior to the expiration of the said six months, the said brother shall, upon apph·
cation for affiliation after the period of six months, be required to pay an additional six months' dues."
This resolution was pre11ented and referred to this committee on Thursday afternoon. The committee bad, at the morning session of that day, presented two
reports upon the same subject, and for some reason failed to make report upon Bro.
ANDEBBON's resolution.
We have again given the subject careful consideration and have examined those
reports somewhat critically. Those reports were adopted by the Grand Lodge and
it was then ruled:
1. That it is the duty of every Master Mason residing in this State to be a
member of some Lodge.
2. If at the time he comes here he is a member of a Lodge in some other
State or Country, he may continue that membership.
3. But if, before coming here, he severs his membership with his home Lodge,
his duty is to make application for membership to some Lodge in this State within
six months from the time he becomes a resident here.
4. If he neglecte to make such application within the time limited, he thereby
deprives himself of the right to demand or receive "any of the rights, privil01tea
or charities of the Order," except the privilege of applying for affiliation upon the
condition precedent of paying to the Lodge to which he would apply a sum equiva·
lent to six months' dues of that Lodge.
5. The sum so required to be .paid is 1imply the condition upon which the
Lod~e is permitted to receive his application. In case his application is rejected,
it will not ·b e returned to him, and in case he is elected to membership it cannot be
applied as payment of his dues for the next six months.

seem to us sufficiently stringent.
It was declar~ in the third of the ancient charges that every brother ought to
~Ion~ to a Lodge "a~d to be subject to its By-Laws and the General Regula.
~:one: That declaration we reiterate in our Constitution, Sec. 1, Art. II, Part V:

Order" if, having resided in this State, he "shall refuse to make application for
me~bership to some Lodge therein." WhE>n he makes applicatiun he does what
he JS called upon to do, and we do not think that any onerous conditions should be
added to those we now impose.
We therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopted.

Bro. WILLIAM CALDWELL BELOHER, from the Committee on Juris·
prudence, presented the following reports :To the M . •• W . '. (hand Lodge of California, :-

The Grand Lodge of Mississippi, at its last Communication in February of this
year, adopted the following preamble, resolutions and rules:WHEBEAB, It is desirable that there should be uniform rules adopted by all
Grand Lodges, relating to the jurisdiction of Lodges over candidates rejected for
initiation, and Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts applying for advancement,
whose place of residence, after petitioning or initiation, is permanently removed
outside of the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge having jurisdiction ov;ir the Lodges
to which they have petitioned, or by which they were initiated; therefore be it
Ruol'Dtid, That the two rules following be proposed to each Grand Lodge with
which this Grand Lodge is in correspondence for adoption, to become the uniform
rules relating to jurisdiction over rejected candidates for initiation and candidates
applying for advancement, who have permanently removed beyond the jurisdiction
of any Grand Lodge into that of another Grand Lodge; and be it further
Ruolved, That said proposed rules be and the same are hereby adopted by this
Grand Lodge to take effect from and after their adoption by any other Grand .
Lodge, as between this Grand Lodge and the Grand Lodge or Grand Lodges
adopting the same ; pr01JidR.d, that the laws, rules and regulations of this Grand
Lodge, as they now stand, shall remain in full force and effect as between this
Grand Lodge and all other Grand Lodges which shall not become parties to the
same, by adopting said rules, to wit :
JURIBDICTION 0VRB PERSONS REJECTED FOB INITIATION.
RULE I. Whenever any person who shall have been rejected for initiation in
any Lodge shall have removed his place of abode into the jurisdiction of another
Lodge, within the jorisdiotion of another Grand Lodge, with the intention of
making it his permanent place of residence, and shall have resided there not less
than one year, and shall again desire to petition for initiation, be may present bis
petition to the Lodge under whose jurisdiction he resides, or to any Lodge which bas
concurrent jurisdiction over that place, which shall thereupon certify the facts to
11he Lodge which rejected him, and if said Lodge shall not, within six months
thereafter, furnish to the Lodge to which said petition is made the grounds upon
which such rejection was made, it may proceed with such petition as in other
cases, and that Lodge may initiate him if elected. Whenever the grounds upon
which the petitioner was rejected are furnished to the Lodge to which he makes
his new petition, it shall judge of the sufficiency thereof, and proceed in its
discretion.

JUBIBDICTION OVER ENTEBIID APPBENTIOES AND FELLOW CRAFTS PETmONING
FOB AoVANOEHENT,
RULE II. Whenever an Entered Apprentice, or Fellow Craft, of a Lodge in
this jurisdiction shall permanently change his place of abode into the jurisdiction
of a Lodge in another Grand Jurisdiction, and shall have resided there not less
than one year, and shall desire to be passed, or raised, be may apply to the, Lodge
under whose jurisdiction he lives, or to any Lodge having concurrent jurisdiction
thereover, and if it shall signify its willingness to receive him, and so certify the
fact to the Lodge which initiated or passed him, it shall thereupon strike his name

'

Grand Lorlge of Oalifamm.

803

from its roll of Apprentices or Fellow Crafts, as the case may be, and all juriedic.
tion over him shall cease; provided, that if the Lodge to which he applies shall
reject his p;itition for advan,cement, the jurisdiction of the Lodge which initiated
or passed him shall, ipso fact.a, be resumed, and hi~ name shall again be entered
upon its roll, with a note of the fact; and provided further, that nothing in this or
the preceding rule shall prevent a Lodge from initiating, passing, or raising a per.
son as the proxy of another Lodge; in which event the person so initiated, passed,
or raised shall become a member of the Lodge for which it acts, if that would be
the effect of being raised in the Lodge for which the deiree is conferred, under the
laws of its Grand Lodge.
The Grand .Lodge of Mississippi has hitherto adhered to the doctrine that a
Lodge, by receiving a petition for the degrees or initiation, thereby acquires per·
petual jurisdiction over the applicant. Thie doctrine is purely American in its
origin and practice, and is not recognized by even a majority of the Grand Lodges
of the United States, and not at all by those of the Dominion of Canada, or, so
far as we are advised, by any Grand Lodge in any other country. In itR strictest
form it means that a rejected applicant can never, under any ·circumstances, make
application to any Lodge other than the one which rejected him, except with its
permission, and that such permission can be granted only by a secret and unanimous ballot: Such is the rule in Pennsylvania, Michigan, South Carolina, Illi.
nois, Oregon, Texas and Arkansas.
In other jurisdictions a majority of the rejecting Lodge may, by a viva 'llOCO
vote, grant the permission.
In others, still, the permission may be granted by less than a majority, as, in
M8.88achusetts, by the Master, Wardens, and two other members.
In a very considerable majority of the Grand Lodges of the United States, the
rule in regard to jurisdiction is practically the same as in California, to wit: That
a Lodge, by receiving the petition of an applicant and refusing to initiate him,
retains no jurisdiction over him in case be removes from its territorial jurisdiction
within the territory of another Lodge in the same State or in another State,
except that it limits the time within which he can make application to any other
Lodge, in the State to twelve months.
In the Grand Lodges of England, Scotland, and Ireland, no such doctrine ever
prevailed. Not long since, the Grand Lodge of Illinois made complaint that a
Lodge under the obedience of the Grand Lodge of Scotland had received the petition of and initiated a resident of the State of Illinois, who, after having been
rejected by a Lodge in that State, had returned to hie old home in Scotland for a
visit, aud, while viijiting there, had been received and initiated by a Scottish
Lodge. A like case occurred here: A party residing in California made application to and was rejeoted by a Lodge in this State. Subsequently he returned to
hie old home in England for a short visit, and, while there, at the instance of relatives who were Masone, he made application for initiation in the Lodge of which
hie relatives were members. His petition was received and be was initiated.
This was done with a full knowledge on the part of the parties proposing him, and
of the Lodge, that he was a resident of California and had been rejected by a
Lodge here.
No complaint has been made in regard to the matter, but we understand that
those three Grand Lodges assert and exercise the right to receive petitions from
persons who are only transiently with them as well as from residents, and that
they allow no claim of jurisdiction dependent upon reeid6DOO, or upon the reception and rejection of a petition. Even in the States of Pennsylvania and Texas,

we understand that an applicant is not restricted to the Lodge within whose terr!·
tory he resides, but may make bis application to any Lodge in the State. The
Lodge's jurisdiction does not seem to attach until his petition baa been actually
presented and received-then it becomes perpetual.
In reply to the complaint from Illinois the Grand Secretary of Scotland replied,
in substance, that bis Grand Lodge did not recognize any claim of jurisdiction
dependent upon a rejection or upon reeidenel';'.
This doctrine has not, so far as we have been able to. diecover, any basis in
reason, justice or authority. We say it has no basis in authority because it
was not declared in the "Ancient Charges" or "Old Regulations," and because
no such rule, doctrine or regulation was ever declared or acted upon bv either
of the Grand Lodges of England, Scotland, or Ireland. It is fair to presume
that if any such rule or doctrine had prevailed iu the earlier days it would have
been carried into the "Ancient Charges" or "Regulations," one or both, and that
it would have become the rule of action in the Grand Lodge of England, which
was the first estabJished Grand Lodge. We are aware, howeYer, that some of the
ardent defenders of 'the rule have referred to the fifth section of the "Ancient
Charges " as declaring, in au bstance, such a rule. That section is entitled, " Of
the management of the Craft while working." The only paragraph In the section
referred to which can, in any way, support their contention, is in these words:None shall discover envy at the prosperity of a brother, nor supplant him, i;ior
put him out of bis work if be be able to finish the same, for no man can fimeb
another's work so much to the Lord's profit, unless be be thoroughly acquainted
with the designs and drafts of him that began it.
Thie is, in substance, just the rule declared at Edinburgh in 1698 by WILLIAK
Smraw, then M&Rter of Work in Scotland, which is given in this wise:• The statutis and ordinanceis to be obseruit he all the Maister-Maissounis within
this Realme sett douu be WILLIAKll SOHAW, Maieter of Wark to hie Maijeetie an<l.
General W ardene of the said Craft, with the consent of the Maieteris efter
epecifeit.
Item. - That na Maister sall tak ane vther Maieteris wark over his heid efter
that the 6ret Maister bes aggreit wt the awnar of the wark ather be contract arles
or verbal! conditione vnder the paine of fourtie pundis.
Item.-Tbat na Maister sall tak the wirkin}!' of ony wark that vther Maisteris
hes wrocht at of befoir vnto the tyme that the first wirkaris be satisfeit for the
wark qubilk thay h:i.if wrocbt vnder the paine foirsaid.
That was a rule made by the Society of Operative Stone Masons, and was
intended to govern the relations and conduct of one member of the Society towards
another. It commends itself as a just rule, and one that we may well make a rule
of ~nduct for ourselves, for it is just as deserving of our observance to-day as it
was of the members of that Society, that we should not be envious of a brother's
prosperity, and should not seek to supplant him in bis business or to drive him
out of it. If, in giving that charge present application, we substitute "Lodite" in
the place of "brother," we are unable to see how it can be made appli~able to the
claim of perpetual jurisdiction over a rejected applicant. In the days of the Society of Stone Masons it never was the rule that, if an applicant was rejected by the
particular branch of the Society located in London as an apprentice, for any reason, be might not thereafter go to Edinburgh or Paris and there awly to be
received as an apprentice. The rule of the Society was that an applicant must be
a good, true and free man, freeborn, and of mature and discreet age, and of good
repute. That was all. and the inquiry was not made of him, and it is not now
made in the Lodges of England, whether or not be has previously made applica-

1894.]

Grand Lo<U.Je of Oal,ifornia.

805

tion elsewhere. Universally the petitioner for initiation must be vouched for by
at least two members of the Lodge to which his application is made, and they
must sign their names to his petition, When the petition is presented, the Lodge
wuet. by vote, determine whether it shall be received. If received, it must be
referred to a committee of investigation, consisting usually of three members of
the Lodge other than those who recommended the petitioner. The report of that
committee being favorable, a ballot may be had; aQd, for the purposes of our argument, we will suppose that a single blackball appears; that the ballot is repeated,
and that the one blackball still appears, and the applicant is declared rejected.
In such a case, we think that the open declaration of five members of the Lodge,
the two who signed the petition and the three members composing the committee
of investigation, that the applicant is worthy, ought to have as much consideration
as the secret declaration of one that be .is not worthy.
The rule has no foundation in reason or justice. It is not reasonable that
the secret ballot of one man, whom we do not know, should have a greater
influence and power over the future life and fortunes of the ·applicant than the
openly declared approval of five whom we do know. It is true that under our
laws, which in that regard are unchangeable, that one has the abec>lute right
by his ballot to say the applicant shall not become a member of the immediate
family to which he belongs, and that without assigning or even being allowed
to assign any reaRon for bis action. But is it reasonable or just that the one
man who cast the rejectmg vote should be able to say to the whole world of
Masons: "I do not like the applicant and because I do not, you shall not receive
him ; my black ball must constitute. an absolute bar to hie admission to the society
of Masons. True, my objeotion to him and my reason for opposing him was
purely personal, merely giving effect to an old grudge, but be shall never be received so long as my vote can prevent it."
If his objection bad been of a character that would commend itself to the consideration of others, then it would have been proper for him to have opposed the
receiving of the petition and to have stated bis reasons. Failing to do that, it was
his duty, if he knew the applicant to be unworthy, to have stated the facts that
in his judlflllent rendered the applicant unworthy to the investigating committee,
in order that that committee might investigate the facts and report accordingly.
Such committees are appointed for the purpose of subjecting the life and character
of the applicant to the most rigid scrutiny. We have a right to presume that
their work is faithfully and honestly done and to rely upon their conclusions.
We do not mean to insinuate even that we would take away or abolish the
secret ballot, if that were a matter open for consideration, but we do mean that it
is neither reasonable nor just that the secret ballot of one should have such a controlling authority over all the world as to prohibit all the rest of the world from
inquiring as to his fitneBB, except with the consent of that one secretly given.
So long M the question is of receiving a new member into bis own immediate
family, we recognize the right of each individual member to reject as abeolnte,
but beyond that we do not recognize it at all.
If there were any basis in reason or justice for thfl rule, it ought to be still more
stringent than it is where most strictly construed. If the one black ball should
have the effect of an absolute and perpetual bar to the reception by any other
Lodge of a peti~ion from the applicant, except with the unanimous consent of the
rejecting Lodge, why should it not have the like effect upon that Lodge too? The
friends of the rule tell us that the one rejecting member may become convinced in
some way that he was wrong, and be ready to repair the wrong if an opportunity

806

Proceedings of the

[Oct.13,

were given him. But it would be equally among possibilities that he might have
died meanwhile, or, if not dead, might be sick and unable to attend.
If the negative ballot of one should constitute a bar to all the world, except
with his consent while living, we do not understand the propriety of removing the
\>ar as soon as death has removed him. The cause that moved him to reject is just
aa potent when he is dead as when he lived.
The first of the rules proposed by our friends in Mississippi provides that, upon
receiving the petition of an applicant who has been once rejected, we must report
the fact to the rejecting Lodge and that such Lodge may, in response, furnish a
statement of the grounds upon which he was rejected, but that, when they are
furnished, we shall be the judges of their sufficiency.
This sounds somewhat strange to us because, if the character of the applicant
were generally known to be bad, we cannot nnde~stand how any two reputable
members of the Lodge could be induced to sign hie petition as vouchers for his
good character, nor how the Lodge could be induced to receive the petition, nor
how, after the ballot had been taken, the Lodge or any of its members, excepting
the one who cast the negative ballot, could know the grounds upon which the
petitioner was rejected. With us the rule is imperative that the ballot must be
secret, and that, when a negative ballot has been cast and the applicant declared
rejected, the grounds or reasons for the rejection are not open for discuSBion and
cannot lawfully be discussed by the party even who cast the rejecting ballot.
It might be very proper that the petitioner should, in all cases, be required to
state in his petition whether or not he had ever been rejected, and, if so, when
and where, because such a statement might put the investigating committee upon
inquiry as to his standing in the community where he had formerly lived, and from
the applicant himself as to the reasons, if he knew or suspected what they were.
There is good reason for requiring previous residence within the particular
juriRdiction before an application can be received, to enable the members to know
the man, and if the time (six months in the particular jurisdiction and twelve
months in the State) is not long enou~h, let us make it longer. So, too, there is
good reason for requiring that a second application shall not be made until the
lapse of a full year from the date of rejection, and, if that is not enough, let us
make the term of probation five years, as in Maine, or seven, as in Rhode Island ;
but, when the term limited has lapsed, let him be free to make application in the
place where he has lived long enough to give the Lodge jurisdiction, and then let
the investigating committee do its duty.
The second of the rules proposed by our Mississippi brethren strikes Ud more
favorably. Our Grand Lodge now claims perpetual jurisdiction over all Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts who have been initiated in its Lodges ; but, in the
case supposed by this Rule II, when an Entered Apprentice removes from the
juri•diction of the Lod11e in which he was initiated and permanently settles or
makes his home in another, and, it may be, distant jurisdiction, we see no good
reason why he should not be allowed to dimit, as is the practice in English Lodges,
or in some other way sever his connection with his Lodge, and be then as free to
make application for advancement in the place of his residence as a dimitted Master Mason would be to make application for affiliation. We do not, however, at
all like the proposition that, after striking from the roll the name of an apprentice
because he had chosen to apply for advancement and to be received to membership
elsewhere, a rejection by the Lodge to which he had applied should, ipao facto,
restore his name to our roll. If he desires to go elsewhere, let him go; but, having gone, and havin~ failed of success, we do not think he should be restored to

1894.]

Grand Lodge of California.

807

his place upon our rolls without a new petition, a new reference, and a new
ballot.
Although we are not pleased with all the details of these proposed rules, yet
we hail the movement as one made in the right direction and deserving the serious
consideration of all Grand Lodges.
Many serious differences have arisen and more are likely to arise by reason of
the great diversity of rules upon the subject of jurisdiction over rejected applicants,
and, in a certain limited senRe, over all persons residing within certain territorial
limits and as well over all who have been initiated in our Lodges. It would undoubtedly be for the interest of all, if all could agree upon aome rules which
should control, and by which all should be bound upon this matter.
When matters of difference arise between nations, they are settled by negotiations, or, aR a last resort, by war.
England, as all know, prior to 1812 claimed perpetual jurisdiction over all
persons born upon her soil, and a right to take them, wherever found, for service
in her army or navy, and from time to time she took, by force from our merchant
ships, men who had abandoned their allegiance to her and had become citizens of
the United States. That claim of perpetual allegiance was settled in our favor by
the war of 1812.
Grand Lodges, happily, neither have nor need to have armies or navies for the
adjustment of their difficulties or the enforcement of their rights, but we can see
that there ought to be what we may call a law of Grand Lodges upon certain
questions of mutual concern, and we know of none of more serious concern than
these questions of jurisdiction. Now each Grand Lodge makes laws for itself
upon this subject, and, when a confilct arises, either passes it without notice or
visits the punishment for the infraction of its law upon the individuals through
whom it occurred, and who for the most part were innocent of any intentional
violation of the law. Thid punishmel).t is generally exclusion of the party from
all recoguition as a Mason in the State. Thus, if one who, as applicant for initiation, had been rejected in Pennsylvania or Illinois, and had subsequently removed
to and become a permanent resident of California, and had, after a residence here
of say ten years, been, according to our requirements, regularly made a Mason,
should return to either of those States and ask for relief, or admission as a visitor
to one of their Lodges, he would be refused admiSBion or relief as an irregular and
clandestine Mason.
In such a case, the Grand Lodge of Illinois would say, as the government of
Great Britain said of the sailor whom she took by force from our merchant ship,
"he owed perpetual allegiance to me, and until I absolve him from that allegiance
he must be subject to all the duties which that imposes."
A very interesting and instructive case of this kind arose some years ago when
a party residing at Troy, New York, made application to a Lodge in that city and
was rejected. Subsequently he removed to Montpelier, Vermont, and, after a
residence of more than a year, made application to a Lodge there and was received,
without any release of jurisdiction being given by, or even asked of, the Troy
Lodge. The matter was brought to the attention of the Grand Lodges of New
York and Vermont, and by them referred to Past Grand Master RooHE, of New
York, one of the abl1ist Masonic jurists in the country.
This was his report and judgment in the case :
In the matter of the complaint of the M. ·. W . '. Grand Lodge of New York,

The law on the point as to which they were so advised differs in the two juris·
dictions of New York and Vermont.
I;n N~w York, a candidate once having :tieen ~ejected in a Lodge cannot be
~~iv~d .m any oth!lr Lodge u1;lleas the one m which he was first rejected waives
JUnsd1ct1on over him, and this no matter bow long a period of time may have
elapsed since the rejection.
In Vermont, he may apply and be elected elsewhere without such waiver, after
the lapse of one year from the date of the rejection.
It thus appears that by the law of New York Aurora Lodge erred in electing
and conferring the degrees on Bro. CURRAN, and tbt by the law of Vermont
.A.ur,ora Lod!f.e also err~ if the year prescribed by th".ir statutes had not then
"xp1red. Still, as I believe they acted m perfect good faith, not knowing that he
had been rejected within the year, and, as moreover the petition thus denied
should never have been balloted on at all, I shall decide that thev complied with
the Vermont law in receiving the application when presented. The question then
arises as to which rule shouid govern the case-that of Vermont or Lhat of New
York?
Ii;i the fi~ pl~e•. it cannot ~ said that ~ny general Masonic rule exists on the
subiect of iunsd1ct1on over reJected material. No one in New York would hold
fo! example, ~hat a b~ot~er. w~o has received the degrees in .one V!lrmont Lod~~
without a waiver of Junsd1ct1on, after the lap•e of a year smce his rejection m
another Vermont Lodge, is for that reason any the less a :Mason in gnod standing
or that anv question can be raised as to the regularity of his status. Such bein~
the case, it would seem that each jurisdiction can lawfully adopt that policy it may
deem most wise; and that, although one Grand Lodge may differ from another
still, as each claims the right to decide for itself, so each must respect the rul~
~01,>ted by t~i; ot~er. Thus we .must here hold t_hat the law of perpetual j_uris·
d1ct1on preva1hng m New York ts the law governmg the question in New York;
and that the law of one year's limitation prevailing in Vermont is likewise and
'
just as truly, the law ll'oveming the question in Vermont.
The second point is then presented ~ to which rule should ~ive way to the

wa1vei: of _JUnsd1ct1on by .A.polW Lodge, such Lodge would have violated the law
by which it should have been g:ovemed, and would be liable to censure. In the
present case, however, Aurom Lodge violated no law prevailing within the State
of :Vermont. The candidate bad resided in Vermont for over a year, and still
resided there, and he had not been rejec&ed by any other Lodge lawfully within
the rear. In DO Grand Jurisdiction other than that of Vermont was he eligible to
receive the .degrees of Masonry. The law as laid down by their Grand Lodge
fully .authonzed Aurora Lodge to receive and act upon the petition, and it cannot
be sa1? that they wer_e bound to know the law prevailing in another State. If, in
so actmg, they had violated any general rule of Masonic jurisprudence or if they
had infrinl?ed any of the landmarks of the Craft, all Masons throughout the world
would unite in condemning their action, and the law of their Grand Lodge could
offer no defense. Aurora Lodge, however, simply did in Vermont a thing which
wo~ld have been contrary to local policy ~nd irregular if done in New York, but
which, when done and where done, was m accordance with law. Bro. CURRAN
Wal!, therefor"., lawfully made a Mason by t~e law p:r;evailing in the jurisdiction in
which he received the degrees, and the legality of this act must be recognized elsewhere. In matters fundamental and of the essence of Freemasonry we may well
refuse~ admit the legality_of e:n act done in another jurisdiction where they have
hee,n v10lated- for that which is there deemed Masonry and Masonic is not that
which we call by the same names here. As to mere queations of local policy
however, we must recognize the right of other Masonic BOdies to decide for them'.
selves, and in Tmch matters an act which is lawful in the place in which it is done
is lawful elsewhere.
I am therefore of the opinion that the complaint herein should not be sustained.
CHARLES ROOME.

of the law, and we trust that our brethren everywhere will give it consideration and

We are very glad that our brethren of Mississippi have brought this subject to
the attention of the Grand Lodges, and hope the rules presented may be so
amended as to be a.oceptable to all and that the law of jurisdiction may become
uniform and univel'l!al.
We could not recommend the adoption of these ntles in the form in which they
are presented, and do not think it would be advisable at this time to propose any
amendments, but we can safely promise our friends everywhere that the Grand
Lodge of California will be ready to join with them in the enactment of some general law that will relieve Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts from its present
claim of perpetual jurisdiction, and will give to them all the liberty they can reasonably ask.
Relative to the effect of a remiBBion of dues by a Lodge.
Bro. CHARLES E. STONE offered this resolution :".Ruvlt>td, That extension of time for payment of dues, under !>Ur Cof!stitution,
doeg not place a brother in position to vote for officers of this Lodge at 1ta annual
meeting, or to hold office therein."
In our report upon No. 12, of the decisions of the Grand Master, we had
occasion to consider the question presented by this resolution, and we repeat the
citations from our Constitution and the Uniform Code of By-Laws, as follows:None but membeN in good standing, 'IDlwBe duea are paw, shall be entitled to
vote at an election, and every voter shall be eligible to any office in the Lodge.Constitution, Sec. 3, Art. I, Part IV.
No member who shall be in arrears for dues at the time of the annual election
shall be permitted to vote or shall be eligible to any oflice.-Uniform Code, Sec. 2,
Art. IX.
It does not seem to us that Bro. STONE'S resolution is any more explicit than
the By-Law above quoted, nor that any Master ought to mistake the meaning.
We therefore recommend that it be not adopted.
Owing to lack of time your committee will be unable to report upon the following matters, viz.:The proposed amendment to the Constitution relative to electioneering for
office, the proposed amendment relative to trials for unmasonic conduct, and the
proposed consolidation of Sincerity and G'1"eenvill,e Lodges.
We therefore recommend that they be referred to our successors.

JONATHAN DRAKE STEVENSON.
It is a most unusual occurrence for a Grand Lodge of Ma.sons to
be called upon to chronicle the death of its first and last Past Grand
Master at the same Annual Co=unication. It forcibly reminds us
of the span of life, and the doubts that compass human existence.
Death is the ultimatum of life ; it puts its seal upon young and
old, and its blight is consummated in mystery and uncertainty. We
honor, side by side, our illustrious dead. The one borne down by the
tide of death in the prime of manhood ; the other bafiling the storms
of well nigh a centnry. The one flushed with the pride of recent
honors; the other in the composure of ripe old age. The one full of '
hope and expectanoy in meeting life's battles; the other a quiet
loiterer on the wayside of destiny. We honor one for hie loyalty and
devotion to the great Brotherhood of California Masonry ; we honor
the other for his aid in eucceesfully esta.blishing the Order on the
western shore of civilization, and for his paternal oversight during all
these passing years.
During the suprema.cy of Greece the young were taught a love and
reverence for the aged that amounted to devotion. They rejoiced
in a father's benediction. The grea.t Masonic hea.rt of Ca.lifornia.
would not be true to the boast of a better civilization in this era did
it not throb e.rdently for the memory of
Jo:trAT.llAN DRAKE Sn:v.KNso:tr,

the first Grand Master of Masons in this jurisdiction.
During all the history of Masonry in California he has been a conspicuous figure in its orga.ni?.a.tion, its growth, and in its assemblages.
He has the honor of first paternal regard, a.nd we bestow it with that
fealty born of principle noble in its inception and sublime in its fulfillment.
For almost forty-four years our venerable brother was a landmark
to Masonry on the Pacific Slope-true and steadfast to the end.
His zea.l i.nd devotion never wavered ; for, although bowed under the
weight of years, far in advance of the allotted age of ma.n, with
feeble frame and tottering steps, he entered the Temple at each Annual Communication to hold communion with hie brethren, many of
whom were unborn at the time when he presided in the Grand Oriental

Mourning Page of the

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

Chair. Hie visits at Grand Lodge were occasions of special moment,
for hie brethren were ever ready to accord to him that homage so
gratifying to one of hie appreciative nature, and to which hie rank
and ripe age so richly entitled him.
Our venerable Past Grand Master was born on the first day of January, 1800. He was made a. Mason in 1821, e.nd for over sev~nty
yea.re he figuratively wrought in the quarries of Zeredatha and forests
of Lebanon, in building and embellishing the social temple so dear to
the heart of one of hie noble nature.
Whether breathing the spirit of patriotism during hie childish
endeavors in a.id of defenses on Brooklyn Heights, when his country
was in peril, whether a. pupil in the cause of liberty under the tutelage of the leaders of the ca.pita.I of the nation, whether in command
of the citizen soldiery in his native State, whether making the long
and perilous voyage around Cape Horn at the head of his famous
regiment, whether delving in the gold fields of hie adopted State,
whetlrer in e.ny public service or in the retirement of private life, he
wa.s ever the same-honorable and upright in his life and character.
To JONATHAN DRAKE STEVENSON was accorded a privilege that·
but few have enjoyed. He lived to witness, in the country of
his birth, the transformation of broad areas of wilderness into great
and prosperous commonwealths ; to watch its growth in population
from a little over five millions to upwards of sixty-five million souls;
to see it girded and interwoven with electric lines and roads of steel;
to see borne upon the bosom of its great rivers, lakes, gulfs a.nd bays,
the commerce of the world. ·
It is not our purpose to attempt the biography of our illustrious
Brother ; for to do so, to use the language of Bro. EDWIN A. SHERMAN, "it would require volumes, for the story of his life is so interwoven with that of our common country and its most distinguished ,
men and statesmen, that in a. brief sketch it would be utterly impossible to telescope or condense the history of so remarkable and wellknown character as that of Colonel JONATHAN DRAKE STKVENSON."

a victim to the destroyer at a time when nature was radiant with verdure and the blossoms of springtime. Just three months after Bro.
STEVENSON had put on immortality, he joined that grand old veteran in the Grand Lodge above.

820

Bro. GRITMAN was born in 1838, in Providence, Rhode Island.
He was equipped for the duties of life with a. finished education, having graduated from Ya.le College. At the time of his death he was the
Cashier of the B~k of Napa, a position he had filled for many yea.re.
He was ma.de a Mason in "Manhattan Lodll,'e," in New York city, in
1865. He seems ever to have had the warmest attachment for Masonry and la.bored zealously to promote its interests. He served as
Chairman of the Committee on Finance for four yea.re, and was then
elected Senior Grand Warden. He was noted for his fidelity in all
his acts, and whatever he underliook was done with precision and dispatch. He was ever the personification of modesty and unostentation.
His warm and genial nature, and his uniform courtesy and kindness,
made him universally popular among his brethren. Honore which
they were pleased to bestow on account of his sterling worth, stirred
the very deptas of his emotions.
When he realized that he bad reached the very moment of dissolution of soul and body, his adieu to the Grand Lodge told in no uncertain tone of the sincere affection he bore his brethren to the very
close of hie peaceful life. Loyalty and gratitude a.re among the sweetest charms of human excellence : these attributes were distinctive
marks in the character of Bro. CHARLES RAY GRITMAN. There was
no sordid residuum in his composition ; if there had been, somewhere
along the pathway of hie life, through the natural channel, it would
have been made known to some of his many friends and associates.
But he preserved his cha.meter above reproach ; and now that he is
gone, it may be truly ea.id of him, his career was the synonym of
purity, and hie example the standard of excellence.
Farewell, beloved Brother I The Grand Lodge returns your affectionate "Good-By," in love, tenderness, and grateful remembrance.
HIRAM NEWTON RUCK.ER,
Past Grand Master.

CHARLES RAY GRITMAN.
Bro. CHARLES RAY GRITMAN, who retired from the Grand Oriental Chair at the Annual Communication in October, 1893, was
summoned from association with his brethren on the fourteenth day
of M.i.y of the present year. He did not survive long enough to receive the teRtimonial which had been ordered by the Grand Lodge in
honor of his services. In the prime of manhood, he was smitten and fell
